title: Advances in tools and strategies for spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression in Caenorhabditis elegans.
authors: Wang, Yi-Meng; Zang, Xiao
abstract: Spatiotemporal manipulation of gene expression is essential for dissecting gene function, elucidating developmental processes, and uncovering complex physiological mechanisms. As a model organism, Caenorhabditis elegans has played an important role in basic biology research and provides an ideal experimental system for achieving such precise control. With the development of single-copy transgenesis, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing, and conditional recombination and inducible systems, the genetic toolkits for spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression, and even at the single-cell-resolution, have been greatly expanded in C. elegans. In this review, we systematically summarize the major strategies for spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression in C. elegans, with a focus on tissue-specific RNA interference, conditional protein degradation systems, inducible transcriptional regulation systems, and recently developed approaches such as Ribo-on/Ribo-off. These methods are compared in terms of regulatory levels, technical advantages, limitations, and suitable applications. Together, these tools cover multiple layers of regulation, ranging from transcriptional and post-transcriptional control to protein-level manipulation, and provide powerful approaches for developmental biology, aging, inter-tissue signaling, and disease models, while also establishing a methodological foundation for dissecting cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous regulatory mechanisms in complex biological processes.

title: Omics-driven improvement of safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.) for climate resilience, oil quality, and high-value metabolites under changing environments.
authors: Ali, Fawad; Ali, Arif; Nadeem, Muhammad Azhar; Baloch, Faheem Shehzad; Kurt, Cemal; Do, Manh Cuong; Yu, Ju-Kyung; Chung, Yong Suk
abstract: Safflower is an Asteraceae oilseed crop valued for its high-quality unsaturated fatty acids ( approximately 90% oleic and linoleic acids), natural floral pigments, and diverse bioactive compounds. These attributes underpin its applications in functional foods, nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals, and various industrial sectors. Safflower inherent tolerance to drought, heat, cold, and salinity positions it as a climate-resilient alternative to more temperature-sensitive oilseeds; however, omics-based research in this crop remains comparatively fragmented. This review consolidates recent advances across major omics domains. Genomics covers chromosome-scale assemblies, GWAS panels, QTL mapping, and diagnostic candidate genes for molecular breeding. Transcriptomics summarizes regulatory networks for flavonoid and oil biosynthesis, stress-responsive transcription factors (NAC, WRKY, bZIP, AP2/ERF), and seed developmental programs. The proteomics section addresses stress-inducible, therapeutic, and storage/lipid metabolic proteins linked to quality and stress adaptation. Metabolomics outlines quinochalcone and flavonoid pathway architecture, color-specific metabolic profiles, and emerging clinical and nutraceutical applications. Phenomics highlights UAV-based high-throughput phenotyping, RGB and multispectral imaging for salt and drought screening, and machine-learning-assisted germplasm authentication. Epigenomics focuses on DNA methylation and miRNA-mediated regulation. Finally, lipidomics and metagenomics consider oil authentication biomarkers, refining optimization, and microbiome-driven nutrient cycling shaping medicinally important compounds. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in multi-omics integration, CRISPR-based functional validation, genomic selection pipelines, and detailed characterization of root-shoot architecture under combined stresses. Addressing these gaps will advance mechanistic understanding of climate resilience and enable the development of stress-tolerant, high-yielding safflower cultivars with improved oil quality and bioactive profiles, thereby supporting climate-resilient production systems and high-value safflower-based products at scale.

title: Draft genome data of Pediococcus acidilactici strain AP1 isolated from common carp (Cyprinus carpio).
authors: Kobilov, Fazliddin; Elova, Nilufar; Murodali, Bobokulov; Gullola, Bekmurodova; Amirsaidova, Dildora; Xidirova, Mastura; Yodgorova, Farangiz; Miralimova, Shakhlo
abstract: This data article presents the whole-genome sequencing and associated genomic datasets of Pediococcus acidilactici strain AP1, isolated from the intestinal tract of a healthy common carp (Cyprinus carpio) obtained from a fish farm in the Tashkent region, Uzbekistan. The datasets comprise raw paired-end sequencing reads, a draft genome assembly, genome-quality assessment reports, structural and functional annotations, and phylogenomic outputs. Whole-genome sequencing was performed using the Illumina MiSeq i100 Plus System with paired-end 2 x 151 bp chemistry. De novo assembly generated a draft genome comprising 19 contigs, with a total length of 2,015,983 bp, an N50 of 388,737 bp, an L50 of 2, and a GC content of 42.02%. CheckM2 estimated 99.99% genome completeness and 0.5% contamination, whereas BUSCO recovered 99.2% of the conserved bacterial single-copy orthologs. Annotation with Prokka v1.15.6 identified 1,897 protein-coding sequences, 52 tRNA genes, four rRNA genes, and one tmRNA. Genome-based phylogenetic and digital DNA-DNA hybridization analyses supported the assignment of strain AP1 to P. acidilactici. Functional annotations generated using Prokka, RAST, eggNOG-mapper, and InterProScan indicated genes putatively associated with carbohydrate fermentation, stress adaptation, exopolysaccharide biosynthesis, peptide transport and proteolysis, cell-surface interactions, and CRISPR-Cas defense. Gene-based functional assignments represent predictions and require experimental validation. The publicly available datasets can support comparative genomic investigations of fish-associated Pediococcus strains and future experimental studies of host-associated and probiotic-relevant traits.

title: Engineering uORFs in wheat improves abiotic stress tolerance without growth penalties.
authors: Si, Xiaomin; Yan, Yonghui; Bai, Shenglong; Guo, Guanghui; Xiao, Panpan; Hu, Mengxiao; Xia, Kai; Ren, Yongqi; Jiang, Jintao; Fan, Rong; Ji, Xiang; Wang, Yue; Li, Hao; Dang, Tingting; Gao, Qinmin; Liu, Luyu; Xiong, Changbin; Liu, Kangpeng; Zhou, Yun; Song, Chun-Peng
abstract: Developing climate-resilient crops is critical for ensuring global food security, yet agricultural productivity is frequently constrained by the trade-off between stress tolerance and growth. This challenge is particularly acute in allohexaploid wheat, a staple crop susceptible to abiotic stresses, underscoring the demand for precise gene regulation. Here, we established a simple, efficient, and transgene-free method for regulating gene expression in allohexaploid wheat by disrupting or creating de novo upstream open reading frames (uORFs) via genome editing. Using ribosome profiling, we identified 1199 actively translated uORFs across the wheat genome and developed a dual-luciferase screening pipeline to pinpoint potent translational repressors of positive regulators of abiotic stress. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the uORFs in TaCIPK14 and TaGGP1 elevated downstream protein accumulation, thereby enhancing drought, cold, and salt tolerance of plants. Furthermore, base editing was employed to generate de novo uORFs in TaMADS26, effectively downregulating gene expression and improving drought resilience. Notably, both the transgene-free uorf(TaGGP1-ACG) and uORF(TaMADS26) mutants conferred pronounced yield advantages under drought conditions without incurring growth penalties under well-watered conditions. This study provides a predictable and precise way for modulating gene expression, enabling the coordinated improvement of stress resilience and agronomic performance in wheat.

title: From oleaginous microalga to marine chassis: synthetic biology and process-aware biomanufacturing in Nannochloropsis.
authors: Wang, Hao; Liu, Jin
abstract: Nannochloropsis has developed from an oleaginous marine microalga valued mainly for eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA)-rich lipids into a credible candidate for marine photosynthetic biomanufacturing. Its toolkit now spans genome resources, efficient nuclear transformation, homologous recombination, CRISPR/Cas editing, marker recycling, defined integration sites, and modular multigene assembly. Researchers have used these capabilities to alter carbon allocation, triacylglycerol accumulation, EPA synthesis and lipid-class partitioning, carotenoid metabolism, recombinant-protein production, specialty-metabolite formation, and cultivation robustness. This review assesses whether these advances are sufficient to support Nannochloropsis as a predictable, reusable, and process-aware chassis. The evidence shows that the genus has moved beyond basic transformability. Targeted genome modification and pathway construction are feasible, and native and non-native products have reached biologically relevant and, in some cases, process-relevant levels. However, outcomes remain strongly influenced by genomic locus, strain background, intracellular compartment, physiological state, and cultivation regime. Platform maturation will therefore depend on reusable genomic architectures, reliable organelle-targeting rules, dynamic regulation, and phenotyping suited to iterative design-build-test-learn workflows. Strain design must also be coupled more closely to cultivation, harvesting, product recovery, and deployment. Product-specific chassis configurations are likely to be more practical than a universal strain for EPA-rich oils, pigments, recombinant products, and specialty metabolites. Nannochloropsis thus provides a useful test of how an industrially relevant, non-model photosynthetic eukaryote can become a more designable marine production host.

title: Advances in influenza A and B virus detection: molecular diagnostics, biosensors, and point-of-care applications.
authors: Huang, Yingqi; Duan, Chen; Deng, Xiyan; Zhang, Xinlan; Wu, Meiqi; Peng, Siqin; Liu, Rushi; Hou, Defu
abstract: Influenza A and B viruses remain major causes of seasonal epidemics and continue to pose substantial challenges for rapid clinical diagnosis and public-health surveillance. Conventional methods, including viral culture, immunological assays, and reverse-transcription real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), provide important diagnostic benchmarks but are constrained by long turnaround times, dependence on specialized equipment, or reduced sensitivity in low-viral-load specimens. This review summarizes recent advances in influenza virus detection, with emphasis on molecular diagnostics, biosensors, point-of-care testing, and high-throughput sequencing. Digital PCR offers precise absolute quantification, whereas isothermal amplification technologies such as reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP) and reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA) reduce reliance on thermal cycling and support portable testing. CRISPR-Cas systems further improve sequence specificity and are increasingly being integrated with isothermal amplification, lateral-flow readouts, and microfluidic platforms. Biosensor strategies based on optical, electrochemical, multimodal, and smartphone-assisted readouts provide promising routes for rapid, multiplexed, and point-of-care detection, although standardization and large-scale clinical validation remain key barriers. High-throughput sequencing complements rapid testing by enabling viral typing, variant monitoring, and emerging-pathogen monitoring. Overall, future influenza diagnostics are expected to move toward integrated, low-cost, "sample-in, answer-out" systems that combine sensitivity, speed, portability, and surveillance connectivity.

title: Development of a Rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b Assay for Dual Detection of Hantaan Virus and Seoul Virus.
authors: Ruowen, Guo; Haitao, Tang; Hongkun, Fu; Weilin, Wang; Baosheng, Yu; Mengya, Xiong; Jia, Xu; Chaojie, Hu; Xiaoyu, Chen
abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1x10(1) copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

title: Unipoint-anchored cascade amplification strategy integrating FUSE probe-activated CRISPR-Cas12a for dual mode osteopontin detection toward osteosarcoma assessment and therapeutic response evaluation.
authors: Zhao, Jie; Gao, Miaomiao; Ding, Hongmei; Song, Youshen; Zhang, Yantao; Ten, Yuze; Wang, Fei; Miao, Zukang; Zhang, Jingyu; Yang, Shuang; Jiao, Jun
abstract: Reliable assessment of disease status and therapeutic response in osteosarcoma remains an unmet clinical need. Integrative bioinformatics analysis and protein-level verification in paired clinical specimens prioritized secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1, osteopontin) as a liquid biopsy target associated with osteosarcoma progression and patient survival. On this basis, CRUMP, a CRISPR-Cas12a and FUSE Probe-based dual-mode biosensing platform, was developed for SPP1 quantification. A bifunctional NH(2)-ZIF-8 probe co-immobilizes the components required for target recognition and Cas12a activation, while MoS(2)@AuNPs interfaces transduce the resulting signals. Signal amplification is achieved through a unipoint-anchored multisite cascade based on a DNA tetrahedron-HCR architecture, enabling one-to-multiple parallel amplification while balancing stability and sensitivity. A single Cas12a cleavage event simultaneously decreases the electrochemical (EC) signal and increases the fluorescence (FL) signal. These reciprocal changes allow the two readouts to provide an internal consistency check for each measurement. Each channel covers more than five orders of magnitude, with detection limits of 167.7 fg/mL for EC and 331.6 fg/mL for FL. The broad measurement ranges allow most serum samples to be analyzed directly, without the per-sample dilution optimization that ELISA requires, and the complete analysis takes only approximately 85 min. Validation across osteosarcoma cell lines, clinical specimens, and tumor-bearing mouse models provided preliminary evidence for the feasibility of CRUMP in SPP1 quantification and endpoint assessment of chemotherapeutic response. By combining biomarker prioritization, biosensor engineering, and preliminary application testing, this work presents CRUMP as a candidate platform for SPP1-based assessment of osteosarcoma and its therapeutic response.

title: Rapid and visual detection of group B Streptococcus based on an ERA-CasMNPs colorimetric biosensor.
authors: Guo, Hua; Jiang, Yayun; Li, Dongmei; He, Kuo; Chen, Yongyi; Li, Yulin; Dai, Shiyu; He, Yang
abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a major pathogen responsible for adverse perinatal outcomes; rapid and accurate detection is crucial for preventing maternal-neonatal transmission and for guiding clinical interventions. Current GBS detection methods are limited by long assay times, insufficient sensitivity, and high equipment and operational requirements, restricting their application in resource-limited settings and rapid detection scenarios. Targeting the cfb gene of GBS, this study developed ERA-CasMNPs by integrating enzymatic recombinase amplification (ERA), CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated specific recognition and trans-cleavage activity of ssDNA, and horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-modified magnetic nanoparticle complexes (MNPs)-based colorimetric signal output. The ERA-CasMNPs biosensor enables rapid and sensitive visual detection of GBS within 85 min, with an LOD(95) of 23.3 copies/muL (95% confidence interval: 15.6-34.8 copies/muL). Moreover, evaluation using 135 cultured clinical bacterial isolates demonstrated that ERA-CasMNPs achieved a sensitivity of 97.33%, a specificity of 98.33%, and a detection accuracy of 97.78%, comparable to qPCR. These results indicate that the ERA-CasMNPs biosensor provides a sensitive and visual method for rapid detection of GBS and supports its potential for further evaluation in resource-limited and rapid-testing settings.

title: Aptamer-CRISPR/Cas as a tool in point-of-care testing of infectious diseases.
authors: Lau, Cia-Hin; Huang, Yumei; Ch'ng, Ewe Seng; Tang, Thean-Hock; Zhu, Haibao; Citartan, Marimuthu
abstract: Aptamers and the CRISPR/Cas system have become the cornerstones of target detections due to their numerous advantages. Aptamers enable direct recognition of non-nucleic acid targets, such as pathogens and antigens, while CRISPR/Cas system drives signal amplification and rapid detection. The combined aptamer-CRISPR/Cas system can overcome the limitations of traditional target detection by realizing field-deployable, highly sensitive, specific, versatile, and rapid assays. Given the increasing number of different aptamer-CRISPR/Cas systems developed recently, particularly for infectious diseases, we provide a comprehensive overview of these platforms designed for detecting significant viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, Monkeypox virus, Hepatitis B virus and bacteria that include Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella. Current challenges that impede the deployment of aptamer-CRISPR/Cas for point-of-care pathogen detection were also mapped, including primary barriers such as clinical matrix effect and stability. Several strategies to mitigate these issues were also set forth, predominantly the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning to accelerate the transition of aptamer-CRISPR/Cas system to the clinical translation and commercialization phase, paving the way towards widespread implementation in global health.

title: Biomaterials for environmental control of AMR dissemination.
authors: Joshi, Mahavir; Kaur, Sukhminderjit; Mouafo, Hippolyte Tene
journal: Journal of infection and public health
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens human, animal, agricultural, and environmental health, driven by horizontal and vertical gene transfer. Conventional wastewater treatment removes 63-94% of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) but fails to eliminate ARGs and antibiotic-resistant bacteria, while generating toxic sludge. This review evaluates advanced biomaterials, including silver and gold nanoparticles, reactive oxygen species, magnetic nanocomposites, targeted disruption of metabolic pathways, carbon-based sorbents, biopolymers, metal-organic frameworks, functionalized enzymes/peptides, and engineered biofilms, for reducing ARG and resistant-bacteria loads, inhibiting horizontal gene transfer, and reducing the selective pressure exerted by residual antibiotics. These approaches offer enhanced performance across wastewater/agriculture/air/food supply chain systems. Challenges in scalability, ecological safety, and regulation remain, requiring integration with AI monitoring, CRISPR tools, and One Health strategies. This review aims to summarize and discuss the literature on the development and use of innovative biomaterial-based intervention strategies that address the environmental aspects of AMR in order to provide a comprehensive overview of what has been learned and developed to date.

title: Protocol for eVLP-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 and prime editing in pancreatic cancer cell lines.
authors: Timmins-Young, Chloe; Cordani, Marco; Giovannetti, Elisa; Aslanoglou, Despoina; Gutierrez, Alvaro; Costello, Eithne; Glenn, Mark
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell lines resist transfection, limiting gene-editing experiments. Here, we present a protocol for delivering CRISPR-Cas9 or prime editors into PDAC cell lines using retrovirus-derived engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs). We describe steps for generating eVLPs, packaging CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoproteins or prime editors with engineered prime-editing guide RNAs (epegRNAs), and transducing human PDAC cells. We use the HEK3 locus and NQO1 (NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1) exon 6 as example edits and controls, respectively. This protocol adapts readily to other genomic sites.

title: Utilization of the CRISPR-Cas system for investigating tuberculosis drug resistance.
authors: Yuan, Yanhui; Deng, Jiahui; Li, Xiang; Zheng, Xi; Tan, Yunhong; Xu, Kun
abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis(TB) presents a significant challenge to global efforts to control the disease. Addressing this issue requires a comprehensive understanding of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb). The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated protein (Cas) system are efficient genome-editing tools for various organisms and have facilitated new research directions regarding drug resistance in M.tb. This review summarizes recent progress in applying CRISPR/Cas technology to investigate drug resistance mechanisms in M.tuberculosis and discusses the potential of the CRISPR/Cas system as an integrated platform to transform research paradigms and enhance understanding of M.tuberculosis drug resistance mechanisms.

title: Alternative and Synergistic Strategies Against Antibiotic-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus in Clinical and Environmental Settings.
authors: Babolhavaeji, Kiandokht; Kazemi, Sima; Etesamifard, Tahere; Solgi, Rahmat
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) poses a serious global health threat, undermining treatment outcomes and necessitating the development of innovative therapeutic strategies. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major contributor to this burden, with increasing prevalence in hospitals, contaminated food, and environmental sources. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further intensified S. aureus resistance due to widespread antibiotic misuse. Biofilm formation, which facilitates the horizontal transfer of resistance genes such as mecA (methicillin resistance gene A), plays a central role in the development of resistance. To counteract antibiotic-resistant S. aureus, alternative approaches have emerged, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), photodynamic therapy (PDT), and drug repurposing guided by artificial intelligence (AI). Cutting-edge technologies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based gene editing and engineered bacteriophages offer promising avenues for targeting resistant strains. Natural compounds such as thymol and chlorogenic acid (CGA) have also shown potential in reducing resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. Effective management of AMR requires strengthened antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs), robust surveillance systems, and public health measures such as proper hand hygiene and environmental sanitation. Combining antibiotic adjuvants (AAs) with existing antibiotics and leveraging bioactive peptides (BAPs) can enhance antibiotic efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-drug-resistant (PDR) S. aureus. This review investigates the prevalence and resistance mechanisms of S. aureus in clinical, food, and environmental contexts, explores promising alternative therapies, and emphasizes the urgent need for global antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) and sustainable intervention strategies.

title: Strategies and mechanisms of precision genome engineering: From gene editing to genome writing.
authors: Huang, Kerui; Tian, Jianhong; Zhao, Wenyan; Zhang, Siqin; Xiang, Lixuan; Yang, Meiqing; Liu, Lu; Huang, Yazhou; Zhang, Ningyun; Sun, Lei; Xie, Peng; Kuang, Nanyu; Zhou, Hong; Qiu, Chengfeng; Yan, Jun; Jiang, Xiaocheng; Tu, Qiang; Wang, Yun; Hu, Haoliang; Zhang, Youming
abstract: Genomic manipulation has advanced from stochastic nuclease-mediated disruption toward programmable, deterministic precision. Early clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) strategies enabled targeted mutagenesis through double-strand breaks; however, their therapeutic application is limited by genotoxicity, chromosomal instability, and dependence on endogenous repair pathways that are difficult to predict. In this review, we examined the transition from gene editing to genome writing, an approach that decouples genomic modification from host repair pathways to better balance efficiency, precision, and payload delivery. We also discussed the principles of precision technologies, including base and prime editors, and described emerging large-scale writers, such as CRISPR-associated transposases and recombinase-based bridge RNAs, which enable the integration of multi-kilobase synthetic modules. Beyond enzymatic mechanisms, we further considered the combined use of generative artificial intelligence, structural biology, and novel delivery architectures as potential strategies to overcome current biological limitations. Taken together, these developments point toward Generative Biology, in which computational design and high-throughput screening transform the genome from a static substrate into a more dynamic model for complex, synthetic functional design.

title: Integrative molecular mechanisms of lodging resistance in rice (Oryza sativa L.) culms: from DELLA-OsGSK2-BZR1 signaling to cell wall engineering and QTL-based breeding.
authors: Sherif, Ahmed; Tang, Cuifeng; Dong, Chao; A, Xinxiang; Sun, Yiding; Yang, Yi; Ge, Na; Nie, Ruimin; Hassan, Amr A; Zhang, Feifei; Yang, Yayun
abstract: Rice lodging, permanent culm displacement from the vertical position, reduces grain yield and quality, potentially causing up to ~80% yield loss. Lodging resistance is a multifactorial trait shaped by stem morphology, internal anatomy, and cell wall chemistry. A central unresolved question in the field concerns the relative contribution of lignin versus cellulose to culm mechanical strength, a debate that has significant implications for targeted breeding and cell wall engineering. This review offers a comprehensive integration of two key questions: (1) What are the current molecular regulatory mechanisms underlying lodging resistance-associated culm traits in rice? (2) How can these mechanisms be translated into effective breeding strategies?. How can these mechanisms be translated into effective breeding strategies? Unlike earlier reviews that focused on individual mechanisms, this synthesis integrates hormonal crosstalk, hierarchical NAC-MYB cascades, emerging evidence for epigenetic regulation, and QTL-based breeding into a unified conceptual framework centered on the DELLA-OsGSK2-BZR1 module. Our synthesis reveals that plant architecture is governed by extensive phytohormone crosstalk centered on the proposed DELLA-OsGSK2-BZR1 module, where gibberellin and brassinosteroid synergistically modulate elongation and thickening, whereas auxin, strigolactone, ethylene, and jasmonic acid fine-tune plant height and tillering. Major-effect loci, such as SCM2/APO1 and SCM3/OsTB1, enable the concurrent improvement of strength and yield, with QTL pyramiding reported to increase culm diameter by up to ~39% in specific genetic backgrounds. Vascular bundle development and cell wall biosynthesis (lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose) are coordinated by hierarchical NAC-MYB transcriptional cascades, with recent advances suggesting epigenetic regulation through DNA methylation, histone modification, and DELLA-mediated chromatin silencing in rice. We further discuss how these mechanistic insights may guide modern breeding through marker-assisted selection, genome selection, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated precision engineering, and ideotype design, providing a roadmap for developing next-generation lodging-resistant rice varieties.

title: Individualized and Platform-Designated Gene-Editing Studies in the Registered Clinical Record: A Case-by-Case Census Against 148 Eligible Studies.
authors: Li, Oscar Mingtian; Li, Yijiang
abstract: Introduction In February 2025, a single infant with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency received a customized base-editing therapy, and individualized gene editing has since been discussed as an emerging category of care. No one has yet counted whether this category exists in the registered study record. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional census of interventional studies of human gene-editing agents registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. Records were retrieved through the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface, version 2, with a verbatim, intervention-scoped query and a fixed census date of 17 September 2026. Eligibility was verified from each record's own fields, and every exclusion is supported by the field value that justifies it. Two independent screening passes classified each eligible record as single-participant or n-of-1, multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated, or conventional cohort. Agreement was quantified with Cohen's kappa and a 95% confidence interval (CI). Records in the individualized and platform classes were re-verified against their complete registry entries and version histories. We also searched public US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) records for the regulatory route of each census record. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. Results Of 212 retrieved records, 64 were excluded, and 148 were eligible. Four eligible records were single-participant or n-of-1 designs, and three were multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated designs, giving a census of seven studies. Of the remainder, 140 were conventional cohorts, and one was an editing arm inside a non-editing platform trial. Version histories confirmed the four single-participant designs; one of them reached an enrolment of one through a revision made before enrolment began. The same histories showed that three other records had an enrolment of one or two only because of termination or under-enrolment. Only two of the 148 eligible records describe a construct designed for the individual participant. No publicly verifiable platform technology designation was located for any census record, and the census query returned no expanded-access record. Of 23 studies completed more than 12 months before the census, five had posted results (21.7%, Wilson 95% CI: 9.7%-41.9%); because this interval is wide, the figure is reported as context only. Agreement on design class was moderate (kappa, 0.540; 95% CI, 0.264-0.815). Conclusions Nineteen months after the first individualized CRISPR treatment, the registry contains seven individualized or platform-designated gene-editing studies, and only two records describe an individualized construct. The regulatory pathway used by the index case was not retrievable from the registry, and no regulatory route could be verified from public records; this is an absence of public evidence, not evidence that no route existed. These counts describe the ClinicalTrials.gov record, not the prevalence of individualized gene editing, and the design-class counts are provisional given moderate agreement.

title: CasNano: An ultracompact CRISPR-Cas12f with a GC-rich PAM for epigenome editing with therapeutic potential.
authors: Kim, Dongkyeong; Huang, Chia-Wei; Pan, Richard; Qian, Junming; Wu, Xuebing; Devinsky, Orrin; Tsai, Yi-Ting; Liu, Shawn
abstract: Clinical use of CRISPR-Cas proteins for genome engineering is constrained by their large size, limiting in vivo delivery. To address this, we engineered an ultracompact and versatile platform from a minimally active, 400-amino acid Cas12f protein from Blautia lenta. A multi-stage strategy of structure-guided protein mutagenesis and systematic single guide RNA (sgRNA) optimization transformed BlCas12f into a "CasNano" as a potent genome targeting tool for mammalian cells. When a catalytically dead CasNano (dCasNano) is fused to a VPR domain, it activates endogenous genes with an efficiency and specificity comparable or superior to the benchmark SpCas9 system for the guide RNAs (gRNAs) and loci tested under equal-mass plasmid transfection; as editor expression was not quantified and stoichiometric differences would, in any case, preclude equivalent normalization, these comparisons describe functional output rather than intrinsic activity. We established the platform's versatility for bidirectional epigenetic editing by fusing dCasNano to a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT3A) for gene silencing or a dioxygenase (TET1) for gene activation. TET1-mediated reactivation persisted for 5 months in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), whereas DNMT3A-deposited methylation was not retained at 2 weeks in a dividing reporter line. CasNano's small size and distinct CCN PAM sequence highlight its potential for future therapeutic applications constrained by viral delivery cargo capacity.

title: DEG2MOL: Conditional Latent Flow Matching for Transcriptome-Guided de novo Drug Design.
authors: Kim, Songhyeon; Lim, Wootaek; Lee, Hawon; Bong, Hyunsu; Kim, Jitae; Jeon, Minji
abstract: Transcriptomic profiles capture cellular responses to perturbations, offering a principled foundation for biologically grounded de novo drug design. However, existing transcriptome-guided generative approaches remain limited in biological specificity, transcriptomic coverage, and evaluation across diverse perturbation contexts. Here, we propose DEG2MOL, a biologically grounded conditioning framework that encodes differentially expressed gene profiles through a Gene Ontology (GO)-informed encoder and maps this representation into the latent space of a frozen, pre-trained scaffold-aware VAE via conditional latent flow matching. When benchmarked against five baseline models, DEG2MOL ranked first by rank-sum aggregation of six metrics in both the random- and scaffold-split evaluations. For two representative compound conditions, GO-informed encoder activations were accompanied by enrichment of the corresponding target-engaging pharmacophores among the generated molecules. In docking case studies of two compound-target pairs, generated molecules showed favorable predicted docking scores and reference-associated contacts. DEG2MOL also generated molecules from shRNA knockdown, CRISPR knockout, and Perturb-seq profiles without additional training, indicating transfer across the perturbation types and profiling platforms evaluated. At the transcriptional level, an in silico gene-expression analysis showed that the predicted signatures of generated molecules were more similar to those of target-matched inhibitors than to those of unrelated inhibitors. The data and code are available at https://github.com/KU-MedAI/DEG2MOL.

title: Natural products targeting mitochondrial homeostasis: a four-dimensional framework integrating dynamics, mitophagy, pharmacokinetics, and translational safety.
authors: Xiang, Zhi-Yun; Yang, Xiu-Hua; Lan, Wen-Ying; Xiao, Xin-Yu; Huang, Qun; Yang, Lin-Lin
abstract: BACKGROUND: Dysregulated mitochondrial dynamics, including fission, fusion, biogenesis, and mitophagy, underlie the pathogenesis of many diseases. Natural products have the potential for multi-target therapy, but insufficient understanding of their mechanisms of action and pharmacokinetic limitations hinder their clinical translation. OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a regulatory framework covering the four dimensions of biogenesis, morphology, quality control, and defense, aiming to systematically clarify how natural products regulate mitochondrial function and critically evaluate their translational potential. The framework emphasizes that inter-organelle contact platforms, such as mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites (MERCs) and mitochondrial-lysosomal contact sites (MLCs), are key sites through which natural products exert regulatory effects. METHODS: Major scientific databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, were searched, and evidence on mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, and toxicology from preclinical and clinical studies was comprehensively reviewed. RESULTS: Natural products can selectively regulate key mitochondrial pathways and regulatory nodes, including the AMPK/SIRT1/PGC-1alpha axis involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, the DRP1 axis involved in mitochondrial fission, and the PINK1/Parkin pathway involved in mitophagy. Representative metabolites include resveratrol, curcumin, and Coptis chinensis-derived alkaloids. A key finding of this review is that the intestinal microbiota plays an important role in converting low-bioavailability precursors, such as tannins, into systemically active metabolites, such as urolithin A (UA), thus inducing mitophagy. Although these metabolites usually show strong activity in vitro, their low oral bioavailability and rapid metabolism lead to significant pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) mismatch, which remains a major obstacle to their clinical translation. CONCLUSION: Natural products are powerful multidimensional regulators of mitochondrial homeostasis. In order to fully realize their therapeutic potential, strategies must be adopted to overcome PK/PD mismatch, including the development of targeted delivery systems, in-depth analysis of microbiome-metabolite interactions, and the integration of artificial intelligence and CRISPR-based technological innovation to support precision therapy.

title: Bacterial Defense and Phage Counterdefense: Unraveling the Molecular Basis of Phage Resistance.
authors: Dutta, Kunal; Velieva, Kira M; Skorb, Ekaterina V; Shityakov, Sergey
abstract: Phage therapy represents a promising strategy against multidrug-resistant bacteria, but its clinical effectiveness is increasingly compromised by the emergence of phage-resistant traits (PRTs). This resistance develops through multiple interconnected mechanisms that operate at different levels of bacterial defense. At the primary level, mutations in phage receptors, cell surface glycoconjugates (lipopolysaccharide, capsule polysaccharide, exopolysaccharide), outer membrane proteins, drug efflux pumps, and surface layer proteins provide the first line of defense by preventing phage adsorption. These receptors are highly diverse across Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive bacteria, and acid-fast bacteria, with PRT being particularly dominant in Gram-negative species. At the secondary level, bacteria deploy sophisticated antiphage defense (APD) systems, including CRISPR-Cas, restriction-modification systems, and abortive infection mechanisms. The recent discovery of over 150 distinct APD systems underscores the remarkable complexity of bacterial immunity. Concurrently, bacteriophages have evolved anti-antiphage defense (AAPD) systems to counter bacterial immunity, establishing a dynamic coevolutionary arms race. This continuous interplay between APD diversification and AAPD counteradaptation drives the rapid emergence of PRT, which threatens the long-term viability of phage therapy. This systematic review examines the molecular basis of phage resistance across diverse bacterial taxa, analyzes the evolutionary and coevolutionary forces shaping APD and AAPD systems, and highlights previously overlooked aspects of phage-bacteria interactions. By integrating these perspectives, we aim to inform strategies for advancing modern phage therapy and guiding future research directions.

title: Validation of a Modular Base Editing Strategy, Free-BE, in Physcomitrium patens, Maize, and Wheat.
authors: Guyon-Debast, Anouchka; Javelle, Marie; Perroud, Pierre-Francois; Pichon, Jean-Philippe; Paul, Wyatt; Nogue, Fabien
abstract: Base editing (BE) technologies enable precise genome modification but often generate undesired editing outcomes, including indels, bystander edits, and editing outside the optimal activity windows. Here, we report a modular BE strategy, termed Free-BE, where the cytidine deaminase and Cas9 nickase are delivered as separate components rather than as a single fusion protein. In the moss Physcomitrium patens, Free-BE showed lower editing efficiency than the conventional fused system (Fused-BE). However, it generated fewer indels, a higher proportion of single-nucleotide edits, and reduced out-of-window editing. Free-BE also altered the spectrum of base substitutions, producing a higher proportion of C-to-G and C-to-A transversions than Fused-BE in P. patens. No mutations were detected at four predicted off-target loci examined in P. patens. We further validated Free-BE in crop systems. In a transient maize protoplast reporter assay, Free-BE achieved targeted base conversions, whereas stable transformation of wheat demonstrated successful editing of endogenous loci, although with lower efficiency than Fused-BE. In wheat, Free-BE similarly reduced multicytidine editing and by-products. Together, these results establish Free-BE as a functional modular BE strategy that broadens the plant genome-editing toolbox and may be advantageous for applications requiring greater control over editing outcomes, despite lower overall editing efficiency.

title: Dynamic phosphorylation of DGCR8 regulates embryonic stem cell differentiation and microprocessor function.
authors: Leong, Ka Weng; Mok, Lawrence; Gu, Karen; Oakhill, Jonathan S; Chong, Mark M W
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
abstract: The Microprocessor complex, minimally composed of DROSHA and DGCR8, is ubiquitously required for microRNA biogenesis. It also regulates the balance between pluripotency and differentiation through mRNA alternative splicing and mRNA cleavage. However, how these various activities are regulated remains incompletely understood. Both DROSHA and DGCR8 are phosphoproteins, and phosphorylation has been reported to influence their molecular functions. In this study, we identified residues in DGCR8 by mass spectrometry that were differentially phosphorylated in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) before and after differentiation into neuronal cells. This included S95 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in undifferentiated cells, and S238 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in differentiated cells. By means of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing of the endogenous Dgcr8 gene, we generated a homozygous S95A mESC clone and a heterozygous S238A/- mESC clone. Both mutants retained an mESC phenotype but exhibited altered Microprocessor-dependent functions and differentiation outcomes. When directed toward the neuronal lineage, the S238A/- mutant displayed elevated mRNA expression of neuronal progenitor markers even after 10 days, while both S95A and S238A/- mutants failed to generate cardiomyocytes in embryoid body differentiation cultures. Furthermore, MEK1/2 inhibition with a highly selective inhibitor partially phenocopied the transcriptional effects of S95A in mESCs, consistent with a potential contribution of ERK/MAPK signaling for S95 phosphorylation. Together, these findings support a role for site-specific DGCR8 phosphorylation in modulating Microprocessor-dependent processes and differentiation in mESCs, establishing DGCR8 phosphorylation as an important regulatory mechanism in the regulation of Microprocessor activity, especially for stem cell differentiation.

title: Mapping the epigenetic regulatory network of cotton single-cell fiber elongation mediated by H3K4me3.
authors: Yu, Mengli; Liu, Le; Guo, Yuling; Xu, Yameng; Li, Yujun; Li, Xiaonan; Wang, Yu; Fan, Liqiang; Yang, Zuoren
abstract: Histone modifications are central to plant development, yet how they coordinate cellular morphogenesis remains poorly understood. Cotton fibers, as single-celled trichomes derived from seed epidermal cells, provide an ideal model to address this question. Multi-omics approaches were used, including cleavage under targets and tagmentation for genome-wide H3K4me3 profiling and transcriptome sequencing. These were integrated with molecular and genetic validation experiments such as virus-induced gene silencing, overexpression, CRISPR/Cas9, yeast one/two-hybrid, electrophoretic mobility shift assay, co-immunoprecipitation, and split-luciferase complementation assays. We identify GhMYBL as a core transcriptional repressor that negatively regulates fiber elongation. GhMYBL is subject to dual control: H3K4me3 governs its transcription, whereas GhHBI1 posttranslationally attenuates its DNA-binding activity. GhMYBL directly represses the positive regulators GhXTH22 and GhALP1, limiting elongation; GhHBI1 relieves this repression, enabling their normal expression and synergistic promotion of fiber elongation. Our results demonstrate that differential H3K4me3 modification orchestrates GhMYBL-mediated transcriptional repression, which is fine-tuned by GhHBI1 interaction to coordinate fiber cell elongation. This study provides mechanistic insights into the epigenetic control of cell elongation and highlights promising targets for cotton fiber improvement.

title: CRISPR screens identify ACSL4 as a key regulator in macrophage activation and metabolic inflammation.
authors: Lin, Yanting; Jing, Dongquan; Liu, Yiming; Gao, Rui; Zhao, Qixiang; Jiang, Xingyu; Da, Huijuan; Ren, Yiming; Cao, Qiuhua; Jiang, Jingwei; Sun, Yuanyuan; Yang, Yong; Gao, Xinghua
abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pro-inflammatory macrophages drive obesity-associated metabolic inflammation. Identifying key regulators of their activation is crucial for new therapies. This study aimed to identify novel regulators of pro-inflammatory adipose tissue macrophage (ATM) activation and assess their therapeutic potential. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: We combined genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening with scRNA-seq data from human adipose tissue and identified long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 4 (ACSL4) as critical for pro-inflammatory ATM activation. Validation used myeloid-specific Acsl4 knockout mice (Acsl4(fl/fl) Lyz2(Cre)) and shRNA-mediated knockdown in macrophage cell lines (RAW264.7, THP-1, and iBMDM). Mechanisms were explored via mutagenesis, immunostaining, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and transcriptional activity assays. A high-throughput screen of 8,685 DrugBank compounds was performed to identify candidates targeting ACSL4. KEY RESULTS: ACSL4 deficiency markedly reduced pro-inflammatory factor expression (Tnfalpha, Il1beta, and Il6). Myeloid ACSL4 deletion protected against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory ATMs and enhanced adipocyte lipolysis and thermogenesis, without affecting food intake, water intake, or locomotor activity in mice. However, glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity were not significantly affected. Mechanistically, ACSL4 contributed to inflammation independent of its enzymatic/ferroptotic functions (Thr328 mutation, troglitazone insensitivity). Instead, ACSL4 translocated to the nucleus in a karyopherin beta1 (KPNB1)-dependent manner. DrugBank screening identified abemaciclib as a potential inhibitor of the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction. Notably, abemaciclib treatment reduced macrophage inflammation and attenuated HFD-induced obesity in mice. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: ACSL4 promotes pro-inflammatory macrophage activation through its KPNB1-dependent nuclear translocation and cooperation with IRF5. Targeting the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic inflammation.

title: The CRISPR-dCas9 epigenetic toolbox: prospects for modulating gene expression in climate-resilient crops.
authors: Quyoom, Bushra; Peer, Latif Ahmad
abstract: CRISPR-dCas9 epigenome editing represents a paradigm shift from static DNA sequence editing to dynamic reprogramming of gene expression, offering a powerful and precise toolbox with the potential to develop stable and climate-resilient crops without altering DNA sequences. The escalating challenges of global food security, driven by climate change and population growth, necessitate innovative crop improvement strategies that extend beyond conventional breeding. Although CRISPR-Cas9 has revolutionized plant biotechnology through direct genome editing, CRISPR-based epigenome editing has emerged as a new frontier. By repurposing nuclease-dead Cas9 as a programmable targeting platform fused to epigenetic effector domains, researchers can precisely modulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence. This approach has already yielded compelling successes, such as the engineering of durable resistance to cassava bacterial blight through targeted epigenetic silencing of a susceptibility gene. This review focuses primarily on the current state of CRISPR-based epigenome editing systems, including acetyltransferases, demethylases, DNA methyltransferases, and deacetylases, and their applications in crop improvement research. We critically evaluate their mechanisms in rewriting epigenetic regulatory information, their demonstrated efficacy in enhancing yield components, disease resistance, and abiotic stress tolerance, and their potential to create stable meiotically heritable epialleles, although most demonstrations remain at the proof-of-concept stage in model plants, with field validation in major crops still limited. This review provides a balanced analysis of key challenges, including editing specificity, context-dependency, delivery limitations, and regulatory considerations. Finally, we outline future directions focusing on technological refinement, multi-omics integration, and field validation. Epigenome editing shows promise as a conceptually distinct and transformative approach in crop biotechnology, through targeted modulation of a plant's epigenetic landscape. However, its full potential hinges on overcoming challenges related to stability, predictability, and field-scale validation.

title: Synthetic Biology Tools and Strategies for Microbial Cell Factory Construction.
authors: Jiang, Jipeng; Zhang, Xin; Zhang, Lixin; Tan, Gao-Yi
abstract: Microbial cell factories have emerged as important platforms for the sustainable production of fuels, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and other value-added bioproducts. Synthetic biology provides a systematic engineering framework for their construction and optimization through standardized biological parts, modular design, and iterative Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles. This chapter summarizes the major tools and strategies for developing microbial cell factories, beginning with the fundamental principles of synthetic biology and the characteristics of representative microbial chassis. Key genetic engineering approaches, including CRISPR-based genome editing, transcriptional and translational regulation, and modular DNA assembly, are discussed together with strategies for metabolic pathway design, enzyme engineering, flux balancing, and dynamic regulation. Genome-scale metabolic modeling, adaptive and directed evolution, and multi-omics analysis are further introduced as systems-level approaches for identifying engineering targets and improving cellular performance. In addition, emerging computational tools, machine learning, artificial intelligence, high-throughput screening, and laboratory automation are highlighted for their roles in accelerating strain development and closing the Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle. Finally, representative applications illustrate the translation of engineered microbial cell factories from laboratory-scale design to industrial biomanufacturing.

title: LipReg4 deletion blocks hypertension induced by gut S. aureofaciens Tu117.
authors: Lv, Xiaowang; Yang, Teng; Wang, Zhiwei; Shen, Hao; Mao, Aiqin; Zhou, Tingting
journal: Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension
abstract: Streptomyces aureofaciens (S. aureofaciens) Tu117 and its metabolite alpha-lipomycin have been implicated in high-salt-induced hypertension. Previous studies showed that high-salt intake increases gut Tu117 abundance and circulating alpha-lipomycin levels. Mechanistically, alpha-lipomycin acts as a TRPV4 antagonist, impairing nitric oxide (NO)- and endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF)- mediated endothelium-dependent vasodilation and thereby promoting vascular dysfunction and blood pressure (BP) elevation. However, whether hypertension is driven by Tu117 itself or specifically by alpha-lipomycin production remains unclear. Here, we generated a LipReg4 deletion mutant strain (DeltaTu117) using Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-Cas9 genome editing to selectively abolish alpha-lipomycin biosynthesis. Deletion of LipReg4 did not markedly affect bacterial growth but completely abolished alpha-lipomycin production. Compared with Tu117, DeltaTu117 failed to increase circulating alpha-lipomycin levels or induce a sustained elevation in BP. These findings identify alpha-lipomycin as the key metabolite mediating Tu117-induced hypertension. They further support a direct role of gut microbial metabolites in host BP regulation.

title: Advances in modeling chromosomal aberrations to recapitulate genomic rearrangements.
authors: Ginestet, Victoria; Schwager, Anna; Vassetzky, Yegor; Shmakova, Anna
abstract: Chromosomal aberrations, including aneuploidies and structural rearrangements, are key drivers of cancer and numerous genetic disorders. Experimental modeling of these alterations is essential for understanding their role in disease initiation and progression. Historically, chromosome engineering relied on methods that lacked precision and could generate off-target genomic damage. Recent advances in genome editing have enabled the precise generation of defined chromosomal abnormalities in human cells. This review summarizes current approaches for modeling numerical and structural chromosomal aberrations, including CRISPR-based chromosome elimination, KaryoCreate, prime editing, programmable recombinases, and RNA-guided bridge recombinases. We also discuss strategies for generating complex chromosomal rearrangements, their applications in studying genome instability, and their limitations. Together, these technologies provide powerful tools to investigate the earliest genomic events underlying cancer and genetic diseases.

title: Primer-programmed circular template generation enables padlock-free rolling circle amplification for low-background CRISPR-based pathogen detection.
authors: Han, Yemin; Yu, Haotian; Lv, Manman; Cheng, Mengqing; Li, Weihao; Ge, Houyang; Gao, Song; Yin, Lu; Ge, Qinyu; Xu, Xinping; Huang, Yan; Sun, Longhua; Lu, Zuhong; Liu, Quanjun
abstract: Rolling circle amplification (RCA) is a powerful nucleic acid amplification strategy, yet conventional RCA-based biosensing often relies on target-specific padlock probes for circular template construction, which increases probe-design complexity and may introduce nonspecific ligation and background amplification. Here, we develop a padlock-free RCA strategy for CRISPR-based pathogen detection through primer-programmed circular template generation (PPCTG) strategy. Asymmetric recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with rationally designed phosphorylated primers generates target-derived single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), which subsequently undergoes universal splint-mediated circularization to form amplification templates without target-specific padlock probes. By integrating target recognition into the amplification-derived ssDNA intermediate, PPCTG couples target amplification with circular template generation while simplifying probe design and reducing nonspecific background. The resulting circular templates support continuous RCA, generating long ssDNA scaffolds that provide abundant activator sites for CRISPR-Cas12a, thereby enabling cascaded signal amplification through trans-cleavage of fluorophore-quencher reporters. The platform achieved a limit of detection of 3.47 aM for Staphylococcus aureus with high analytical specificity. Moreover, extraction-free detection was demonstrated in crude sputum and exhaled breath condensate, with recovery rates of 96.4%-105.5% and good agreement with qPCR results. Overall, PPCTG provides a padlock-free strategy for programmable circular template generation and integrates target amplification, RCA, and CRISPR-Cas12a signal amplification into a streamlined workflow, offering a low-background and ultrasensitive approach for pathogen detection in complex biological matrices.

title: Development and Evaluation of an RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a Molecular Assay for Rapid Diagnosis of Theileria annulata Infection in Bovines.
authors: Mondal, Aditi; Saravanan, B C; Singh, Prachand Pratap; Madhankumar, P; Sankar, M; Mahajan, Sonalika; Dey, S; Pawaiya, Rajveer Singh
abstract: Tropical theileriosis, caused by Theileria annulata, continues to be the most significant tick-borne disease affecting cattle, particularly in endemic regions where it leads to significant production losses. Prompt and reliable diagnosis is critically important for timely treatment and disease control; however, conventional diagnostic methods have important limitations. Microscopic examination lacks sensitivity, particularly in carrier animals, while PCR requires specialized laboratory infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, a fluorescence-based RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay targeting the multicopy mitochondrial cytb gene was developed for rapid detection of T. annulata. Five RPA primer pairs were designed and evaluated, and primer set-5, generating a 324-bp amplicon, exhibited the best amplification performance. A CRISPR RNA (crRNA) was designed within the selected amplicon to enable specific Cas12a-mediated target recognition. The assay was completed within 50 min and demonstrated no cross-reactivity with DNA from Theileria orientalis, Babesia bigemina, Babesia bovis, Anaplasma marginale, and bovine host DNA, confirming excellent analytical specificity. Sensitivity analysis using recombinant plasmid DNA demonstrated a detection limit of approximately ten copies per reaction. The field evaluation of the assay was done by testing 206 bovine field samples. showed that the developed assay identified 163 positive samples, exceeding the detection rates obtained by PCR (151 positives) and microscopy (116 positives). On comparison with PCR, the assay achieved 100% diagnostic sensitivity, 78.18% specificity, 92.64% positive predictive value, 100% negative predictive value, with an overall agreement of 94.17%. These findings indicate that the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a platform is a rapid, sensitive, and accurate molecular diagnostic approach with strong potential for field application and point-of-care diagnosis of bovine tropical theileriosis, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

title: Ddx1 is essential for zebrafish development to adulthood but has no detectable effect on the response to tilapia lake virus (TiLV) in larvae.
authors: Pooranachandran, Niedharsan; Mojzesz, Miriam; Starzyk, Justyna; Zawisza, Maria; Chromiec, Adam; Widziolek, Magdalena; Prajsnar, Tomasz K; Surachetpong, Win; Chadzinska, Magdalena; Adamek, Mikolaj; Rakus, Krzysztof
abstract: DExD/H-box RNA helicases are multifunctional regulators of RNA metabolism and some are associated with host defence against viruses. However, the in vivo roles of individual family members remain insufficiently characterised. Ddx1 is one such example, implicated in antiviral signalling as well as in the replication of several viruses. In this study, we investigated the function of Ddx1 during vertebrate development and viral infection in zebrafish (Danio rerio) model using both loss-of-function and gain-of-function approaches. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of ddx1 resulted in viable embryos and larvae without overt developmental abnormalities; however, knockouts failed to survive to adulthood, indicating that Ddx1 is required for later stages of development. To assess its role in antiviral defence, ddx1 knockout and wild-type larvae were experimentally infected with tilapia lake virus (TiLV), a virus known to induce a strong type I interferon response in zebrafish. Survival rates, viral loads, and expression of selected type I interferon pathway genes (rig-I, ifnphi1, mxa) were comparable between genotypes, demonstrating that Ddx1 is not essential for the larval antiviral response to TiLV. Consistently, overexpression of ddx1 did not enhance resistance to infection. Together, these findings indicate that while Ddx1 is critical for zebrafish survival to adulthood, it does not play a measurable role in early antiviral immunity against TiLV in zebrafish larvae.

title: Integrative proximity labeling and multiomic profiling uncover domain-specific interactomes and molecular vulnerabilities of oncogenic PI3K.
authors: Lee, Donghee; Koh, Jin; Choi, Sun Hee; Kim, Jong Hyuk
abstract: Activating mutations in PIK3CA (encoding the p110alpha kinase) are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers in human tumors. The two major hotspot mutations, E545K (helical domain) and H1047R (kinase domain), both hyperactivate PI3K-AKT signaling, yet they exhibit distinct functional behaviors and differential drug sensitivities. The mutation-specific protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks underlying the differences, however, remain largely unexplored. In this study, we established experimental approaches to identify proteins in proximity to oncogenic PI3K using biotin ligase-based proximity labeling. Our data revealed that the PIK3CA H1047R and E545K mutants fused to BioID2 formed structurally distinct complexes, each associating with unique proximal proteins identified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Further integration of the PPI networks with CRISPR dependency screens and multiomic profiling mapped the divergent functional interactomes of p110alpha hotspot mutants. H1047R exhibited a synthetic lethal dependency on the adaptor protein TAB2, which is associated with aggressive clinical phenotypes in breast cancer. Distinctly, E545K interacted with core subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, corresponding to a globally repressive chromatin state at distal enhancers. This SWI/SNF association also revealed a mutation-specific epigenetic vulnerability, with E545K-mutant cells displaying increased sensitivity to EZH2 inhibitors. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the molecular network complexity of oncogenic PI3K can be interrogated through proximity labeling and that distinct PIK3CA point mutations rewire non-overlapping PPI networks, revealing domain-specific dependencies. Our study provides a framework for mapping mutation-specific interactomes and offers molecular insights and potential therapeutic strategies for PIK3CA-mutant tumors.

title: Oocyst wall protein EtOWP6 is critical for sporocyst formation and developmental progression in Eimeria tenella.
authors: Jia, Liushu; Wang, Jinwen; Wang, Qingjie; Wang, Lu; Zhu, Shunhai; Zhao, Qiping; Wu, Shanbo; Han, Wenqi; Bai, Jaiyu; Zhao, Fanghe; Yu, Yu; Han, Hongyu; Dong, Hui
abstract: Transmission of apicomplexan parasites-including Eimeria, Toxoplasma, and Cryptosporidium-relies on the environmentally resilient oocyst wall, a bilayered structure whose integrity is maintained by cysteine-rich oocyst wall proteins (OWPs). Yet the functional roles of these conserved proteins remain poorly defined. Here, we characterize EtOWP6, a conserved OWP in Eimeria tenella, the causative agent of avian coccidiosis. Immunofluorescence reveals that EtOWP6 localizes specifically to wall-forming bodies and oocyst/sporocyst walls during sexual development. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout demonstrates that EtOWP6 is essential for sporocyst formation, with deficient parasites exhibiting malformed sporocysts, developmental arrest in vitro, and an in vivo reduction in oocyst output exceeding 85%. The knockout strain is highly attenuated yet retains partial immunogenicity. Transcriptomic analysis reveals that EtOWP6 deletion induces widespread transcriptional reprogramming, disrupting genes critical for developmental regulation and oocyst wall biogenesis. Our findings establish EtOWP6 as a critical regulator coupling structural integrity with developmental progression in Eimeria, and more broadly, highlight OWPs as conserved targets for transmission-blocking interventions across apicomplexan parasites.

title: DNA assisting CRISPR-Cas13a activation regulating assay for detection of DNA mutation and miRNAs.
authors: Wan, Changqing; Liu, Wenzheng; Pan, Shutao; Wang, Xiaoxiang; Zhou, Jingcong; Hu, Yibo; Li, Pengcheng; Nie, Xiaoqi; Liao, Yangwei
abstract: Cas13a is an RNA-targeting effector system with exceptional sensitivity, essential for applications such as mutation discrimination, RNA biomarker quantification and dynamic monitoring. However, precise control over its activation kinetics and thermodynamics remains a fundamental challenge, limiting its use in nucleic acid detection. Here, we present the DNA-Assisting CRISPR-Cas13a Activation Regulating (DACAR) Assay, which employs a single-stranded DNA blocker to occupy the crRNA spacer. Through programmable toehold-mediated strand displacement (TMSD) and toehold-exchange (TE) reactions, DACAR is able to control the thermodynamics and kinetics of Cas13a activation at two different levels. Systematic modulation of toehold length and direction yields a tunable cleavage rate gradient, while TE-based free-energy tuning facilitates an ON/OFF gating mode. For single-nucleotide variant (SNV) discrimination, DACAR-TE amplifies thermodynamic mismatch effects, achieving a discrimination factor of 162.4 and a detection limit of 0.05% mutant abundance for the KRAS G12D mutation. The Switch-DACAR system also enables sequential detection of miR-155 and miR-21 in a single tube, with a detection limit of 10 pM. To sum up, DACAR provides a unified, programmable framework for precise molecular-level control of Cas13a, advancing its potential in diagnostics and molecular logic.

title: Quadruple HLA-I/II gene homo/heterozygous knockout hESC line: generation, multi-omics profiling, pluripotency, and immunogenicity.
authors: Zhang, Linghan; Cai, Bo; Li, Xiaoxiao; Liu, Yanxing; Lu, Ping; Liu, Yuqin; Lei, Wenzhuo; Mao, Genhong
abstract: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) exhibit pluripotency, self-renewal, and broad therapeutic potential in diverse disease contexts. Meanwhile, allogeneic grafts derived from hESCs are confronted with the formidable challenge of immune rejection. Specific human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) are critically involved in mediating transplant rejection, thus establishing HLA-deficient stem cells can be an important step toward achieving immune evasion. However, there is currently no consensus on which gene editing strategy can reduce hESC immunogenicity to a level suitable for broad clinical applications. This study performed HLA-A/-B gene hetero/homozygous knockout in an HLA double-knockout hESC line using a CRISPR/Cas9 system, established HLA-DRA(-/-)/-DQA1(-/-)/-A(+/-)/-B(-/-) knockout monoclonal cell lines, and revealed the multi-omics profiles, along with preserved pluripotency and trends to reduced immunogenicity of the hESC lines, through multi-omics analyses, in vitro assessment of pluripotency-related gene expression, in vivo teratoma formation assays and xenotransplantation experiments in mouse models. This study presents two novel monoclonal HLA genes homo/heterozygous knockout hESC lines, along with their multi-omics landscapes, pluripotency and immunogenicity. The findings exhibit crucial application potential and reference value in the development of hypoimmunogenic hESCs for their universal clinical use.

title: Programmable and selective silencing of oncogenic fusion transcripts by CRISPR-Cas13b via breakpoint sequence recognition.
authors: Hu 胡文欣, Wenxin; Chen 陈竑霖, Honglin; He, Steven; Casan, Joshua M L; Shembrey, Carolyn; Li, Sharon; Brown, Lauren M; Zhao, Andrea; Truong, Lynda; Buchner, Isabella; Vassiliadis, Dane; Hughes, Timothy P; White, Deborah L; Carmichael, Catherine L; De Weck, Antoine; Voskoboinik, Ilia; Gouil, Quentin; Trapani, Joseph A; Ekert, Paul G; Sadras, Teresa; Fareh, Mohamed
abstract: Oncogenic gene fusions are key drivers of cancer, yet most remain undruggable by current therapies. Here, we establish CRISPR-PspCas13b as a personalizable platform for systematic silencing of various fusion transcripts. We reveal that recognition and cleavage of the breakpoint sequence by PspCas13b disrupt the fusion transcript, resulting in efficient protein depletion. PspCas13b cleavage produces aberrant, translation-incompetent target RNA species, a subset of which harbors internal deletions proximal to the cleavage site. We demonstrate that targeting the BCR::ABL1 breakpoint sequence efficiently degrades both wild-type and drug-resistant BCR::ABL1 mutants, which are the primary drivers of tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and relapse in chronic myeloid leukemia. Molecular profiling revealed that PspCas13b impairs BCR::ABL1 tyrosine phosphokinase activity and triggers extensive transcriptomic and proteomic remodeling, leading to erythroid differentiation and apoptosis in drug-resistant cells. Beyond BCR::ABL1, personalized design of PspCas13b effectively silences other undruggable oncogenic fusions. Collectively, this study establishes a molecular framework for precise targeting of undruggable or drug-resistant oncogenic transcripts.

title: Chemogenetic ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 CRISPR screen uncovers HAPSTR1/HUWE1 axis in chromatin proteostasis and cell cycle control.
authors: van Overbeek, Nila K; Clijsters, Linda; Wirth, Martina; de Graaf, Ilona J; de Lint, Klaas; Uruci, Sidrit; Teunisse, Amina F A S; Akimov, Vyacheslav; de Ru, Arnoud H; Vukic, Maja; Kirdok, Idil; Daxinger, Lucia; van Veelen, Peter A; Blagoev, Blagoy; Luijsterburg, Martijn S; Wolthuis, Rob M F; Berlin, Ilana; Vertegaal, Alfred C O
abstract: In this study, we sought to comprehensively map ubiquitin signaling networks at the crossroads of cellular proliferation and proteostasis, both crucial in cancer. Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screening in the presence of the ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 identified 239 genes whose ablation sensitizes cells to ubiquitination blockade. Follow-up studies reveal a role for the nuclear protein, C16orf72/HECT, UBA, and WWE domain containing E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1 (HUWE1)-Associated Protein modifying Stress Responses (HAPSTR1), in chromatin proteostasis and DNA replication. We show that HAPSTR1 recruits the E3 ligase HUWE1 to the chromatin, keeping the chromatin-associated proteome in check, and is itself turned over by HUWE1 during cell cycle progression. Structural modeling of the HAPSTR1/HUWE1 complex, supported by mutational analysis, demonstrates that loss of HUWE1 binding renders HAPSTR1 unable to support cellular proliferation when ubiquitin signaling is suppressed. Consequently, HAPSTR1 ablation impairs clearance of chromatin-associated proteins, triggering global transcriptional and proteostatic adaptations. Under diminished ubiquitin signaling, these adaptive mechanisms give way to replication stress and premature S phase entry, culminating in cell cycle collapse and DNA damage. Our findings uncover protein networks exhibiting synthetic lethality with ubiquitin signaling blockade and highlight vulnerabilities of actively proliferating cells to proteostatic imbalance at the chromatin.

title: A conserved Hox9-10 code underlies the early establishment of hind appendage progenitors in zebrafish and the Iberian ribbed newt.
authors: Nakazawa, Hidemichi; Urakawa, Kohei; Maeno, Akiteru; Fujibayashi, Towa; Ishizaka, Mizuki; Ishizu, Atsuki; Asano, Touma; Matsubara, Haruka; Takeuchi, Takashi; Watakabe, Ikuko; Higashijima, Shin-Ichi; Abe, Gembu; Kawamura, Akinori
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: The acquisition of paired appendages was a key innovation in vertebrate evolution. Although HoxA/D paralog groups (PGs) 9-13 play central roles in patterning paired fins and limbs, the evolutionary origin of this paired appendage-patterning system remains unknown. Here, we show that HoxA/D PG9-10 genes are essential for the early establishment of pelvic fin progenitors in zebrafish, and that Hox9-10 function is similarly required for hindlimb progenitor formation in the Iberian ribbed newt. In zebrafish, combined disruption of five HoxA/D PG9-10 genes abolishes the detectable pelvic fin progenitor population, resulting in complete loss of pelvic fins. A Tg(hoxa10b:EGFP) reporter labeled cells in the presumptive pelvic fin field before pelvic fin bud formation. Importantly, simultaneous CRISPR-mediated disruption of all seven Hox9-10 paralogs in the Iberian ribbed newt similarly impaired the establishment of hindlimb progenitors, suggesting that an early requirement for Hox9-10 function in hind appendage development predates the divergence of ray-finned and lobe-finned vertebrates. Together, these findings identify an evolutionarily conserved role for posterior Hox9-10 genes in the initial establishment of hind appendage progenitors. Because overlapping posterior Hox paralog groups are subsequently deployed during paired appendage patterning, this early Hox9-10 requirement provides a developmental link between the posterior axial Hox code and the paired appendage-patterning system. Our results are therefore consistent with the hypothesis that recruitment of a posterior Hox code into hind appendage progenitor formation contributed to the evolutionary assembly of the vertebrate paired appendage-patterning system.

title: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers in cancer: emerging platforms for molecular imaging, biosensing, and precision oncology.
authors: Akbarin, Mohammad Mehdi; Farjami, Zahra; Alvarez, Hugo Ramirez
abstract: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers have emerged as powerful molecular tools for cancer imaging, biosensing, and biomarker detection due to their high specificity, low background fluorescence, and genetic encodability. These short RNA molecules activate fluorescence upon binding specific fluorogens, enabling real-time visualization of intracellular targets and dynamic molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances in RNA structural engineering, fluorophore optimization, and biosensor integration have significantly expanded the translational applications of fluorogenic aptamers in oncology. This mini-review summarizes the structural principles, fluorescence activation mechanisms, and cancer-related applications of fluorogenic RNA aptamers and related nucleic acid biosensors. Foundational studies describing the architecture of fluorogenic aptamer families, including Spinach, Broccoli, Mango, Pepper, Squash, and Beetroot, are discussed with emphasis on G-quadruplex-mediated fluorogen stabilization and fluorescence enhancement. Furthermore, recent developments in CRISPR/Cas-assisted fluorogenic biosensors, dual-color RNA imaging systems, fluorogenic DNAzymes, and amplification-driven aptamer platforms are highlighted. Direct applications across multiple malignancies, including brain, breast, colorectal, liver, lung, prostate, and skin cancers, demonstrate the growing utility of these technologies for tumor-associated RNA detection, epigenetic biomarker analysis, molecular imaging, and therapeutic monitoring. In addition, advances in fluorescence brightness, structural stability, and multiplex imaging strategies have improved the sensitivity and adaptability of fluorogenic RNA systems for complex biological environments. Despite current limitations related to RNA stability, intracellular delivery, and tissue penetration, fluorogenic RNA aptamers represent highly promising tools for next-generation precision oncology. Continued integration with nanotechnology, live-cell imaging, artificial intelligence, and molecular diagnostics is expected to enhance further their clinical and translational potential in cancer research and personalized medicine.

title: Modeling Moyamoya disease using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and organoids.
authors: Kim, Jong-Tae; Youn, Dong Hyuk; Jung, Harry; Lee, Ji Hyeon; Hong, Eun Pyo; Kim, Youngmi; Cho, Kyu-Won; Lee, Jae Jun; Jeon, Jin Pyeong
abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.
