RESULTS: The results demonstrated that the overexpression of MSMEI_4050 decreased rifampicin resistance in M. smegmatis, whereas the opposite effect was observed upon MSMEI_4050 inhibition. Molecular docking analysis revealed a positive value of the change in Gibbs free energy estimation between MSMEI_4050 and rifampicin, suggesting that no direct protein‒drug interaction occurs at the active site of the protein. CONCLUSIONS: MSMEI_4050 expression is associated with rifampicin resistance; further studies are needed to understand the role of MSMEI_4050 in the mechanism underlying rifampicin resistance.

title: CRISPR-based interrogation of alternative lengthening of telomeres: mapping dependencies, stress-buffering pathways, and therapeutic vulnerabilities.
authors: Lannoo, Ruth; Bechter, Oliver; Daelemans, Dirk
abstract: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere maintenance mechanism that supports the growth of approximately 5-10% of human tumors and represents an attractive but insufficiently explored therapeutic target. CRISPR-based functional genomics has emerged as a powerful approach to systematically interrogate ALT biology and identify genetic dependencies associated with the ALT state. In this Review, we discuss the CRISPR-based strategies applied to ALT, including hypothesis-driven targeted loss-of-function screens, phenotype-driven optical screens, in silico mining of large-scale dependency datasets, and genome-wide screens in ALT-adjacent states. Across these approaches, recurrent dependencies converge on pathways mediating replication stress buffering, DNA repair, and telomere maintenance, including FANCM, SMARCAL1, and SUB1. Collectively, these findings support a model in which ALT-positive cells rely not on a unique ALT-specific factor, but rather on stress-buffering mechanisms that prevent chronic telomeric dysfunction from triggering replication catastrophe and cell death, highlighting these pathways as promising candidates for further therapeutic investigation.

title: Emerging stem cell strategies for neurodegenerative diseases.
authors: Hardjo, Marhaen; Sophian, Alfi
abstract: Degenerative diseases continue to impose a substantial global health burden with limited curative options. Neurodegenerative diseases, the principal focus of this review, are among the largest contributors to this burden. Stem cell therapies have emerged as a promising approach, offering the potential to replace lost cells, modulate pathological microenvironments, and restore tissue function through both direct cell replacement and paracrine mechanisms. However, conventional stem cell strategies encounter persistent obstacles including immune rejection, tumorigenicity, poor engraftment, and limited long-term efficacy in chronic disease settings. This narrative review synthesizes recent and emerging innovations in stem cell therapy for neurodegenerative diseases across four major domains: (i) emerging mechanisms of stem cell action, including activation of dormant neural stem cells (NSCs), exosome-based cell-free therapies, and rejuvenation of aged stem cells; (ii) emerging cell types such as pre-morula stem cells (PMSCs), perinatal stem cells, SSEA-4+ human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUC-MSCs), and iPSC-derived mesenchymal progenitor cells (MiMPCs); (iii) advanced delivery platforms including three-dimensional (3D) biomaterial scaffolds, injectable hydrogels, and stem cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CMNPs); and (iv) gene-editing strategies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9-mediated generation of hypoimmunogenic induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines for allogeneic, off-the-shelf cell therapies. Key translational gaps, including standardization of exosome isolation and scaffold fabrication protocols, long-term safety and immunogenicity assessment, and ethical and regulatory frameworks, are critically evaluated, and future research directions are proposed. In addition, the review states the level of evidence (in vitro, animal, or human) supporting each approach and summarizes their clinical status in a single table. Addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to realizing the full potential of stem cell-based regenerative medicine for degenerative diseases.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen reveals that Wnt signaling regulates lipid accumulation in APOE4 oligodendrocytes.
authors: Akay, Leyla Anne; Bright, Anna; Dong, Daiyun; Smith, Ethan D; Hurt, Robert C; Boix, Carles A; Louderback, Kate; Medrano, Janine; Sun, Dingcheng; Lin, Haonan; King, Oisin; Welch, Gwyneth M; Nawaid, Hiba; Agbas, Emre; Jiang, Alan; Bubnys, Adele; Cheng, Ji-Xin; Blanchard, Joel W; Tsai, Li-Huei
abstract: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, yet the cellular mechanisms linking APOE variants to disease risk remain unclear. We previously found that APOE4 expression causes lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes, reducing myelination, but the underlying mechanisms were unknown. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) sequencing in human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived oligodendrocytes, we identified decreased Wnt signaling and overactive glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B) as key regulators of lipid-droplet accumulation. Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of GSK3B reduced lipid droplets in APOE4 oligodendrocytes and increased myelination in three-dimensional iPSC-derived brain organoids. Pharmacological GSK3B inhibition also reduced lipid droplets and improved myelination in APOE4;PS19 tau transgenic mice. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework linking Wnt/GSK3B signaling to APOE4-driven disruptions in oligodendrocyte lipid metabolism and myelination, pointing to GSK3B as a potential therapeutic target for APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease.

title: Lactate dehydrogenase A-dependent redox control of selective mRNA translation directs monocyte fate commitment.
authors: Yang, Ning; He, Huixia; Liu, Xin
abstract: Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation is a central process that shapes immune responses across diverse contexts, yet how inflammatory cues engage metabolism to instruct monocyte fate commitment remains unclear. Here, using a CRISPR-based metabolic screen combined with monocyte-specific perturbations in bacterial lung infection, we identified lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) as a key metabolic regulator of monocyte commitment to the nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2)(+) macrophage fate in vivo. LDHA-dependent cytosolic nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD(+)) regeneration enabled selective hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1alpha) translation through its 5' untranslated region (UTR) and is associated with structural remodeling of this region. HIF1alpha then functioned as a downstream effector that promoted the NOS2(+) macrophage fate. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) further acted as an upstream metabolic priming signal that enhanced LDHA-dependent HIF1alpha regulation and supported this differentiation process. Together, these findings suggest that metabolic redox state regulates monocyte fate commitment through selective mRNA translation coupled to RNA structural remodeling.

title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation.
authors: Thapa, Christina; Oh, Emily K; Sirkin, David; Lahey, Jennifer; Diaz de Leon Guerrerro, Sol; McCarroll, Ada; Gowda, Prarthana; Zhang, Hanwen; Barishman, Alexandra; Peyton, Lilia; Zhang, Siwei; Pollak, Rebecca M; Hart, Ronald P; Pato, Carlos N; Kreimer, Anat; Mulle, Jennifer G; Sanders, Alan R; Pang, Zhiping P; Duan, Jubao
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Beyond prediction: The evolving role of artificial intelligence in genome editing.
authors: Shin, Soochul; Uhm, Heesoo; Kim, Yong-Woo; Im, Hyeon Woo; Bae, Sangsu
abstract: Since the discovery of the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)-associated (Cas) system, genome-editing technologies have advanced rapidly, and the field has expanded substantially. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) has progressed at an unprecedented pace and is transforming genetic engineering. Early AI applications primarily addressed predictive tasks, including guide RNA (gRNA) activity, off-target effects, and editing outcomes for CRISPR-Cas nucleases, base editors, and prime editors. Recently, transformer-based protein language models (PLMs) and generative AI have expanded the role of AI beyond prediction to direct molecular design. Thus, AI-driven frameworks can now evolve genome-editing proteins, design molecular architectures, and generate de novo genome-editing enzymes. This review discusses how AI is reshaping genome engineering, from gRNA activity prediction to the design of next-generation editors.

title: Evaluating a CRISPR-based sterile male for Drosophila suzukii (Diptera: Drosophilidae) control.
authors: Lee, Jana C; Skabeikis, Dominick; Eswar, Anirudh; Saa, Emilie; Gamez, Maria G; Sellman, Anne; Lyons, Noelle; Gamez, Stephanie
abstract: Spotted-wing drosophila (SWD), Drosophila suzukii Matsumura, is a serious invasive pest of small fruits. The novel precision-guided Sterile Insect Technology (pgSIT) uses CRISPR technology to simultaneously produce sterile males and eliminate female offspring. Testing their performance in the laboratory is required before field testing is permitted. We evaluated pgSIT males with wild males regarding suppressing infestation and survivorship. In large cage trials in the laboratory, a 5:1 ratio of sterile to wild males led to a 35% or 41% reduction in offspring, and a 10:1 ratio led to 52% reduction. This indicates that sterile males were mating with wild females when wild males were present. In survivorship trials, median longevity was 1 d shorter among sterile males than wild males kept in large, ventilated cages. Finally, we performed predator feeding assays to address regulatory concerns of pgSIT technology. Green lacewing larvae, Chrysoperla rufilabris, that fed on wild or pgSIT SWD larvae developed similarly into pupae and adults. While pgSIT flies would not be present in the field at the larval stage, this test revealed no discernible impacts when predators fed on it. Rather, pgSIT males would be delivered in release boxes at the pupal stage. We found that SWD pupae, wild or sterile, were not a good food source for lacewing larvae to complete development. Given the results, further field research is warranted to test the efficacy of these sterile male SWD.

title: Decoding cellular vulnerabilities for interpretable drug response prediction.
authors: Chen, Chonghao; Du, Yulei; Jiang, Yaxin; Wang, Yuanfang; Tang, Di; Ding, Xiaofan; He, Mian
abstract: Accurate prediction of anticancer drug response remains challenging because conventional approaches based on chemical structures and baseline molecular profiles do not directly capture drug-induced perturbations or cellular dependencies. Here, we present vulnerability-guided cascaded attention transformer (VCAT), which integrates Connectivity Map (CMap)/Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures (LINCS)-derived consensus transcriptional signatures with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-supervised cellular representations through adaptive encoders and dual stream cascaded attention. Across four data splitting strategies, VCAT outperformed conventional machine learning and published deep learning models, achieving the best performance in 11 of 12 classification split metric comparisons. Ablation analyses showed that CRISPR-derived vulnerability features complement baseline gene expression and that the proposed interaction architecture further improves prediction. VCAT also enhanced continuous IC50 prediction and generalized across Cancer Therapeutics Response Portal (CTRP), Profiling Relative Inhibition Simultaneously in Mixtures (PRISM), patient-derived organoids, and hepatocellular carcinoma cohorts. Attention based prioritization and integrated gradients jointly highlighted biologically relevant genes, while knockdown of cytosolic iron-sulfur assembly component 3 (CIAO3), methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase 2 (MTHFD2), and WD repeat domain 1 (WDR1) increased sorafenib sensitivity in hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines. These findings support integrating drug-induced perturbations with genetic vulnerabilities for accurate, interpretable, and transferable anticancer drug response prediction.

title: Genetic and Epigenetic Manipulation Using CRISPR Techniques in Ewing Sarcoma.
authors: Knott, Maximilian M L; Li, Jing
abstract: CRISPR-based technologies have transformed experimental biology by enabling precise, efficient, and programmable manipulation of the genome and epigenome. This chapter provides a comprehensive and practical guide to genetic and epigenetic editing using CRISPR technology, with a particular focus on applications in Ewing sarcoma cell models. We describe strategies for CRISPR-mediated gene knockout (CRISPR KO) via nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ), precise gene knock-in (CRISPR KI) through homology-directed repair (HDR), and reversible transcriptional modulation using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and CRISPR activation (CRISPRa). We emphasize the use of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery of Cas9 and single guide RNAs, which offers improved editing efficiency, reduced off-target activity, and enhanced safety compared to plasmid-based approaches. Detailed protocols are provided for guide RNA design, RNP assembly, electroporation-based delivery, single-cell cloning, and molecular validation of edited clones. In addition, we outline best practices for HDR template design, discuss strategies to improve KI efficiency, and address common challenges such as polyploidy, variable editing rates, and DNA-mediated cytotoxicity. For CRISPRi and CRISPRa applications, we describe plasmid-based systems employing catalytically inactive Cas9 fused to transcriptional repressors or activators, enabling potentially tunable and reversible control of endogenous gene expression. Throughout the chapter, practical advice, troubleshooting tips, and critical considerations are included to facilitate successful implementation across diverse experimental settings. Collectively, this chapter serves as a detailed methodological resource for researchers aiming to employ CRISPR-based engineering for functional studies.

title: Ewing Sarcoma-Specific (Re)Expression Models.
authors: Knott, Maximilian M L; Cidre-Aranaz, Florencia
abstract: Gene expression and knockdown systems are powerful tools for studying the function of single genes and their interactions within pathways. Plasmid transfection and viral transduction have revolutionized the field of molecular biology and paved the way for various gene-editing strategies such as TALEN, Zink finger nucleases, and ultimately CRISPR. In Ewing sarcoma (EwS), almost as many genes are repressed by the expression of EWSR1-FLI1 as are upregulated by the fusion oncogene. Here, we present a useful point-by-point protocol for generating transgene expression systems in EwS that allow (conditional) re-expression of a gene of interest. We provide an extensive instruction on molecular cloning, plasmid generation, viral transduction, and expression validation. Finally, we address common problems and highlight potential pitfalls that can be easily avoided with thoughtful guidance.

title: In-vivo CRISPR/Base-Editing "One-Shot" Therapies Targeting PCSK9.
authors: Nelson, Benjamin; Khera, Amit
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To assess and present the current state of gene editing for reduction of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) with emphasis on technology and ongoing trials for genetic editing of protein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9). RECENT FINDINGS: There are two ongoing clinical trials in humans to edit PCSK9 using CRISPR-Cas9 base editing technology packaged within lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Preliminary interim and preclinical data suggest that this strategy is effective for long-term reduction of PCSK9 and LDL-C following a single IV infusion. Monoclonal antibodies that neutralize circulating PCSK9 have demonstrated the utility of PCSK9 inhibition for reducing LDL-C and ASCVD. Although there is an increasing number of pharmacologic strategies for inhibiting PCSK9, gene editing is an attractive option due to its potential to permanently reduce circulating PCSK9 levels and by extension LDL-C and ASCVD. There are two ongoing clinical trials in humans investigating the safety and efficacy of gene editing for PCSK9 with encouraging preliminary results. In this review, we will describe the background of PCSK9 as a target, the gene editing machinery and the preliminary results. We also explore the unique safety challenges of this technology and propose considerations for appropriate patient populations to maintain net positive benefits despite unknowns.

title: Disruption of the CRL5 ubiquitin ligase complex enhances engineered T-cell persistence under chronic tumor antigen exposure.
authors: Bachl, Stefanie; Ching, Carter; Talbot, Alexis; Forget, Antoine; Kale, Nupura; Kochendoerfer, Clara; Nyberg, William A; Li, Zhongmei; Chen, Peixin Amy; Kennedy, Patrick H; Liu, Qi; Muldoon, Joseph J; Liu, Chang; Cusing, Gwendolyn; Arang, Nadia; Krogan, Nevan J; Allen, Greg M; Marson, Alexander; Dodgson, Stacie E; Eyquem, Justin; Carnevale, Julia
abstract: Engineered T-cell therapies are limited by progressive dysfunction under chronic tumor antigen exposure, and genetic perturbation of negative regulators has emerged as a promising strategy to sustain effector activity. We reanalyzed a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen in primary human T cells under repetitive tumor stimulation; protein-protein interaction mapping revealed seven members of the Cullin-RING Ligase 5 (CRL5) complex as an enriched hit cluster. Knockout of any of these members (CUL5, ARIH2, RNF7, UBE2F, UBE2L3, CISH, DCUN1D3) enhanced tumor serial killing, and CUL5, the complex scaffold, emerged as the strongest target. CUL5 knockout T cells exhibited sustained cytotoxicity, elevated effector cytokine production, and fewer exhaustion marker-positive cells while retaining antigen specificity and cytokine dependence. Quantitative ubiquitylation proteomics in resting, and acutely and chronically stimulated T cells mapped CRL5-dependent candidate substrates beyond the canonical JAK/STAT axis, including nutrient transporters, receptor trafficking proteins, and TCR signaling components. The benefit of CUL5 knockout extended across CARs targeting CD19, BCMA, and HER2 with different costimulatory domains, and to 1XX-modified CAR and HLA-independent TCR architectures. Combining CUL5 ablation with a tumor-induced IL-2 circuit produced tumor control across nine rounds of repetitive stimulation, whereas either modification alone eventually failed. In vivo, CUL5 knockout BCMA CAR T cells were enriched in the bone marrow following repeated tumor rechallenge and exhibited enhanced ex vivo cytotoxicity after nearly 90 days in tumor-bearing mice. These findings position CUL5 perturbation as a strategy to improve T-cell persistence and the efficacy of adoptive cell therapies, potentially with engineered cytokine support.

title: Cullin-5 RING E3 ligase limits CD8(+) T-cell persistence and effector responses during chronic antigen stimulation.
authors: Saco, Justin D; Karin, Daniel; Patten, J J; Bachl, Stefanie; Ching, Carter; Kale, Nupura; Fan, Yichen; Medina, Egmidio; Naser Al Deen, Nataly; Champhekar, Ameya; Kaelin, William G; Schulman, Brenda A; Campbell, Katie M; Carnevale, Julia; Puig-Saus, Cristina; Ribas, Antoni
abstract: T-cell exhaustion limits durable antitumor responses and remains a barrier to adoptive cell therapies (ACT) in solid tumors. To identify regulators of T-cell persistence, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in primary human CD8(+) T cells expressing an NY-ESO-1-specific T-cell receptor and subjected them to repeated tumor cell rechallenge. These screens revealed enrichment of single-guide RNAs targeting components of Cullin-RING E3 ligases, particularly Cullin-5 (CRL5) assemblies comprising CUL5, RNF7, and ARIH2. Disruption of CRL5 genes in T cells preserved cytotoxic activity and enhanced cytokine production while sustaining effector-associated transcriptional programs and suppressing exhaustion-related signatures. Pharmacologic inhibition of cullin neddylation with the NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor MLN4924 recapitulated CRL5 loss and enhanced T-cell effector function in vitro. In a human melanoma xenograft model, ACT with CRL5-deficient T cells improved tumor control. Together, these findings identify CRL5 as a negative regulator of T-cell fitness and a potential therapeutic target to enhance ACT durability in solid tumors.

title: Genomic dissection of divergent selection reveals a roadmap for reciprocal improvement of Chinese and American soybean.
authors: Jiao, Chengzhi; Li, Delin; Zhang, Hao; Zhang, Zhongren; Wang, Xueqing; Yan, Long; Zheng, Tianqing; Zhao, Chaosen; Qiu, Hongmei; Xing, Guangnan; Hu, Guoyu; Liu, Like; Wang, Qiang; Huang, Wen; Wang, Xing; Wang, Yumin; Miao, Long; Li, YanFei; Jing, Xin; Fang, Xiaojian; Tian, Yu; Li, Ying-Hui; Wang, Xiaobo; Qiu, Li-Juan
abstract: Soybean (Glycine max [L.] Merr.) was domesticated in China over five millennia ago; yet, its global expansion has resulted in two distinct, independently evolved breeding pools in China and the Americas. While regional breeding has optimized specific traits, a comprehensive roadmap for the reciprocal exchange of these "breeding-specific" beneficial alleles is lacking. Here, we performed a large-scale genomic dissection of 2,377 soybean accessions, integrating 8.4 million high-quality SNPs with multi-environment phenotyping across 11 locations. Through genome-wide association studies (GWAS), we identified 261 significant loci (223 novel) governing six key agronomic traits, revealing that Chinese and American germplasms have accumulated distinct sets of beneficial alleles of seed size/protein in China and oil/yield in the Americas. To harness this untapped potential, we developed the Soybean Targeted Improvement Navigation System (STINS), a framework integrating population genomics, GWAS, and genomic selection (GS). We demonstrate the potential of targeted beneficial allele introgression between populations via gene modification for rapid trait improvement. Proof-of-concept functional evaluation through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of GmST05 in an American cultivar and overexpression of a resistant GmSNAP18 haplotype in a Chinese cultivar provided experimental support for STINS-predicted targets for protein content and SCN resistance improvement. Our study provides a navigable genomic resource for "knowledge-driven design breeding", offering a blueprint for the global exchange of elite alleles to ensure future food security.

title: A programmable aptamer-triggered B-PER/CRISPR cascade amplification platform for ultrasensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus.
authors: Jiang, Jialin; Peng, Yuan; Ma, Wenjie; Zhang, He; Xiong, Shaoqing; Fu, Xin; Li, Jinyan
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
abstract: Rapid and sensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is critical for food safety and public health. Herein, this work developed an ABC (aptamer-B-PER-CRISPR) cascade detection platform, where B-PER stands for bidirectional primer exchange reaction, that integrates aptamer-mediated target recognition, B-PER isothermal amplification, and CRISPR/Cas12a trans-cleavage for highly sensitive and specific detection of S. aureus. Upon target recognition, the trigger strand T is released from the aptamer-T duplex, initiating B-PER to generate abundant products containing sequences recognized by the guide RNA (gRNA), which activate Cas12a to cleave the reporter probe, generating a detectable fluorescence signal. Under optimized conditions, the platform exhibited a linear range of 10(2) to 10(10) CFU per mL with a regression equation of F(520 nm) = 575.36 log C + 3246.47 (R(2) = 0.9992) and a limit of detection of 13 CFU per mL. The assay showed excellent specificity for S. aureus, with negligible cross-reactivity toward Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Salmonella. Recovery tests in spiked milk samples yielded average recoveries of 98.9-100.7%. Overall, the ABC platform offers high sensitivity, excellent specificity, robust anti-interference capability, and operational simplicity, demonstrating great potential for rapid and reliable detection of foodborne pathogens in complex matrices.

title: Gene regulatory behaviors of mutant CRX proteins demonstrated with late-stage human retinal organoids.
authors: Mullin, Nathaniel K; Voigt, Andrew P; Lamba, Deepak A; Chirco, Kathleen R
abstract: Variants in the transcription factor CRX cause a spectrum of retinal degenerative disorders including Leber congenital amaurosis 7 (LCA7). LCA7-associated variants exert a dominant effect in developing photoreceptor cells, leading to cellular dysfunction and poor to absent visual acuity in patients. Here, we dissect the allelic heterogeneity of LCA7 using multimodal single-cell gene expression and chromatin accessibility analysis of retinal organoids. We generated mature (240 day) retinal organoids from patient-derived iPSCs carrying missense (K88Q) and nonsense (T155fs) variants, as well as from CRISPR-corrected control lines. We show that these variants, while both causing LCA7, produce unique transcriptional changes in human photoreceptors. Furthermore, the K88Q variant causes aberrant chromatin accessibility at sites typically bound by non-photoreceptor retinal transcription factors, indicating a partial derangement of normal retinal cell fate programming. This work demonstrates the gene regulatory mechanisms of pathogenicity of two disease-causing CRX variants in human retinal cells.

title: Cells heal themselves: gene-edited hematopoietic stem cells restore frataxin deficiency in multiple organs.
authors: Osborne, Lucy R
abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a triplet repeat expansion disorder with multisystem, progressive symptoms caused by reduced frataxin protein levels and compromised mitochondrial function. Restoration of frataxin protein is a focus of clinical trials involving adeno-associated viral vectors, but substantial barriers exist because of the immune response they elicit. In this issue of the JCI, Sivakumar et al. harnessed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of endogenous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to excise the frataxin gene (FXN) repeat expansion ex vivo, followed by autologous transplantation. A single, systemic infusion of corrected HSPCs resulted in long-term engraftment and sustained multiorgan benefit in a humanized mouse model of FRDA. This improvement in brain, cardiac, and pancreatic symptoms, mediated by myeloid progeny of the engrafted stem cells, provides strong support for the potential effectiveness of this approach in humans and bypasses the need to correct the FXN deficiency in the affected tissue and cells directly.

title: Edited HSPCs rescue frataxin deficiency and inflammation-driven multisystemic pathology in Friedreich's ataxia mice.
authors: Sivakumar, Anusha; Corl, Alexis N; Munoz, Keneth Jordan; Arumugam, Subhashini; Gunes, Betul B; Solis, Angelyn B; Murthy, Rishika; El-Hachem, Lilas Rony; Pizzo, Donald P; Blair, Ian A; Rojsajjakul, Teerapat; Mesaros, Clementina; Wan, Xinlong; Rainaldi, Joseph N; Badell-Grau, Rafael A; Khare, Veenita; Thai, Kevin Eric; Biederman, Kavya; Cherqui, Stephanie
abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a multisystemic neurodegenerative disorder caused by GAA repeat expansion in intron 1 of frataxin (FXN), resulting in FXN deficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction. Current therapies do not correct the underlying genetic defect. Here, we demonstrate that ex vivo CRISPR/Cas9 excision of the GAA expansion in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) provides durable, systemic therapy for FRDA. A single infusion of gene-edited Sca1+ HSPCs, mPPL-001, into myeloablative, humanized YG8JR mice resulted in long-term engraftment of donor-derived cells across hematopoietic and FRDA-affected tissues. mPPL-001 increased FXN expression and corrected multiple key pathogenic drivers of FRDA, including mitochondrial stress, microglial and macrophage activation, and inflammatory signaling. These coordinated effects improved motor functions, preserved cerebellar architecture, mitigated cardiac pathology, and promoted survival of insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. Collectively, these findings establish FXN-edited autologous HSPCs as a one-time, disease-modifying therapy for FRDA and support advancement toward a first-in-human trial.

title: Gene therapy for non-obstructive azoospermia: therapeutic avenues and translational pathway to clinical application.
authors: Jiang, Man-Xi; Jing, Tao; Feng, Huai L; Zhu, Yan
abstract: Non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) represents the most severe male infertility. Although microsurgical testicular sperm extraction combined with intracytoplasmic sperm injection offers opportunities, approximately 50% of NOA patients still fail to obtain sperm for clinical treatments. Fortunately, the emergence of precision medicine, particularly advances in gene therapy, has opened new therapeutic avenues for NOA in preclinical studies, demonstrating proof-of-concept in animal models. This review examines current progress in NOA gene therapy. Firstly, three principal therapeutic strategies: lipid nanoparticle-mediated mRNA delivery for transient protein replacement, CRISPR-based gene editing for permanent correction, and stem cell-based approaches combined with genetic modification are comparatively analyzed. Subsequently, particular emphasis is placed on recent breakthroughs in testicular mRNA delivery that have successfully restored spermatogenesis in NOA mouse models, resulting in viable offspring. Furthermore, the delivery technologies including adeno-associated viral vectors, and non-viral methods are critically evaluated to assess their respective advantages, limitations, and suitability for different testicular cell types. The review also addresses critical safety considerations, such as off-target effects, germline transmission risks, and epigenetic consequences. Finally, we discuss the translational roadmap toward clinical application, and how the obstacles including delivery optimization, long-term safety validation, and the regulatory pathways to affect the transition from preclinical proof-of-concept to first-in-human trials.

title: Generation of lachrymatory factor synthase-suppressed onion (Allium cepa L.) by Agrobacterium-mediated gene transfer for CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.
authors: Tamaru, Shoya; Imai, Shinsuke; Watanabe, Satoshi; Ikegai, Tatsuya; Kondo, Sachie; Igawa, Tomoko; Kamoi, Takahiro
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Lachrymatory factor, an irritating volatile compound that induces tearing, is produced when onion bulbs are cut or chopped. Lachrymatory factor synthase (LFS)-specific suppression in onion may reduce the lachrymatory effect and enhance flavor and health-functional properties. Genome editing enables precise modification of target genes in plant genomes. However, no reports targeting genes controlling onion-specific traits have been published. Therefore, we aimed to generate onion plants with reduced LFS activity via clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) genome editing. METHODS: Calli induced from primary roots were transformed with Agrobacterium tumefaciens carrying expression cassettes for CRISPR/Cas9, guide RNA, green fluorescent protein (GFP), and hygromycin resistance; callus lines with a high frequency of stable GFP expression were selected as "elite callus lines" suitable for transformation. Cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS), heteroduplex mobility assay (HMA), and Sanger sequencing confirmed mutations introduced into the LFS gene, and plants were regenerated from the confirmed LFS-edited callus lines. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: The LFS enzyme activity was lower in the leaves and bulbs of the LFS-edited plants than in those of control plants, while the LFS-edited plants exhibited severe growth abnormalities and failed to set seed, possibly due to long-term culturing to maintain the elite callus line. The present study demonstrates the feasibility of onion genome editing to modify a specific onion trait, namely, LFS activity. Our findings provide a basis for further development toward the ultimate goal of producing tear-free onions with enhanced health-functional properties.

title: Starch characteristics distinguish malt from non-malt barley and can be modulated via SBEIIb promoter editing.
authors: Li, Mengdi; He, Peixin; Cai, Kangfeng; Yao, Jie; Huang, Danyin; Zhang, Guoping; Ye, Lingzhen
abstract: Barley is classified as malt or non-malt barley according to its end use, yet the role of starch characteristics in determining malt quality remains poorly understood. In this study, we systematically compared starch content, composition, granule structure, and thermal properties between six malt and six non-malt barley varieties. Compared with non-malt barley, malt barley exhibited significantly higher total starch (TS) content, a lower amylose/amylopectin (Am/Ap) ratio, and a larger area of large starch granules (LSGs), features that may collectively enhance the contact surface for hydrolytic enzymes during mashing. Thermal property analysis further revealed a narrower gelatinization temperature range (R) in malt barley, indicating more synchronized and potentially more efficient starch gelatinization. Based on these distinct starch traits, we employed novel CRISPR/Cas9-mediated editing of the SBEIIb promoter to generate novel barley accessions. The resulting promoter-editing SBEIIb mutants showed a significantly reduced Am/Ap ratio, closely mimicking the altered starch profile potentially relevant to malt quality related traits of elite malt barley varieties, without affecting total starch content or grain morphology. Mechanistically, this compositional shift was associated with altered starch-associated genes expression, demonstrating that targeted promoter modification is a promising strategy for malt barley improvement while avoiding the pleiotropic defects commonly caused by coding-region knockouts. These findings reveal fundamental differences in starch properties between malt and non-malt barley and provide both genetic resources and a feasible breeding strategy for developing superior malt barley cultivars.

title: Primordial germ cell-derived macrophages as a platform to study host-pathogen interactions.
authors: Panda, Sudeepta Kumar; Dehdilani, Nima; Tellez, Guillermo; Torres, Ricardo Corona; Taylor, Lorna; Cody, Charlotte; Halabi, Samer; Wu, Zhiguang; Hawken, Rachel; Stevens, Mark P; McGrew, Mike J
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chickens play a crucial role in global food security but are susceptible to a plethora of avian and zoonotic pathogens. Understanding the contribution of pathogen and host factors during infection is important for the design of strategies to control avian diseases, but it is hampered by the lack of reliable and varied avian cell lines for in vitro studies. Macrophages are key components of the innate immune system. They serve as a first line of defense against many infectious agents and help to orchestrate adaptive immune responses. Primary macrophages derived from chickens are limited in number, short-lived in culture, and difficult to genetically manipulate. METHODS: Here, we established a protocol where chicken primordial germ cells are differentiated into macrophage-like cells, which provide a continuous in vitro supply of functionally active macrophages. RESULTS: Chicken primordial germ cell-derived macrophages (PGCdMs) had similar molecular, transcriptional, and functional characteristics to chicken bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs). PGCdMs phagocytosed and killed Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, a zoonotic pathogen commonly transmitted to humans via contaminated poultry products. Moreover, gene-edited PGCdMs were produced by applying CRISPR/Cas9 to the parental PGCs. The knockout of the major signaling molecule MyD88 in PGCdMs revealed that PGCdMs underwent rapid apoptosis after stimulation with lipopolysaccharide. CONCLUSIONS: Taken together, chicken PGCdMs will be a valuable cellular resource for studying mechanisms underlying resistance to avian and zoonotic diseases.

title: Integrated multi-omics and genome mining strategies for activating cryptic polyketide biosynthetic gene clusters in Streptomyces: an overview.
authors: Santhoshkumar, R; Mohamed, Hafid; Jemo, Martin
abstract: Beneficial microbes from soil or marine habitats are promising sources for discovery of new bioactive compounds for medicine and agriculture, largely through biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) that encode the production of complex natural products for drug and antibiotic discovery. However, most BGCs are transcriptionally silent under standard testing conditions and may require a complex, integrated approach for activation. In this review, we revisit previous approaches to activating BGCs, focusing on polyketides. We additionally discuss how integrating genome mining strategies with multi-omics integration, synthetic biology methods, and precise genome-editing tools is providing increasingly precise strategies for the discovery and engineering of polyketide-producing Streptomyces. We further discuss how to couple artificial intelligence (AI)-designed promoters could enable the production of novel compounds with improved yields, expanded chemical diversity, and enhanced industrial potential. We further examine how state-of-the-art CRISPR-Cas systems, including base editing, facilitate precise editing of high-GC-content genomes while circumventing the genome instability and Cas9-associated cellular toxicity that frequently accompany double-strand break formation in Streptomyces, and how chromatin topology rewiring dismantles transcriptional silencing. Unlike reviews that address genome mining, pathway engineering, or genome editing as separate approaches, this review presents an integrated framework linking computational BGC prediction, multi-omics validation, and precision engineering to prioritize and activate cryptic polyketide pathways in Streptomyces. We propose comprehensive computational genomics prediction approaches and integrate them with experimental validation through promoter engineering, transcription factor decoys, and chassis strain optimization, highlighting how these methods and tools are advancing the field from descriptive BGC catalogs to scalable, predictive models for next-generation drug discovery. Future efforts to couple AI-generated, sequence-orthogonal promoter libraries with biology-based modeling hold great promise.

title: Nanozyme-based biosensors for pathogenic microorganism detection: a mini-review.
authors: Yang, Ting; Ling, Yuting; Zhang, Enmei; Li, Jin
abstract: Nanozyme technology has surfaced as a game-changing tool in the detection of pathogenic microorganisms, serving as an appealing substitute for traditional biosensing methods. This review first highlighted the unique catalytic mechanisms of nanozymes, including peroxidase-like, catalase-like, oxidase-like, and superoxide dismutase-like activities, which are fundamental to their usefulness. Second, we explored mainstream biosensing platforms, such as colorimetric/lateral flow assays, electrochemical sensors, fluorescent/dual-modal systems, and nanozyme-CRISPR synergistic approaches. Each of these systems benefited from the stability, tunability, and cost-effectiveness of nanozymes. Third, the applications of nanozyme-based biosensors in the diagnosis of clinical pathogens, the detection of foodborne bacteria, and the monitoring of environmental microorganisms were further analyzed. Finally, the future directions of nanozyme-based biosensors were discussed to advance their clinical and industrial translation.

title: Gut microbiota-cancer crosstalk: emerging molecular targets for personalized cancer treatment- a comprehensive review.
authors: Negi, Pooja; Upreti, Arpita; Budhlakoti, Preeti; Sen, Amit Kumar; Danu, Mitali; Tewari, Sumit; Joshi, Nirmal; Chandra Joshi, Deepak
abstract: Cancer remains a major global health challenge, and growing evidence indicates that the gut microbiota plays an important role in cancer initiation, progression, metastasis, and response to treatment through complex interactions with host signaling, metabolism, and immunity. This comprehensive narrative review discusses the molecular mechanisms underlying gut microbiota-cancer crosstalk, with particular emphasis on dysbiosis, microbial metabolites, immune modulation, and microbiota-regulated oncogenic pathways, including TLR/NF-kappaB, Wnt/beta-catenin, JAK/STAT, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, and Hippo-YAP signaling. The review also examines emerging molecular targets, including microbial extracellular vesicles, bacterial small RNAs, ferroptosis-related mechanisms, and microbiota-mitochondria interactions. In addition, current microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies, such as fecal microbiota transplantation, engineered bacterial therapeutics, CRISPR-based microbiome engineering, and microbiome-informed approaches to precision oncology are discussed. Relevant peer-reviewed literature published primarily within the recent 5-year period was considered from major scientific databases and publisher platforms, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Springer, Elsevier, and MDPI. Overall, the available evidence suggests that gut microbiota represents an important component of the tumor ecosystem and may provide promising biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Integration of microbiome research with multi-omics and artificial intelligence may further support the development of personalized cancer treatment.

title: Rapid and Sensitive Detection of USP26 Cluster Variants Based on CRISPR/Cas12a.
authors: Li, Ning; Huo, Yongkun; Zhao, Yanan; Liu, Chao; Zhang, Zhe; Chen, Kaizhao; Chen, Longjun; Liu, Xiaonan; Lin, Ziyang; Sun, Ling; Jiang, Hui; Wang, Xinjie; Li, Wei
abstract: USP26 gene variants have been reported to be associated with male infertility, such as non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA), oligozoospermia, and asthenoteratozoospermia, and may be associated with altered sperm sex chromosome segregation patterns. Among the reported variants, USP26 cluster variants (c.370_371insACA/c.494 T > C/c.1423C > T) represent a frequently reported variant pattern in certain populations. Rapid and convenient detection of USP26 cluster variants may serve as a powerful tool for male infertility-associated cohorts. Here, we develop a CRISPR/Cas12a-based assay to rapid detection USP26 variants in human samples. Candidate CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) and RPA primers were screened and optimized, followed by incorporation of restriction enzymes to reduce wild-type-derived amplification interference. Using controlled artificial DNA mixtures, the assay detected mutant-template fractions down to 5% under the tested conditions. The complete workflow could be performed within 60 min using basic laboratory equipment. The results of the CRISPR/Cas12a system are consistent with Sanger sequencing in 91 male infertility research samples. Overall, our study establishes a rapid molecular detection method for detecting USP26 cluster variants and provides an alternative approach for genetic studies of male infertility-associated cohorts.

title: Pathogenicity assessment of a bicuspid aortic valve-associated ELASTIN variant using a zebrafish model.
authors: Bernard, Victor G; Theron, Alexis; Drouard, Aurelien; Avierinos, Jean-Francois; Jopling, Chris; Zaffran, Stephane; Faucherre, Adele
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is one of the most common congenital heart defects but its genetic basis remains incompletely defined. Extracellular matrix components play key roles in outflow tract (OFT) and valve development, but their contribution to BAV is not fully established. Following the analysis of a cohort of BAV patients, we identified a family harbouring a rare human ELASTIN (ELN) variant (p.Gln691X). Here, we investigated the pathogenicity of this variant using an in vivo zebrafish model. METHODS: We generated a zebrafish elna/b double knockout (KO) using an RNAless CRISPR Cas9 strategy to avoid genetic compensation. Cardiovascular morphology and function were assessed in mutant embryos. To evaluate pathogenicity of the human ELN p.Gln691X variant, mutant and control embryos were rescued by mRNA injection encoding either WT human ELN or the p.Gln691X variant. RESULTS: elna/b double KO zebrafish exhibited cardiovascular defects including OFT anomalies, reduced stroke volume and dysmorphic aortic valves, highlighting Elastin's critical role in cardiac development. We then used this model to test the ELN variant identified in the BAV family. We found that wild-type ELN mRNA was able to restore normal cardiac function and morphology, whereas the variant ELN mRNA failed to do so. DISCUSSION: Our study establishes a robust in vivo model to assess ELN variant pathogenicity and provides evidence linking ELASTIN to BAV, opening new avenues for uncovering the genetic mechanisms underlying BAV.

title: MerR-type regulator ZccR links zinc homeostasis to biofilm formation and interspecies competition in Streptococcus mutans.
authors: Pan, Yangyang; Xu, Zhaonan; Wang, Shuyu; Xu, Muxin; Dong, Haiyun; Mei, Liqin; Zhang, Keke
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Zinc is widely present in the oral microenvironment and can influence the growth of oral bacteria. ZccR is a MerR-type transcriptional regulator that controls zinc efflux in Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans), but its role in biofilm virulence and interspecies competition with oral commensals remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the role of ZccR in the formation of single-species biofilms of S. mutans and dual-species biofilms with oral commensal streptococci, and its underlying regulatory mechanisms. METHODS: We constructed an in-frame zccR knockout mutant of S. mutans. The growth curve, crystal violet staining, anthrone method, scanning electron microscopy, fluorescence in situ hybridization, and deferred antagonism assay were used to assess growth, biofilm development, dual-species biofilm composition, and interspecies competitive capacity. RNA-seq was employed to identify genome-wide transcriptional alterations, and promoter-lacZ reporter strains were constructed to confirm the transcriptional regulation mode of ZccR on zccE and on itself. RESULTS: The deletion of zccR significantly suppressed biofilm formation and water-insoluble exopolysaccharide production of S. mutans at 150 muM Zn(2+), a concentration that only modestly affected planktonic growth. In dual-species biofilms containing Streptococcus gordonii (S. gordonii), the mutant exhibited reduced oxidative stress tolerance and weaker inhibition of S. gordonii, despite upregulation of bacteriocin genes. RNA-sequencing identified 89 differentially expressed genes (67 upregulated and 22 downregulated), including downregulation of the mutanobactin cluster and FAD-dependent oxidoreductases, upregulation of iron-uptake genes, induction of HomR-tcy-linked cystine-uptake pathways, glutamine biosynthesis, and CRISPR-Cas genes, and a shift from sucrose import (scrA/msmX) toward lac-dependent lactose/galactose metabolism. Most of these shifts tracked intracellular zinc accumulation rather than direct ZccR control. Promoter-lacZ assays revealed that ZccR activates zccE and represses its own promoter, and zinc acts on these promoters through ZccR-dependent and ZccR-independent routes. CONCLUSIONS: ZccR links zinc homeostasis with biofilm formation and oral interspecies ecology of S. mutans, thus offering a future intervention point for cariogenic biofilm control.

title: Cardiac xenotransplantation: from concept to clinical reality.
authors: Abdelrehim, Ahmed A; Gray, W Hampton; Sorabella, Robert A; Broyles, Matthew G; Ghanbari, Farshad; Hughes, Charlie; Johnson, Lindsay; Padilla, Luz A
abstract: Advanced heart failure afflicts over 6 million adults in the United States alone, yet fewer than 4,000 donor hearts become available for transplantation each year. Mechanical circulatory support devices extend survival for many of these patients, but device-related complications, anatomic contraindications, and limited applicability to certain populations leave a substantial unmet need. For decades, xenotransplantation (XTx)-the transplantation of organs across species-has been proposed as a means of closing this gap. The discovery of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, improved immunosuppressive strategies, and refined preclinical models have accelerated the field at an unprecedented pace. Multi-gene-edited porcine donors now survive for more than 200 days in orthotopic non-human primate models, and two compassionate-use pig-to-human cardiac transplants at the University of Maryland (2022 and 2023) demonstrated the feasibility of clinical cardiac XTx for the first time. Parallel progress in kidney XTx has yielded the first FDA-cleared investigational new drug application and the initiation of a formal clinical trial in late 2025. In May 2026, the FDA granted clearance for the first-ever cardiac XTx clinical trial (EXPRESS), using a 10-gene-edited porcine heart. The 2026 International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation Consensus Statement now provides a structured framework for recipient selection, immunologic assessment, and outcome benchmarking in cardiac XTx. Antibody-mediated rejection remains the dominant barrier, as both clinical cases ended in xenograft failure driven by antipig antibody responses despite aggressive immunosuppression. Porcine cytomegalovirus reactivation, coagulation dysregulation, and xenograft overgrowth represent additional obstacles that demand resolution before broader clinical application. The optimal immunosuppressive regimen for human recipients has yet to be defined, and long-term zoonotic surveillance protocols require further standardization. With the first cardiac XTx clinical trial now cleared by the FDA, the field continues to face not only the remaining immunologic and virologic hurdles but also the ethical, regulatory, and equity considerations that will shape how this therapy is introduced. This review synthesizes the historical, scientific, and clinical foundations of cardiac XTx, appraises the current evidence, and outlines the path toward responsible clinical translation.

title: Precision Medicine in Sickle Cell Disease: From Molecular Pathways to Curative Strategies.
authors: Tluli, Dina; Tluli, Omar; Karen, Abdelrahman A; Abujbara, Mahd M; Sorour, Omar; Abdelhamid, Alaa; Ghith, Dahab; Yassin, Mohamed A
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a monogenic beta-globin disorder characterized by hemoglobin S polymerization, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion, yet it exhibits remarkable clinical heterogeneity. Despite advances in supportive care and disease-modifying therapies, substantial variability in severity, treatment response, and long-term outcomes persists. Therefore, this review aims to examine the biological and clinical foundations of precision medicine in SCD, emphasizing genomic modifiers, molecular pathways, and phenotype-driven therapeutic strategies. Key pathogenic pathways including hemoglobin polymerization, vascular adhesion, and inflammatory and oxidative amplification have enabled the development of targeted agents such as hydroxyurea, voxelotor, crizanlizumab, and L-glutamine, each demonstrating domain-specific targets. Pharmacogenomic insights, particularly involving fetal hemoglobin regulatory loci (e.g. BCL11A and HBS1L-MYB), further elucidate variability in disease expression and therapeutic response. Emerging curative approaches, including allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, lentiviral gene addition, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing, represent transformative applications of precision hematology. Collectively, these advances support a paradigm shift from generalized symptom management toward biologically informed, individualized care. Continued integration of genomic profiling, biomarker stratification, and equitable implementation frameworks will be essential to translate precision strategies into sustainable improvements in global SCD outcomes.

title: Cleavage Activity Adjustment of the CRISPR/Cas System for Enhanced Diagnostics.
authors: Zhao, Yining; Qiao, Panpan; Yang, Min; Chen, Ling; Zhang, Juan; Li, Genxi
abstract: The CRISPR/Cas system, known for its high precision and efficiency in genome editing, has garnered significant interest and demonstrated potential in diagnostics, owing to advantages such as sensitivity and cost-effectiveness. However, the application of the CRISPR/Cas system in diagnostics is constrained by two inherent challenges. On one hand, the sensitivity of the CRISPR/Cas system for the direct detection of low-abundance targets remains to be further improved for the demands of practical detection. On the other hand, the integration of nucleic acid amplification with the CRISPR/Cas system in one-pot assays presents difficulty of balance between target amplification and cleavage of Cas proteins. To overcome these constraints, researchers have encouragingly developed diverse strategies for precisely adjusting the cleavage activity of the CRISPR/Cas system. This review systematically summarizes advancements across six major strategies, including protein engineering, crRNA engineering, activator engineering, reporter engineering, the influence of metal ions and small molecules, and aggregation-mediated enhancement. These approaches either enhance cleavage efficiency for amplification-free, ultrasensitive detection, or temporarily suppress the cleavage activity to coordinate kinetics in integrated one-pot systems. Furthermore, future perspectives are discussed, which will contribute to the development of cleavage activity adjustment of the CRISPR/Cas system, providing insights for next-generation diagnostic technologies.

title: Beyond Viruses: Transposons and CRISPR-Programmable Nonviral Systems for Genome Engineering.
authors: Singh, Satnam; Panchal, Omkar Vikram; Ivics, Zoltan
abstract: Human gene therapy has been transformed by repurposing mobile genetic elements as tools for efficient gene delivery and precise genome modification. Viruses, transposons, and retrotransposons mobilize genetic material through distinct mechanisms with distinct advantages for genome engineering platforms with therapeutic potential. This review describes the mechanisms, performance characteristics, and translational relevance of nonviral methods of gene transfer and genome engineering, with emphasis on engineered systems such as the Sleeping Beauty (SB) and piggyBac (PB) DNA transposons, R2 retrotransposon-based platforms, CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs), and prime editing (PE). Clinical trials using both SB- and PB-engineered cells have shown feasibility by demonstrating sustained therapeutic effect through stable transgene integration, such as CD19-directed CAR-T cell therapy for hematological malignancies. These transposon-based vectors enable robust gene transfer for cell engineering, but are fairly promiscuous with respect to where in the genome they insert their genetic cargo. On the contrary, R2-derived systems and CASTs represent promising technologies for programmable insertion, but are still under preclinical development. CRISPR-based PE provides a distinct route to precise sequence correction without double-strand breaks and is particularly attractive for the correction of monogenic disorders. Taken together, these technologies define a continuum from natural genome mobility to clinically relevant genome engineering. Continued optimization of delivery, targeting, and editing fidelity will determine how rapidly these approaches move from experimental innovation into routine clinical use.

title: Integrated Antigen-DNA Co-Detection Using Digital Microfluidics for Improving Diagnostic Accuracy in POCT Analysis.
authors: Chai, Fengli; Li, Fenggang; Zhang, Jiangjiang; Li, Zheng; Zhai, Jianzhao; Ying, Binwu; Zhang, Shuailong; Jiang, Xingyu
abstract: Simultaneous detection of protein and nucleic acid (NA) provides complementary information essential for accurate analysis of complex samples. Conventional approaches for the analysis of protein and NA typically rely on separate workflows and instruments, limiting the reliability of point-of-care testing. Here, we present a digital microfluidics-based dual-mode molecular assay for simultaneous detection of both protein and NA from the same microscale sample. The protein is captured by a gold nanoparticle-antibody conjugate, while NA is enriched by magnetic beads. Magnetic manipulation separates the protein-containing fraction from NA, enabling separate analysis of the two molecular classes within an automated workflow. By integrating the analysis of protein and NA, the platform enables more accurate analysis than either modality alone. In 56 clinical samples, the combined analysis of hepatitis B surface antigen and DNA reduces the false-negative rate to 1.79%, compared with 12.5% for HBsAg alone. In food safety assays, simultaneous detection of Staphylococcus aureus-associated toxins and PMA-treated bacterial NA provides information not only on protein-based toxins, but also the presence and viability of bacteria within milk. This automated DMF-based dual-mode molecular assay provides a highly integrated strategy for multimodal POCT and public health risk assessment.

title: CRISPR-Scan: Cas13a Mismatch Tolerance Enabled Ultra-Multiplexed Detection of Same-Site Indels in Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
authors: Bai, Linlin; Wang, Bei; Shi, Mingmin; Liu, Dianwei; Ji, Huimin; Wang, Ting; Wang, Ziwei; Guo, Kaiming; Dou, Xinyang; Qian, Chunyan; Zhang, Fang; Wang, Yongming; Mao, Hongju; Wang, Rui
abstract: Detection of gene mutations related to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is crucial for its early diagnosis, personalized treatment, and recurrence monitoring. However, accurate detection of diverse mutations occurring at the same locus remains technically challenging. The CRISPR/Cas system, with its unique programmable nucleic acid recognition capabilities, provides a promising solution. Here, we elucidated that CRISPR/LwaCas13a is tolerant to consecutive substitutions but highly sensitive to insertions or deletions (indels) at specific positions of the spacer sequence, enabling rational CRISPR RNA (crRNA) design for multiplex detection of same-site indels. Guided by these principles, we achieved effective detection of ultra-multiplex nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) c.863_864 4-bp insertions with a single crRNA, while maintaining specificity against the wild-type transcripts. We further established a one-pot CRISPR system, CRISPR-Scan, by integrating recombinase polymerase amplification with LwaCas13a cleavage. CRISPR-Scan enabled detection of mutations in backgrounds as low as 0.01%. In clinical validation, it identified NPM1 mutations in 43 of 120 AML patients, consistent with next-generation sequencing (NGS). Continuous monitoring of four AML patients indicated early recurrence with higher sensitivity than first-generation sequencing (FGS) and full concordance with NGS. A microfluidic chip and portable device further facilitate accurate AML mutation detection. This platform offers an efficient and convenient approach for early AML diagnosis and measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring.

title: CRISPR-backpacked macrophages for immune activation against bone metastasis.
authors: Luo, Wen; Feng, Shujun; Wang, Yufei; Gu, Junhui; Yang, Jingjing; Jiang, Dan; He, Bangshun; Yin, Yi; Song, Yujun

title: Restoration of infectivity-virulence and toxin biosynthesis in Botrytis cinerea B459 via upstream-targeted marker-free CRISPR/Cas9 editing of the transcription factor Bcin04g03490.
authors: Coca-Ruiz, Victor; Saborido-Torres, David; Malvestiti, Michele C; van Kan, Jan A L; Benito, Ernesto P; Aleu, Josefina; Collado, Isidro G
abstract: Botrytis cinerea is a polyphagous fungal pathogen affecting a wide range of ornamental and agricultural crops. Previous studies on natural populations have revealed substantial intraspecific morphological, physiological, and genetic diversity. The field isolate B459 exhibits a distinctive mycelial phenotype, characterized by the lack of sporulation and sclerotia formation, and is unable to infect Vitis vinifera or Phaseolus vulgaris leaves, gerbera petals and tomato fruits. Genetic analysis traced these phenotypes to a mutation in the transcription factor gene Bcin04g03490, introducing a premature stop codon and resulting in a truncated protein. To further investigate the function of Bcin04g03490, CRISPR/Cas9-based strategies were employed to generate B459 transformants either carrying a functional B05.10 allele under the control of the constitutive olicC promoter from Aspergillus nidulans integrated at the niaD locus, or repaired at the endogenous locus through a marker-free approach involving targeted cleavage upstream of the repair template. In both cases, restoration of sporulation and pathogenicity was observed. Notably, complemented and repaired strains also recovered the toxin profile characteristic of the reference aggressive B05.10 isolate, including the production of botrydial (sesquiterpene) and botcinins (polyketides), indicating reactivation of key secondary metabolism pathways. These findings extend the functional scope of Bcin04g03490, demonstrating that it controls developmental processes, pathogenicity, and secondary metabolism pathways critical for virulence. Furthermore, this work provides a proof-of-concept for long-range homology-directed repair in B. cinerea at the Bcin04g03490 locus, offering valuable methodological insights for marker-free genome editing in filamentous fungi.

title: Zein-based hybrid nanocarriers for non-viral gene delivery: A review.
authors: Alsinglawi, Dua; Moursy, Enass Serry; Kasurka, Bilgesu; Al-Quraishi, Zainab; Ho, Vanessa Gi San; Dufes, Christine
abstract: Gene therapy and RNA-based therapeutics are increasingly limited by the challenge of delivering fragile, anionic nucleic acids to the correct intracellular compartment. Zein, the principal maize prolamin, has attracted interest as a biodegradable, self-assembling carrier that can protect cargo and be combined with polymeric, lipidic, targeted and biomimetic components. This review critically evaluates zein-based systems for plasmid DNA, siRNA, antisense oligonucleotides and related nucleic-acid cargos. Native zein is best regarded as a protective and sustained-release matrix rather than a stand-alone high-efficiency transfection vector. In contrast, hybrid systems can add nucleic-acid condensation, colloidal stabilization, targeting and intracellular-trafficking functions through components such as chitosan, polyethylenimine, dendritic poly(l-lysine), lipids and targeting ligands. Direct evidence of endosomal escape remains limited, with only one reviewed study providing imaging evidence consistent with improved lysosomal escape. Cargo-specific evidence is strongest for plasmid DNA, with functional proof-of-concept also reported for selected siRNA and antisense oligonucleotide systems, whereas robust mRNA translation and CRISPR genome editing have not yet been demonstrated with zein-based carriers. The translational rationale for zein lies not in superior intrinsic transfection efficiency, but in route-specific protection, sustained release, hydrophobic drug co-loading and use as a biodegradable scaffold within multifunctional hybrids. Zein-based gene delivery remains preclinical and requires stronger mechanistic, cargo-specific and route-specific validation.

title: Engineering the microbial architects: a genetic revolution in bio-electrochemical hydrogen production.
authors: Kumar, Pankaj; Sharma, Stuti; Sakshi; Rana, Abhishek; Vaidya, Manisha; Singh, Ashish Kumar Lakhveer
abstract: Microorganisms, endowed with extraordinary metabolic versatility and environmental adaptability, represent a transformative frontier for addressing global sustainability imperatives. Engineering microbial systems through regulatory network rewiring and synthetic biology-driven functional augmentation substantially amplifies their biotechnological utility. Herein, we review the convergence of synthetic biology, bio-electrocatalysis, and reactor engineering as an integrated framework for sustainable biohydrogen production. Comparative analysis with conventional hydrogen generation strategies underscores the superiority of bioelectrochemical systems (BESs), which simultaneously enable wastewater valorisation and clean hydrogen production through microbially driven electron transfer cascades. Moreover, the mechanistic electron generation-to-hydrogen conversion continuum highlights the indispensable dominance of biotic catalysis. Furthermore, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated multiplex genome editing is examined as a precision tool surpassing traditional mutagenesis approaches for pathway optimisation. Key electrogenic taxa, their electrochemical interfaces and influences within BESs architectures, prevailing technological bottlenecks in scalability, techno-economic feasibilitites and forward-looking strategies toward wholly biological, scalable hydrogen production systems are critically featured.

title: Suppression of plant immune responses enhances Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana.
authors: Kang, Yu; Xie, Fen; Bai, Ge; Zhao, Jianguo; Zhang, Yifeng; Feng, Yang; Fu, Yaning; Wang, Aping; Zhang, Giping
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana is widely used for recombinant protein production and gene-function studies. However, agroinfiltration can activate host stress and defense responses, thereby limiting heterologous protein accumulation. To distinguish Agrobacterium-associated transcriptional responses from effects of the infiltration procedure, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) using an infection group (GV3101 carrying empty p1300), a buffer-only mock-infiltration group (Mock), and untreated wild-type (WT) plants. Relative to the mock group, the infection group contained 3529 upregulated and 2487 downregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with enrichment of defense- and stress-associated pathways, including "response to stress," "plant-pathogen interaction," and "plant MAPK signaling pathway". Tobacco rattle virus (TRV)-based virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of selected candidates showed that silencing the ERF transcription factor PTI6 (pathogenesis-related genes transcriptional activator PTI6) increased GFP accumulation, and combined silencing of PTI5 and PTI6 produced a stronger effect than either single knockdown. Independent genetic testing using an eds1 CRISPR mutant further showed that loss of EDS1 (enhanced disease susceptibility 1) markedly enhanced transient expression of both GFP and GP3L-Flag, supporting a suppressive role of EDS1-associated immune signaling in agroinfiltration-mediated transient expression. In addition, stable NahG-Myc transgenic N. benthamiana lines derived from independent transformation events showed enhanced GFP accumulation, whereas HOS15 (high expression of osmotic stress-induced gene 15)-Flag lines did not improve transient expression under our conditions. Together, these results indicate that host immune responses can constrain transient expression and identify EDS1, PTI5/PTI6, and salicylic acid (SA)-related signaling as useful genetic targets for improving N. benthamiana as a transient expression chassis.

title: The neuropathy-causing GARS1(∆ETAQ) mutation drives pathology in subsets of motor and sensory neurons in mice.
authors: Simkin, Rebecca L; Paulo-Ramos, Aurelie; Lang, Qiuhan; Rhymes, Elena R; Surana, Sunaina; Villarroel-Campos, David; Snape, Louisa; Liu, Sijiang; Bellanti, Roberto; Veleva, Elena; Drotsevitch, Vlada; Swann, Owen; Heslegrave, Amanda; Zetterberg, Henrik; Lunn, Michael P; Burgess, Robert W; Sleigh, James N
abstract: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2D (CMT2D) results from gain-of-function mutations in GARS1, which encodes glycyl-tRNA synthetase (GlyRS), the enzyme responsible for charging transfer RNA (tRNA) with glycine. There are several CMT2D mouse models, but Gars(∆ETAQ/+) is the only one that bears a patient-sourced mutation. Created using CRISPR/Cas9 to model a 12-nucleotide de novo GARS1 deletion identified in an unusually severe CMT2D patient, Gars(∆ETAQ/+) mice have previously been shown to display several neuromuscular phenotypes: motor axon loss, denervated neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) and reduced muscle function. Here, we extend these analyses to provide a more comprehensive understanding of both motor and sensory nerve deficits across hind- and fore-limbs. At 3 months, Gars(∆ETAQ/+) mice possess sex-independent alterations in the levels of neuropathy biomarkers - including decreased NfL and increased periaxin - alongside reduced muscle endurance and strength, and impairments in the sensory modalities of mechanosensation, proprioception and nociception. Underpinning these dysfunctions, we identified site-specific defects comprising altered sensory neuron populations, muscle spindle loss, reduced motor neuron size, disrupted NMJ innervation and maturation, and reduced axonal transport of signalling endosomes in vivo. Together, these experiments show that Gars(∆ETAQ/+) mice display robust and selective peripheral nerve pathology that manifests in a general length-dependent fashion, priming this CMT2D allele for testing treatments and evaluating mechanisms underlying peripheral nerve vulnerability.

title: Dysregulated Retinal DPP10 Expression with Single Cell-based Next Genomic Sequencing Profiling in X-linked Juvenile Retinoschisis.
authors: Cheng, Han-Ping; Ching, Lo-Jei; Wang, Chia-Hao; Mahardhika, Muhammad Reza Putra; Ou-Yang, Huan; Lee, Chun-Yuan; Chang, Yuh-Lih; Tsai, Der-Chong; Hsu, Chih-Chien; Hwang, De-Kuang; Chiou, Shih-Hwa; Chen, Shih-Jen; Lin, Tai-Chi; Yang, Yi-Ping
abstract: X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) is a hereditary retinal dystrophy resulting from mutations in the retinoschisin (RS1) gene, which lead to progressive structural abnormalities in the retina and consequent visual impairment. Despite this, the molecular mechanisms through which RS1 mutations induce cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling during disease progression remain inadequately elucidated. To delineate transcriptional changes associated with RS1 mutations, we conducted single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered Rs1(emR209C) knock-in mouse model. Integrative analysis with the Mouse Retina Cell Atlas demonstrated that rod photoreceptors exhibited the most significant transcriptional dysregulation among retinal cell types. Notably, dipeptidyl peptidase-like protein 10 (DPP10) was progressively and markedly upregulated, predominantly within photoreceptors, as the disease advanced. These findings were corroborated by immunofluorescence staining, quantitative PCR, and western blot analyses, which confirmed increased retinal DPP10 expression concurrent with a gradual decline in RS1 levels. To explore the functional implications of DPP10 dysregulation, we developed Y79 retinal cell models expressing either wild-type RS1 or the XLRS-associated RS1 R209C variant. Cells expressing the RS1 R209C mutation exhibited elevated DPP10 expression alongside reduced viability. Crucially, siRNA-mediated knockdown of DPP10 partially rescued cell viability and was associated with reduced GRP78/BiP expression in RS1 R209C-expressing cells, supporting potential functional relevance between DPP10 upregulation and mutant RS1-induced cellular stress. Furthermore, circulating DPP10 concentrations were significantly increased in patients with XLRS compared to control subjects. Collectively, these results identify DPP10 as a molecular alteration associated with RS1 mutation and suggest its potential as a circulating biomarker candidate for XLRS.

title: Unified hybrid RNA-regulated CRISPR diagnostic for concurrent Mycobacterium tuberculosis detection and rifampicin resistance profiling.
authors: Yang, Xinggui; Zeng, Xiaoyan; Qi, Guorong; Wang, Jiangfei; Wei, Xiaoyu; Hu, Qianfang; Huang, Junfei; Chen, Yijiang; Xie, Yaxing; Li, Ying; Zhong, Yuting; Li, Shijun; Yang, Xiaolan
abstract: CRISPR-based nucleic acid detection is challenged by protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) dependency, amplicon consumption and single-tube multiplexing barriers, and poor discrimination of single-nucleotide variations (SNVs). These limitations are particularly acute in detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) and rifampicin (RIF) resistance mutations for tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics. Herein, we devised TB-SCANER, a broad-spectrum, one-pot CRISPR-Cas12a diagnostic platform for MTB detection and RIF resistance profiling. The assay employs two unlocking single-stranded RNAs (uLsRNAs) transcribed from RPA products to unlock four cis-cleavage-locked CRISPR-Cas12a systems via distinct locking single-stranded RNAs (LsRNAs), establishing a two-to-four hybrid logic: one uLsRNA carries a single unlocking module for the M channel (targeting mpb64 gene), whereas the other contains three tandem modules engaging LsRNAs for subregions R1, R2, R3 within rpoB gene. With genomic DNA, detection limits are 50 fg/reaction ( approximately 10 copies) for mpb64 and 500 fg/reaction ( approximately 100 copies) for rpoB. The assay reliably identified clinically dominant rpoB mutations (Leu511Pro, Asp516Gly, His526Tyr, Ser531Leu) and low-prevalence variants (Ser522Met, His526Arg, Leu533Pro). For cultured isolates, TB-SCANER was 100% concordant with Sanger sequencing for RIF resistance mutation profiling; in clinical samples, it matched Xpert for MTB detection (100%), outperformed culture sensitivity (100% vs. 93.8%), and was fully concordant with Sanger sequencing for RIF resistance, eliminating Xpert's false-positive while identifying all resistant strains. Collectively, TB-SCANER is a rapid, accurate, low-cost, one-pot CRISPR diagnostic that overcomes multiplexing barriers, enabling concurrent MTB detection and RIF resistance profiling particularly in resource-limited settings, and features built-in adaptability to other pathogens.

title: Generation of a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic control iPSC line (NIMHi001-A-1) from a Parkinson's disease Patient-Derived iPSC line carrying the LRRK2 I1371V mutation.
authors: Banerjee, Roon; Singh, Khushboo; Gogoi, Ujaswini; Ramprasad, Vedam; Pasricha, Gunisha; Nair, Jiny; Kumari, Riyanka; Yadav, Ravi; Kamble, Nitish; Holla, Vikram; Pal, Pramod Kumar; Datta, Indrani
abstract: We report NIMHi001-A-1, a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic iPSC line derived from a patient line carrying a heterozygous LRRK2 missense mutation GRCh38 chr12:g.40308618A > G [(MANE transcript NM_198578.4:c.4111A > G); p.Ile1371Val] associated with familial Parkinson's disease. Sanger sequencing confirmed successful correction. The line retained iPSC morphology and expressed pluripotency markers (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2, TRA-1-60, SSEA4) by immunofluorescence, gene expression analysis, and flow cytometry. Normal karyotype (46, XY) and complete genetic identity with the parental line were established by STR profiling. No off-target modifications were detected. The line demonstrated trilineage differentiation potential and tested negative for mycoplasma, providing an isogenic platform to investigate LRRK2 I1371V-specific pathomechanisms and evaluate therapeutic strategies.

title: Pooled Screening of Cancer Cell Lines Identifies Vulnerability to Polyunsaturated Fatty-Acid-Induced Ferroptosis.
authors: Pan, Zijian; Han, Jingrong Regina; Naowarojna, Nathchar; Graham, Emily T; Roth, Jennifer A; Wang, Wenyu; Xie, Guanglei; Wang, Xi; Li, Haoxin; Zou, Yilong
abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are essential nutrients supporting numerous cellular processes in normal and neoplastic cells, yet PUFA-containing phospholipids predispose cells to ferroptosis. How cancer cells from various lineages or genetic backgrounds proliferate in the presence of PUFA remains poorly understood. Here, by systematically profiling various fatty acids using a barcoded and pooled cancer cell line library, we show that a subset of cell lines is sensitive to PUFA treatment at concentrations comparable to physiological levels. We demonstrate that PUFA treatment alone is sufficient to induce ferroptosis in these cell lines that are also vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition. By correlating patterns of PUFA sensitivity with cancer cell line features including basal mRNA transcript levels, we show that PUFA sensitivity is positively associated with fatty acid binding protein 1 (FABP1) expression. Additionally, by profiling a diverse collection of fatty acids and analogs, we find that ferroptosis in cancer cells can be effectively induced by conjugated linolenic acids, in addition to PUFAs containing 1,4-pentadiene groups. Genome-wide CRISPR modifier screens in the PUFA-sensitive ES2 cells reveal a pro-ferroptosis pathway defined by enzymes that convert PUFAs to membrane-associated phospholipids, and an anti-ferroptosis pathway that segregates PUFAs by delivering them to lipid droplets. Together, we present the first comprehensive data set of PUFA-induced ferroptosis sensitivity in a collection of 554 cell lines from 19 primary lineages and suggest a potential therapeutic avenue to induce tumor cell ferroptosis using dietary metabolites.
