title: Integrative multi-omics reveals CUL4B as a modulator of macrophage pyroptosis and innate defense against Staphylococcus aureus.
authors: Askarian, Fatemeh; Sun, Daniel; Tat, Jasmine; Sorrentino, James T; Kousha, Armin; Sauceda, Consuelo; Yendluri, Siri; Yan, Yu; Yau, Ka Pui Sharon; Masson, Helen; Wozniak, Jacob; Pettersen, Kristin; Chavarria, Natalie; McLaren, Ella; Gage, Hunter; Hoffman, Alexandria; Davis, Stanley; Tsai, Chih-Ming; Monk, Jonathan; Meier, Angela; Sakoulas, George; Mollnes, Tom Eirik; Vaaje-Kolstad, Gustav; Cornax, Ingrid; Zhou, Pengbo; Johannessen, Mona; Gonzalez, David J; Lewis, Nathan E; Nizet, Victor
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (SA) causes a broad range of invasive human diseases, increasingly complicated by antibiotic resistance. Macrophages (MPhi) play a central role in innate immunity, yet key aspects of their interaction with SA remain incompletely understood because of the pathogen's diverse immune evasion strategies. Using multi-omics and systems-level analytics, we identified the E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin 4B (CUL4B) as a host factor that modulates MPhi responses to SA infection. CRISPR-mediated deletion of CUL4B in human THP-1 MPhi enhanced intracellular bacterial killing, reduced cell death, decreased caspase-1 activation, and lowered interleukin-1beta production, consistent with altered inflammasome signaling. In a murine methicillin-resistant SA (MRSA) pneumonia model, CUL4B deficiency improved pulmonary bacterial clearance, reduced bacteremia, and decreased inflammatory tissue injury. Whole-lung and serum proteomics further revealed increased antimicrobial protein abundance and reduced markers of inflammatory damage. Together, these findings identify CUL4B as a regulator of MPhi inflammatory responses during MRSA infection and suggest a potential host-directed pathway that could be leveraged to improve outcomes against this major pathogen.

title: Modeling patient variants of Cnot1 and Cdc42bpb results in distinct forms of congenital diaphragmatic hernia in mice.
authors: Bogenschutz, Eric L; Carpenter, Cynthia; Wong, Ameleen; Palmer, Kristina; Mehta, Aalekh S; Ledermann, Yannick; Heffner, Caleb; Snow, Kathy J; Bult, Carol; Shen, Yufeng; Donahoe, Patricia K; Rowbotham, Samuel P; High, Frances A; Chung, Wendy K; Murray, Stephen A
abstract: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a severe congenital anomaly characterized by impairment of both diaphragm and lung development in utero. CDH presents as a spectrum of forms and severities, with diaphragm defects arising in the dorsal/posterior region typically correlating with more severe pulmonary disease and higher risk of mortality than those appearing in ventral/anterior regions. The genetic etiology underlying CDH is complex, with many implicated genes showing variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance in both human patients and mouse models. Here we present in vivo validation of two genes previously unassociated with CDH: the CDC42-interacting kinase CDC42BPB; and CNOT1, a scaffolding protein of the CCR4-NOT protein complex, critical for mRNA regulation through modifications such as deadenylation. Each gene was found to have a damaging, de novo missense variant in a recent large-scale CDH patient sequencing screen. Loss of Cdc42bpb leads to ventral diaphragmatic hernias, heart septal defects, and minor lung epithelial differentiation defects in mouse embryos. Installation of the orthologous patient-specific missense variant through CRISPR/Cas9 editing leads to less severe ventral diaphragm defects. Mouse embryos with either one or two copies of the orthologous Cnot1 variant, c.1867C > T (p.R623W), develop dorsal diaphragmatic hernias with low (<50%) penetrance, and mutants showed alterations in mRNA isoform expression consistent with the molecular role of Cnot1 in RNA splicing. These results underscore the power of in vivo functional modeling to validate genes and patient-specific variants uncovered by patient sequencing, reveal two previously unrecognized genetic causes of CDH, and highlight the heterogeneity of different patient anatomic presentations.

title: Peptide signaling in the paraventricular thalamus is essential for disrupted adult reward behaviors consequent to early-life adversity.
authors: Floriou-Servou, Amalia; Weber, Ryan; Chen, Yuncai; Tetzlaff, Madison R; Kooiker, Cassandra L; Birnie, Matthew T; Short, Annabel K; Roberts, Roshae C; Liang, Heidi Y; Gantuz, Magdalena; Hardy, Mason; Justice, Nicholas; Mortazavi, Ali; Baram, Tallie Z
abstract: Early-life adversity (ELA) is strongly linked to emotional disorders characterized by dysregulated reward behaviors. However, the mechanisms by which transient neonatal experiences generate enduring, sex-specific alterations in brain function remain unresolved. Paraventricular thalamus (PVT) neurons are selectively activated during ELA and contribute to disrupted adult reward behaviors. Here, we explore the molecular mechanisms behind these enduring, sex-specific disruptions. Combining activity-dependent genetic labeling with translating ribosome affinity purification, we find distinct gene translation programs in ELA and control mice of both sexes. Notably, the receptor for the neuropeptide corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor type 1 (Crhr1), is differentially expressed across rearing and sex in response to reward. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Crhr1 deletion exclusively in early-life-activated PVT neurons normalizes reward behaviors in both male and female adult ELA mice. Thus, CRHR1 signaling in adult PVT neurons activated by ELA is a required and potentially targetable mechanism underlying sex-specific, ELA-induced disruptions of reward behaviors.

title: RNA-Based Therapies for Lipoprotein(a) Reduction: Antisense Oligonucleotides, Small Interfering RNAs, and Emerging Platforms.
authors: Parcha, Vibhu; Bittner, Vera A
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined, and causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and calcific aortic valve stenosis. Elevated Lp(a) affects approximately 20% of the global population and is not meaningfully modified by lifestyle intervention or existing lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy. This review summarizes the biology of Lp(a) as a therapeutic target, evaluates the efficacy of currently available lipid-lowering agents against this target, and describes the mechanistic principles, clinical evidence, and unresolved questions associated with RNA-based and emerging small-molecule and gene-editing approaches to Lp(a) reduction. RECENT FINDINGS: Four RNA-directed agents targeting hepatic apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)] synthesis have entered phase 2/3 development. This includes pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), and olpasiran, zerlasiran, and lepodisiran, which are N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). Phase 2 data demonstrate Lp(a) reductions ranging from 79% to approximately 97% on a placebo-adjusted basis, approaching the practical limit of apo(a) suppression, with favorable short-term safety profiles. A fifth, structurally distinct siRNA conjugated with GalNAc at both strand termini has recently completed first-in-human testing, sustaining reductions up to 97% through 48 weeks after a single dose without injection-site reactions. Recently, the topline results of phase 3 Lp(a) HORIZON (pelacarsen) were released and demonstrate a substantial Lp(a) reduction without meeting the trial's primary composite cardiovascular endpoint. Two further outcomes trials, OCEAN(a)-Outcomes (olpasiran) and ACCLAIM-Lp(a) (lepodisiran), remain ongoing. An oral small molecule, muvalaplin, achieved comparable reductions in phase 2 testing. Lastly, early non-human primate data, together with a completed phase 1 trial of an analogous CRISPR-Cas9 construct targeting a related hepatic lipid gene, support the feasibility of a CRISPR-Cas9-based gene-editing approach capable of durable apo(a) suppression from a single administration. The pharmacology of Lp(a) suppression is now well characterized across three distinct therapeutic modalities. Whether the magnitude of biochemical reduction observed translates into a meaningful and safe reduction in cardiovascular events across different populations remains undetermined and will be addressed by the ongoing outcomes trials.

title: HNF4-alpha Knockout Promotes HepG2 Cell Migration and Reduces Mitochondrial Membrane Potential under Hypoxic Conditions.
authors: Saleh, Tareq; Ismail, Mohammad A; Surakhy, Mirvat; Nairat, Fairouz; Gharandouq, Mohammad H; Ali, Dema; Barham, Raghda; Aldiqs, Razan; Al-Abdallat, Khairallah; Zihlif, Malek; Ababneh, Nidaa A
abstract: INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVE: Hypoxia is a critical component of the tumor microenvironment contributing to metabolic reprogramming and drug resistance. Subsequently, elucidating the molecular mechanisms involved in hypoxia regulation in tumor cell models is essential. METHODS: This study used CRISPR/Cas9 to knock out hepatocyte nuclear factor 4-alpha (HNF4-alpha) and hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1-alpha) in HEPG2 cells. This study then assessed the effects of both knockouts (KO) on proliferation, migration, drug sensitivity, mitochondrial membrane stability, and gene expression in HEPG2 cells under both hypoxic and normoxic conditions. RESULTS: Our data demonstrate that HIF1-alpha KO, but not HNF4-alpha KO, sensitizes HEPG2 cells to doxorubicin under hypoxic conditions. Additionally, the KO of both HIF1-alpha and HNF4-alpha enhances cell migration, irrespective of oxygen levels. Importantly, both HIF1-alpha and HNF4-alpha are required for cellular response to hypoxia and the maintenance of mitochondrial function, as evidenced by the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential increase under hypoxia in KO cells. Microarray-based transcriptomic profiling of HEPG2 cells revealed separation between HNF4-alpha and HIF1-alpha KO cells and controls under hypoxic versus normoxic conditions, with a markedly higher number of differentially expressed genes in hypoxia (up to 5,595 genes; adjusted p < 0.05, log2FC +/-1.5). Both HNF4-alpha and HIF1-alpha contribute to hypoxia-responsive pathways, with impaired induction of key genes such as VEGFA and AK4 in KO cells, while GSEA indicated minimal effects of HNF4-alpha loss under hypoxia but pronounced metabolic pathway disruption in HIF1-alpha KO cells. Moreover, key regulators of mitochondrial function and mitophagy, including FUNDC1, MIEF1, and MIEF2, were upregulated in control hypoxic cells but not in KO cells. DISCUSSION: These findings suggest that, in this single HEPG2 cell line model, HNF4-alpha contributes to the regulation of cell migration and mitochondrial stability under hypoxic conditions. CONCLUSION: Further investigation into the role of HNF4-alpha in tumor biology is encouraged.

title: MLH1 p.His112Arg Variant Is Associated With Increased Cancer Susceptibility.
authors: Elfatih, Amal; Tout, Issam; Doha, Najwa Ahmad; Arja, Tala Abu; Mohammed, Idris; Abdelrhaman, Doua; Hasan, Waseem; Saad, Chadi; Mbarek, Hamdi; Mifsud, Borbala; Da'as, Sahar Isa
abstract: Lynch syndrome, a prevalent hereditary cancer predisposition, is frequently caused by pathogenic variants in the MutL homolog 1 (MLH1) mismatch repair gene. However, a significant proportion of MLH1 missense variants remain classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), creating clinical ambiguity. Functional validation assays in vertebrate models are crucial to assess the pathogenicity of these VUS. We previously reported the rare MLH1 NM_000249.4:c.335A>G (p.His112Arg) variant in individuals with cancer histories within the Qatar Genome Program. To assess its functional impact, we established the MLH1 p.His112Arg variant in the human colorectal cancer cell line, COLO205, using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Isogenic wild-type (WT) and variant-carrying cells were xenotransplanted into the zebrafish. Tumor growth was quantified via fluorescence microscopy at 24 and 72 h post-injection. Zebrafish xenografted with MLH1 p.His112Arg cells exhibited a significant increase in tumor area compared to WT. This accelerated growth was associated with a significant upregulation of the proliferation marker MKI67 in variant-carrying tumors, while cyclin D1 (CCND1) and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) (key regulators of cell cycle progression and DNA replication, respectively) expression remained unchanged, despite a tendency for increased expression. Furthermore, our functional characterization of the MLH1 p.His112Arg variant in COLO205 cells showed an enhanced proliferation capacity compared to the WT cell line, as well as increased cell viability and decreased apoptotic susceptibility when subjected to methylation-induced DNA damage. The MLH1 p.His112Arg variant confers a tumor-promoting phenotype in an in vivo zebrafish model, providing functional evidence that supports its reclassification from VUS to likely pathogenic.

title: Chemically composed Cas9 (ChemComCas9) for spatio-temporal regulation and precision genome engineering applications.
authors: Das, Pallabi; Samoi, Tuhin Baran; Maji, Basudeb
abstract: Chemically composed Cas9 (ChemComCas9) has emerged as a highly versatile CRISPR enzyme, offering tunable, on-demand, and targeted control over genome engineering functions. Despite its programmable, sequence-specific activity, uncontrolled or prolonged exposure to Cas9 can lead to severe genotoxicity, restricting its enormous clinical potential. To circumvent its non-specific and uncontrolled activities, Cas9 has been chemically modified for spatio-temporal and precision control. For developing such ChemComCas9, the WT Cas9 has been chemically modified using either its surface-exposed natural cysteine or by the installation of additional cysteine residues, or an unnatural amino acid has been incorporated for chemical modification. Such strategies include the incorporation of peptides, polymers, antibodies, stimuli-responsive moieties, and biorthogonal conjugation techniques that allow external control over Cas9 activation, localization, and activity. In addition, various short peptides have been either genetically fused or chemically conjugated for spatiotemporal regulation and probing. These approaches enable conditional activation of Cas9 in response to light, small molecules, or intracellular triggers, thereby minimizing off-target effects and increasing editing efficiency. In this review, we discuss a systematic evolution of chemically composed Cas9 (ChemComCas9) for precision genome engineering and gene therapy applications.

title: Mechanotransduction through LFA-1 controls upstream migration in the KG-1a stem cell line.
authors: Mochida, Ai; Valerio, Emily; Burkhardt, Janis K; Hammer, Daniel A
abstract: Immune cell recruitment into tissues requires cells to migrate on the endothelium while overcoming shear forces. Many extravasating cells, including T lymphocytes and hematopoietic stem cells, migrate upstream against the direction of shear flow on ICAM-1. Upstream migration has been shown to depend on intracellular signaling through Crk family adaptor proteins following engagement of lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1). Because upstream migration is an important illustration of leukocyte mechanotransduction, we sought to identify key intracellular regulators of upstream migration using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing and the KG-1a stem cell line. We made targeted deletions of molecules that function downstream of LFA-1 to regulate actin polymerization, link integrin signaling to the actin cytoskeleton, or form scaffolding complexes with Crk proteins. We found that CrkL, CasL (also known as HEF1 or NEDD9), L-plastin (LCP1) and RIAM (APBB1IP) are crucial for dynamic F-actin-rich lamellipodia and upstream migration. Although WASP (WAS), Hem1 (NCKAP1L), EVL and vinculin were found to be dispensable for upstream migration, pan-formin inhibition with SMIFH2 revealed a role for formins in upstream migration. This study illustrates the role of LFA-1 mechanotransduction in driving F-actin assembly at the leading edge to drive upstream migration.

title: CRISPR-HAWK: haplotype- and variant-aware guide design toolkit for CRISPR-Cas.
authors: Kumbara, Alisa; Tognon, Manuel; Carone, Giulia; Fontanesi, Arianna; Bombieri, Nicola; Giugno, Rosalba; Pinello, Luca
abstract: MOTIVATION: Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations. RESULTS: We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79 648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing. AVAILABILITY: CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK.

title: Biotechnological Approaches to Biofilm-Targeted Antifungal Therapy in Recurrent Vulvovaginal Candidiasis.
authors: Hassan, Nazia; Ali, Asgar
abstract: Recurrent Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (RVVC) is increasing worldwide, with biofilm persistence and antifungal resistance limiting treatment options. The combined use of antifungal treatments with antibiofilm agents has become a promising strategy. This review explores advanced therapeutic approaches, their limitations, and prospects. Overgrowth of vaginal Candida inflames the mucosa, causing itching, dryness, and whitish discharge. Biofilm formation worsens the condition, contributing to treatment failure, resistance, and recurrence. Conventional antifungal modalities are often inadequate against these multidimensional biofilm assemblies. Combining natural and synthetic antifungal agents with antibiofilm adjuncts has shown improved outcomes by targeting Candida cells within biofilms. This review compiles studies on multicomponent approaches to managing vaginal Candida infections, focusing on pan-Candida species to clarify species-specific resistance and persistence. Host factors in non-virgin women, a highly affected population, are examined alongside regional data on recurrence and treatment failure. Together, these insights highlight the microbiology of Candida biofilms, host and regional influences, and the socio-economic burden of RVVC, while emphasising the translational importance of combination therapy and biotechnology-driven innovations such as molecular docking, nanocarriers, CRISPR-based gene modulation, and engineered probiotics.

title: Structural basis of assembly-dependent activation of the MAD3-MAD4 nuclease in the Pseudomonas aeruginosa MADS defense system.
authors: Zhang, Jin; Li, Zengru; Ye, Le; Hou, Yaoyao; Liu, Ke; Min, Jinrong
abstract: The methylation-associated defense system (MADS) is a bacterial antiphage immune system that cooperates with CRISPR-Cas systems to restrict phage infection. Within MADS, the MAD3-MAD4 module has been proposed to function as an ATPase-nuclease module related to the OLD nuclease family, but the molecular basis of its assembly and function remains unknown. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, biochemical assays, and mutagenesis to elucidate the architecture and assembly mechanism of the MAD3-MAD4 complex. We found that MAD3 and MAD4 assemble into a stable 2:2 heterotetramer. Structural and biochemical analyses revealed that MAD3 alone lacks detectable ATPase activity, whereas MAD4 is insoluble when expressed alone. Assembly of the MAD3-MAD4 complex induces a conformational rearrangement in which MAD3 adopts an ATPase-competent dimeric conformation, while MAD4 is stabilized through intersubunit interactions. This heterotetrameric assembly exhibits both ATPase and DNA cleavage activities. Overall, our findings reveal the molecular basis of MAD3-MAD4 heterotetramer assembly and provide the first structural and biochemical insights into the function of the MAD3-MAD4 module within the MADS defense system.

title: Exploring tumor-derived exosomes as promising antigenic platforms: novel vaccine and immunotherapy strategies for "cold" colorectal cancer.
authors: Liu, Xiaoting; Wang, Xiaoyan
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a formidable clinical challenge, largely due to the prevalence of microsatellite-stable tumors characterized by an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME) that is resistant to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Tumor-derived exosomes (TEXs) play a paradoxical dual role in this landscape. Native TEXs actively orchestrate immune evasion by delivering immunosuppressive molecules, such as programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta), which impair cytotoxic T-cell function and promote the expansion of regulatory T cells and M2 macrophages. Conversely, TEXs possess inherent biocompatibility and naturally harbor a broad repertoire of tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, positioning them as potential cell-free platforms for cancer vaccination. Current evidence demonstrates that native TEXs establish their immunosuppressive niche primarily through the systemic PD-1/PD-L1 axis and microRNA-driven macrophage polarization. However, preclinical studies indicate that exosome engineering strategies-such as masking surface PD-L1 or loading vesicles with immune adjuvants, siRNAs, or CRISPR components-can effectively neutralize these suppressive traits and amplify antigen presentation. While clinical data in CRC remain limited, engineered TEXs exhibit strong preclinical promise for synergizing with ICIs to reprogram cold CRC into immune-responsive "hot" tumors. Advancing these early-stage therapies from the bench to the clinic will require overcoming significant translational hurdles, particularly regarding standardized isolation protocols and scalable manufacturing.

title: Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys.
authors: Zhang, Zhengjia; Han, Diangang; Wei, Qiujiang; Fu, Xuewei; Yan, Yongqing; Li, Dandan; Xin, Jige
abstract: As the non-human primate models with the closest genetic relationship to humans, laboratory monkeys are indispensable in life sciences research, drug development, and biological product evaluation. However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry-for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. The diversity, complexity, and clinically insidious nature of diseases in laboratory monkeys impose stringent demands on veterinary diagnostic capabilities. This review summarizes the current status and recent advances in mainstream veterinary diagnostic techniques applied to laboratory monkey disease surveillance. We analyze the specific applications, strengths, and limitations of molecular, immunological, imaging, and conventional microbiological methods for detecting major viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens of laboratory monkeys, covering quantitative PCR (qPCR), CRISPR-based assays, ELISA, IFA/IHC, and other established platforms. By comparing these techniques across sensitivity, specificity, cost-effectiveness, and operational feasibility, we delineate their suitability for distinct use cases: high-precision laboratory testing, large-scale colony screening, and point-of-care clinical diagnosis. Current veterinary diagnostic assays for laboratory monkeys achieve robust analytical performance. In several studies, qPCR delivers 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for B virus detection, digital PCR (dPCR) attains a limit of detection as low as 45 copies/ml for monkeypox virus; and CRISPR/Cas-based assays have demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical validation cohorts. Building on these advances, we further identify practical bottlenecks in diagnostic deployment and propose targeted countermeasures. Finally, we explore emerging trends and application prospects for point-of-care testing, multiplex pathogen detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis, which collectively support the development of accurate, efficient, and intelligent disease diagnostics for laboratory monkeys. This work aims to provide a theoretical and practical reference for clinical practice and scientific research focused on laboratory monkey disease prevention and control.

title: Programmable synthetic engineering of adaptive microbial cell factories: from amide transforming enzymes to advanced biocatalytic systems.
authors: Fatima, Syeda Warisul; Alam, Shahenvaz
abstract: Microbial cell factories integrate metabolic engineering, synthetic regulation, protein engineering, and computational design to improve catalytic performance and process robustness. Within this landscape, amide transforming enzymes provide diverse functions ranging from nitrogen metabolism and hydrolysis to covalent protein remodeling. This review examines amidases, asparaginases, glutaminases, nitrilases, nitrile hydratases, acylases, and carbamylases, with particular emphasis on microbial transglutaminase (MTGase). MTGase is distinguished by its ability to catalyze covalent epsilon-(gamma-glutamyl) lysine crosslinking through acyl transfer reactions, enabling protein stabilization, molecular assembly, immobilization, and spatial organization of catalytic systems. This review critically examines the transition from classical amide transforming enzymes toward engineered biocatalytic systems and evaluates how MTGase could be leveraged as a protein level control component in microbial cell factories. Experimental developments in MTGase production, structural and protein engineering, synthetic genetic circuits, CRISPR based regulation, metabolic control, nanobiomaterials, and spatial biocatalysis are evaluated alongside computational approaches including AlphaFold assisted structure prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, machine learning guided mutagenesis, and metabolic modeling. Emphasis is placed on experimentally validated outcomes and current limitations. Key unresolved barriers include intracellular off target crosslinking, proteostatic burden, variable crosslink stoichiometry, limited temporal control of MTGase activity, chassis dependence, and industrial scale up. Where direct evidence is lacking, prospective applications are distinguished from established capabilities and corresponding engineering strategies are proposed. Collectively, this review envisions MTGase as a controllable protein level platform for synthetic biology, while defining the evidence, limitations, and experimental requirements needed for its broader application in microbial biotechnology.

title: Advances in iron-storage protein-based MRI reporter genes: from molecular mechanisms to translational imaging applications.
authors: Li, Haoxiang; Huang, Yucun
abstract: Non-invasive monitoring of cellular and molecular events is essential for advancing precision medicine. While exogenous probes often suffer from signal dilution, iron-storage protein-based MRI reporter genes offer an alternative for longitudinal tracking, because contrast is regenerated by the cells themselves. Especially ferritin and its engineered variants have attracted growing interest due to their ability to regulate intracellular iron and generate endogenous T2/T2* contrast. This review summarizes the molecular mechanisms and design principles of iron-based MRI reporter genes, and examines recent developments including CRISPR-mediated integration and manganese-dependent "Bright Ferritin" platforms, which generate positive T1 contrast but require repeated administration of exogenous manganese. Preclinical studies have tracked cellular dynamics in vivo and monitored transgene expression after viral gene delivery, although the evidence base remains almost entirely preclinical. Nevertheless, a persistent challenge lies in generating sufficiently strong MRI contrast while maintaining the delicate balance of intracellular iron metabolism on which these reporters depend. By linking molecular design to imaging performance, this review distinguishes what has been demonstrated experimentally from what remains prospective, and identifies the quantitative and safety questions that stand between the current evidence and clinical use.

title: An FTA card-based CRISPR/Cas12a platform with isothermal amplification for portable tuberculosis diagnosis.
authors: Xing, Jiayin; Zhao, Xiangxiang; Wang, Gaojie; Ren, Shilong; Chen, Lei; Diao, Wenbin; Qu, Meihua; Chang, Zhimin; Wang, Xiaoqian; Zhao, Shihao; Zhang, Yong; Song, Ningning
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains a major global public health threat, imposing significant socioeconomic burdens. Current molecular diagnostics rely heavily on nucleic acid extraction and specialized equipment, which limits their use in resource-limited settings. We developed a rapid, sensitive platform suitable for point-of-care detection by integrating FTA cards with ERA/RT-ERA amplification and CRISPR/Cas12a, enabling direct analysis of samples without conventional nucleic acid purification. Leveraging FTA cards for efficient nucleic acid release and stable preservation, we established assays targeting IS6110, esxB, gyrB, and the RNA target ASdes. Integration of FTA-based sample processing, ERA/RT-ERA amplification, and Cas12a detection enables fast and reliable identification of nucleic acid markers. The detection limits were 12.5 pM for IS6110, 6.25 pM for esxB, 25 pM for gyrB, and 12.5 pM for ASdes. Our results showed strong concordance between endpoint fluorescence and qPCR results, demonstrating robust quantitative performance for both DNA and RNA targets. In clinical serum samples, the fluorescence readouts and lateral flow strip outputs showed strong concordance with quantitative PCR results across all four targets. Collectively, the FTA-ERA-CRISPR/Cas12a platform serves as a practical and offers a reliable approach for rapid tuberculosis diagnosis at the point of need. This integrated multiple distinct targets strategy provides a versatile framework for portable molecular diagnostics and holds promise for improving TB case detection in resource-limited settings.

title: Development and preliminary validation of an omp25-based RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a visual assay for rapid screening of brucellosis-associated Brucella DNA.
authors: Zhang, Yu; Zhang, Shuairan; Yin, Cai; Jin, Minjing; Zang, Xiaona; Wu, Yawen; Bai, Taotao; Ma, Long; Wang, Xiaoliang; Shi, Yong; Li, Zhixin
abstract: Brucellosis remains an important zoonotic disease for livestock production and public health, creating a need for rapid molecular screening methods with limited equipment requirements. We developed a visual recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)-CRISPR/Cas12a assay targeting a 642-bp region of the Brucella omp25 gene. Comparative sequence analysis was used to assess target conservation, after which four RPA primer pairs and two CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) were experimentally screened. RPA3-crRNA1 produced the strongest fluorescence response and was used for assay optimization. The final Cas12a reaction contained 250 nM Cas12a, 200 nM crRNA, and 200 nM single-stranded DNA fluorescent reporter. RPA amplification and Cas12a detection required 20 min each, and positive reactions produced visible yellow-green fluorescence under 470-nm blue light. No cross-reactivity was observed with the non-target pathogens included in the experimental panel. In silico comparisons with selected phylogenetically related taxa identified sequence differences within the final RPA3 primer-binding sites and crRNA1 recognition region, supporting a low predicted risk of sequence-based cross-reactivity for the taxa examined. Using purified plasmid DNA, the lowest DNA concentration detected under the experimental conditions tested was 2.72 copies/muL of input template, corresponding to an estimated 13.6 copies per RPA reaction. Among 96 bovine nasal swab samples collected during routine surveillance, agreement analysis against the qPCR comparator showed concordant results for 93 of 96 samples, with positive percent agreement (PPA), negative percent agreement (NPA), and overall percent agreement (OPA) of 100.00, 93.75, and 96.88%, respectively; three qPCR-negative samples showed weak RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a fluorescence and could not be independently resolved. Because the target region is conserved in the vaccine strains A19, S19, and RB51, the assay is intended for preliminary screening of brucellosis-associated Brucella DNA rather than species identification or differentiation of vaccine-derived and wild-type DNA. Broader validation with additional specimen types and specificity panels is required before routine diagnostic application.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated Correction of the SLC25A38 Mutation in a Patient With Sideroblastic Anemia.
authors: Yazdanparast, Shokoufeh; Galehdari, Hamid; Khatami, SaeidReza; Hoveizi, Elham; Jaseb, Kaveh
abstract: BACKGROUND: The SLC25A38 is one of the genes of the heme biosynthesis pathway and disruptive alterations therein cause autosomal recessive congenital sideroblastic anemia (CSA). Primary patient-derived fibroblasts can be used as a valuable source for disease modeling, cell therapy studies, and the generation of induced pluripotent stem cells. In addition, they are easy to isolate and grow rapidly in vitro. Therefore, effective gene correction in these cells could be an important step towards personalized therapies. METHODS: In this study, fibroblast cells were isolated from a CSA patient and stained, determined by flow cytometry, and detected by immunocytochemistry. Subsequently, transfection optimization was performed with Lipofectamine. RESULTS: After 24 h of transfection with Cas9/sgRNA3 expression plasmid and single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) donor, a transfection efficiency of 49.64% was achieved. The presence of the ssODN donor in the target gene region was examined by PCR-RFLP and PAGE, observing two fragments with approximate sizes of 116 and 161 bp. These results are consistent with insertion of the ssODN donor into the target gene region in fibroblast cells isolated from the patient. CONCLUSIONS: The findings of this study indicate that the use of the CRISPR/Cas9 system with the designed oligo donor, under the tested conditions, has the potential to produce the expected changes at the target gene locus in patient fibroblast cells. Complementary studies using sequencing, along with examining different transfection conditions, could help more accurately confirm the findings of this study and further optimize this approach for future studies.

title: Elevational melanism in East African Honey Bees involves a Major-Effect locus.
authors: Mazzoni, Marco; Loidolt, Florian; Kersten, Sonja; Otieno, Mark; Njovu, Henry; Lasway, Julius Vincent; Scheiner, Ricarda; Hasselmann, Martin
abstract: Thermal melanism, whereby darker pigmentation occurs in colder environments, is a widespread pattern, yet its genetic and physiological basis in eusocial insects remains poorly understood. East African honey bees (Apis mellifera) occupy elevational gradients in which highland populations are darker, larger, and more cold tolerant than lowland conspecifics. Here, we integrated population genomics, structural variations, and functional genomics to investigate elevational melanism. We sampled, phenotyped and resequenced 139 workers from five East African mountain systems. A genome wide association study identified 977 Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) significantly associated with abdominal pigmentation, with a single, peak at the ebony ortholog AmEbony on chromosome 1. Allelic variation at AmEbony formed three genetic clusters tracking a continuous pigmentation gradient, and 77 divergent SNPs (DXY = 1) almost perfectly discriminated dark from light bees. Two inversions (r7, r9), previously linked to high elevation adaptation, were detected across additional mountain systems and enriched in dark, highland genomic backgrounds, but did not replace AmEbony as the primary pigmentation locus. CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of AmEbony in A. m. carnica produced darker adults in a qualitative comparison, supporting a conserved role in pigmentation. Head RNA-seq and GENIE3 analysis identified recurrent genotype-associated modules involving oxidoreductase activity and odorant binding. Because population structure covaries with elevation and pigmentation, the GWAS supports AmEbony as a major-effect locus but cannot identify causal variants. Similarly, head-expression data identify molecular changes associated with AmEbony disruption, but cannot establish whether they contribute to pigmentation or whether naturally segregating East African alleles act through the same pathways.

title: Association of Xeroderma Pigmentosum group F (XPF) with epigenetic regulation of T helper cell differentiation in coronary artery disease-associated prostate cancer.
authors: Singha Deo, Anisha; P, Shrijana; Karun, Shreya; S U, Sruthika; Mukherjee, Oishi; George, Melvin; Sarkar, Koustav
abstract: BACKGROUND: Coronary artery disease (CAD) and prostate cancer share common genetic and epigenetic risk factors. Xeroderma Pigmentosum group F (XPF), a DNA repair endonuclease, has been implicated in genomic stability and epigenetic regulation. This study investigated the association between XPF expression and epigenetic changes during T helper (TH) cell differentiation in CAD-associated prostate cancer (CAD-PC). RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: CD4(+) T cells isolated from healthy controls and CAD-PC patients were subjected to CRISPR/Cas9-mediated XPF knockout or overexpression. TH cell differentiation, chromatin enrichment, global m6A RNA methylation, DNA methylation, R-loop formation, and tumor cell cytotoxicity were evaluated using molecular and functional assays. RESULTS: XPF overexpression was associated with increased TH1 differentiation and elevated expression of XPF and TP53, whereas TH2, TH17, and Treg-associated markers were reduced. Increased enrichment of XPF and H3K4me3, together with reduced HDAC1, gammaH2A.X, and H3K27me3 enrichment, was observed at the TBX21 and IFNG loci. XPF overexpression was also associated with increased global m6A RNA methylation, reduced DNA methylation at TH1-associated loci, decreased R-loop accumulation, and enhanced tumor cell cytotoxicity in vitro. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that XPF expression is associated with a TH1-skewed epigenetic and immune profile in CAD-PC. However, the absence of disease-specific comparison groups and in vivo validation limits mechanistic interpretation, and further studies are required to establish causality. The present findings demonstrate an association between XPF and the observed TH1-associated epigenetic changes.
