title: Impact of p53 Target Genes on Drug Resistance in TP53-Mutated B-Cell Precursor Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.
authors: Nguyen, Thao T T; Tamai, Minori; Akahane, Koshi; Komatsu, Chiaki; Kagami, Keiko; Qi, Xuekang; Aswad, Luay; Miyake, Kunio; Kasai, Shin; Somazu, Shinpei; Watanabe, Atsushi; Goi, Kumiko; Oshima, Koichi; Imanaga, Hiroshi; Semba, Yuichiro; Sanada, Masashi; Lehtio, Janne; Goto, Hiroaki; Minegishi, Masayoshi; Inaba, Toshiya; Iwamoto, Shotaro; Maeda, Takahiro; Jafari, Rozbeh; Inukai, Takeshi
abstract: TP53 mutations are linked to poor prognoses in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL), indicating that specific p53 target genes may contribute to drug resistance. Although the impact of specific genetic alterations on drug sensitivity has been reported in BCP-ALL, the effects of TP53 mutations on sensitivity to individual agents remain poorly defined in the clinical setting because of the use of combination chemotherapy regimens. In the present study, we addressed this issue through two complementary analyses using a large panel of BCP-ALL cell lines. Initially, 30 cell lines harboring TP53 mutations demonstrated significantly greater resistance to daunorubicin (DNR), mafosfamide (MAF; an active analog of cyclophosphamide), 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and prednisolone compared to 46 cell lines without mutations. Second, 11 CRISPR/Cas9-mediated TP53-knockout sublines derived from cell lines with wild-type TP53 recapitulated resistance to DNR, MAF, and 6-MP, as well as to vincristine (VCR) and cytarabine (Ara-C). Consistent with these findings, re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets revealed significant enrichment of TP53 gRNAs in cells treated with DNR, MAF, 6-MP, Ara-C, and VCR. Furthermore, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of p53 target genes in the two cell line models, along with re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets, identified BAX, BBC3, and FDXR as key p53 target genes associated with multidrug resistance. These results highlight the potential value of targeting these p53 downstream pathways to improve outcomes in TP53-mutated BCP-ALL cases.

title: Klhl41b orchestrates sarcomere assembly and growth to drive skeletal muscle hypertrophy in vivo.
authors: Han, Hyewon; Tate, Grace R; Shi, Janet; Bongiorno, Alfredo H; Mansur, Arian; Widrick, Jeffrey; Gill, Sehajpreet; Karimi, Esmat; Granzier, Henk; Moore, Jeffrey R; Gupta, Vandana A
abstract: BACKGROUND: Nemaline myopathy (NM) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous disease caused by mutations in sarcomere-associated genes, with congenital forms representing the most severe end of the spectrum. Recessive mutations in KLHL41 underlie a severe congenital NM characterized by sarcomeric disorganization and impaired muscle growth. The in vivo mechanisms by which KLHL41 governs sarcomere assembly and growth remain poorly understood. METHODS: We generated zebrafish models of KLHL41 deficiency by the CRISPR-Cas9 approach to examine the temporal and molecular basis of sarcomere assembly defects in NM. The phenotypic and physiological characterization of skeletal muscle defects was investigated by birefringence, spontaneous coiling, spontaneous swimming behavior, and force generation assays. Structural analyses by electron microscopy and immunofluorescence assessed myofibril organization and sarcomere structures across developmental time points. Quantitative proteomics and biochemical assays were performed to identify perturbations in sarcomeric proteins and associated molecular pathways. RESULTS: We show that Klhl41b is essential for the formation and organization of sarcomeres, supporting both radial and longitudinal muscle growth. Loss of Klhl41b resulted in reduced sarcomere size, defective sarcomere assembly followed by progressive destabilization of sarcomeres, nemaline body formation, and reduced muscle function. Proteomic analysis in Klhl41b-deficient zebrafish revealed reduced abundance of the sarcomeric troponin complex proteins, altered abundance of components of the translational machinery, and increased abundance of components of atrophy-associated pathways. CONCLUSIONS: These data show that Klhl41b is required for sarcomere assembly and growth, and its deficiency drives a cascade of structural and molecular changes underlying skeletal muscle hypotrophy and NM pathology. These findings advance our understanding of disease mechanisms and may inform targeted therapeutic strategies to restore sarcomere integrity and muscle function.

title: U2 snRNP inhibition hampers pancreatic cancer cell viability by disrupting DNA repair proficiency and mitotic checkpoint integrity.
authors: Panzeri, Valentina; Pieraccioli, Marco; Ruta, Veronica; Manno, Maria Vittoria; Caggiano, Cinzia; Hartem, Duaa; Riente, Alessia; Milletti, Giacomo; Quero, Giuseppe; Alfieri, Sergio; Lopez-Gil, Juan Carlos; Galvan-Del-Rey, Ana; Guerra, Carmen; Maulucci, Giuseppe; Sette, Claudio
journal: Journal of experimental & clinical cancer research : CR
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer with remarkably poor prognosis. Splicing dysregulation is emerging as a hallmark and possible therapeutic target of PDAC. METHODS: We performed high-throughput RNA sequencing analyses in PANC-1 cells treated with three drugs targeting the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U2 snRNP): Pladienolide B, Thailanstatin A and Indisulam. The efficacy of splicing inhibitors, Talazoparib, Alisertib, AZD7762 and Barisertib, alone or in combination, was assessed in PDAC cells and patient-derived organoids (PDOs) by cell viability assays. RT-PCR, western blot and cell cycle assays were performed to evaluate the expression of DNA repair and mitotic genes and the execution of mitosis. PANC-1 cells were engineered to stably co-express GFP-tagged H2b histone and RFP-tagged beta-tubulin by CRISPR/Cas-9 technology and used for time-lapse confocal microscopy and immunofluorescence analyses. RESULTS: Genes encoding for the U2 snRNP, which recognizes the 3' splice site, are upregulated in advanced PDAC. U2 snRNP-targeting drugs impair the DNA damage response (DDR) pathway in homologous recombination-proficient PDAC cells and PDOs, thus enhancing their sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. Genes whose splicing was disrupted by all three drugs are characterized by higher expression, more exon-intron junctions, weak 5' splice sites and atypical GC content. These features are enriched in mitotic genes (e.g. AURKA, AURKB, CHEK1), whose expression is strongly deregulated by splicing perturbation. Accordingly, splicing inhibition causes severe mitotic defects, leading to the accumulation of cells with misaligned condensed chromosomes on monopolar or bipolar spindles. Notably, high expression of AURKA, AURKB and CHEK1 correlates with poor prognosis in PDAC patients, whereas combined treatments with inhibitors of these mitotic kinases strongly impair the viability of PDAC cells and PDOs. CONCLUSIONS: These findings uncover gene features associated with sensitivity to splicing inhibitors in PDAC cells and suggest that the DDR and mitosis are biological processes highly sensitive to splicing perturbation.

title: CRISPRa screen unveils noncanonical NF-kappaB to boost the antitumor activity of TCR-based CAR-T cells.
authors: Yu, Hanyang; Wu, Yingxin; Liu, Yue; Wei, Ruxue; Zhou, Zhixiao; Yu, Li; Lin, Xin; Wang, Jiasheng
abstract: Engineering autologous T cells for adoptive therapies has revolutionized cancer treatment, yet limited persistence remains a major barrier to robust clinical responses and durable disease control. Although costimulation with 4-1BB markedly improves CAR-T-cell persistence, no comparably effective approach has been identified to enhance persistence in T-cell therapies that rely on native TCR signaling, including conventional TCR-T cells and synthetic T-cell receptor and antigen receptor (STAR) T cells. To identify intrinsic persistence regulators in a TCR-based context, we performed an in vivo CRISPR activation screen in STAR-T cells and identified the noncanonical NF-kappaB axis, with RELB as the top hit. Direct RELB overexpression, however, exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, motivating a translational alternative: overexpression of p52, the ncNF-kappaB transcription partner of RELB. Under prolonged antigen exposure, p52 overexpression sustained proliferation, preserved effector functions, and increased the intratumoral trafficking potential, particularly in CD8(+) T cells, thereby yielding superior tumor control. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling revealed coordinated upregulation of cell cycle programs and chemokine receptors, along with downregulation of apoptosis and exhaustion-associated modules. Moreover, p52 overexpression restored RELB nuclear translocation in the context of PD-1/PD-L1 engagement, indicating partial resistance to checkpoint-mediated suppression and sustained ncNF-kappaB activity in PD-L1(hi) immunosuppressive environments. Collectively, our findings identify p52 as an antigen-dependent enhancer of ncNF-kappaB, conferring durable persistence and checkpoint resilience on TCR-based T cells and providing a feasible strategy to improve therapeutic effects in solid tumors.

title: Author Correction: Engineered CRISPR-OsCas12f1 and RhCas12f1 with robust activities and expanded target range for genome editing.
authors: Kong, Xiangfeng; Zhang, Hainan; Li, Guoling; Wang, Zikang; Kong, Xuqiang; Wang, Lecong; Xue, Mingxing; Zhang, Weihong; Wang, Yao; Lin, Jiajia; Zhou, Jingxing; Shen, Xiaowen; Wei, Yinghui; Zhong, Na; Bai, Weiya; Yuan, Yuan; Shi, Linyu; Zhou, Yingsi; Yang, Hui

title: TET2 loss triggers ssDNA gap accumulation and heightened PARP inhibitor sensitivity.
authors: Agashe, Sumedha; Athreya, Nidhi; Jacobs, William; Letson, Christopher T; Sviderskiy, Vladislav O; Rouault, Celia D; Xie, Yixuan; Bras-Costa, Carolina; Zahn, Emily; Kendall, Mary Claire; Meroni, Alice; Wood, Matthew; Soares, Barbara; Shao, Jin; Cox, Maggie J; Batista, Luis Francisco Zirnberger; Challen, Grant A; Krais, John; Walter, Matthew J; Oh, Stephen T; Garcia, Benjamin A; Edwards, John; Verma, Priyanka; Vindigni, Alessandro
abstract: Somatic mutations in the de novo methyltransferase DNMT3A and cytosine demethylase TET2 are common in age-related clonal hematopoiesis and hematopoietic neoplasms. TET2 mutations, unlike DNMT3A mutations, increase sensitivity to PARP inhibitors (PARPi). We find that TET2 loss, but not DNMT3A loss, alters DNA replication fork progression upon treatment with PARPi Olaparib, resulting in longer DNA replication tracts and increased DNA breaks. This reveals a new link between abnormal fork elongation and PARPi sensitivity in TET2-deficient cells. The elongated forks of TET2-deficient cells contain PRIMPOL-dependent single-stranded (ss)-DNA gaps. This phenotype is dependent on the catalytic activity of TET2 and is mitigated by TET1/3 depletion. Furthermore, TET2 loss causes an imbalance in cytosine methylation and an increase in 5hmU modifications. These modifications are processed by SMUG1, creating abasic sites, detectable via a modified DNA fiber method. A CRISPR screen identified the base excision repair nuclease APE1 as linked to increased PARPi sensitivity in TET2-deficient cells. We propose that abasic sites, skipped by PRIMPOL repriming, lead to ssDNA gaps that are converted into DNA breaks by APE1, increasing PARPi toxicity. Finally, we identify TET2 mutations as an unrecognized predictor of PARPi response in bone marrow samples from patients with myeloid malignancies.

title: Targeting the HIF-1alpha-BSG metabolic circuit reverses enzalutamide resistance in prostate cancer.
authors: Guo, Xiuchen; Huang, Jiacheng; Chen, Zhiwei; Liao, Haihong; Xu, Yulin; Yu, Yongjiang
abstract: BACKGROUND: Enzalutamide resistance limits durable control of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), but the mechanisms coordinating metabolic adaptation, cellular plasticity, and residual androgen receptor (AR) signaling remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether BSG, encoding basigin/CD147, contributes to this resistant state. METHODS: We integrated reanalysis of an androgen-responsive reporter-based CRISPR activation screen with bulk and single-cell transcriptomic datasets, clinical specimens, and outcome data. Reciprocal BSG loss- and gain-of-function experiments were performed in parental and enzalutamide-resistant LNCaP and C4-2 cells. Drug response, cellular plasticity, glycolytic activity, hypoxia/HIF1A perturbation, pathway-directed inhibition, and resistant xenografts were evaluated. RESULTS: BSG-activating guides were enriched in unsorted and androgen-responsive, but not androgen-independent, enzalutamide-resistant populations. BSG was elevated in resistant models and high-Gleason-score tumors, and high expression was associated with shorter progression-free survival. Single-cell analysis identified a CRPC-enriched tumor-cell state with high BSG and SLC16A3 expression, increased glycolysis and hypoxia-related activity, enhanced developmental plasticity, and retained AR-target gene expression. BSG depletion increased enzalutamide responsiveness and suppressed proliferation, clonogenic survival, migration, invasion, sphere formation, and stemness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition programs in resistant cells, whereas BSG overexpression produced reciprocal effects in parental cells. BSG depletion reduced AR and PSA abundance in LNCaP EnzR cells. It also reduced extracellular acidification, lactate production, glucose uptake, and the abundance of HK2, LDHA, MCT1, and MCT4. Hypoxia or HIF1A overexpression increased BSG-associated metabolic and plasticity programs, whereas BSG depletion attenuated most HIF-1alpha-induced changes without materially reducing HIF-1alpha. In resistant xenografts, BSG depletion or PX-478 enhanced tumor suppression by enzalutamide. CONCLUSIONS: BSG contributes to an AR-retaining, hypoxia-associated glycolytic and plastic state that supports enzalutamide resistance.

title: Single-gRNA CRISPR/eCas9-mediated simultaneous targeting of cIAP1 and cIAP2 in colorectal cancer cells: RNA-seq reveals distinct transcriptomic and apoptotic responses.
authors: Batir, Muhammet Burak
abstract: Cellular inhibitor of apoptosis proteins 1 and 2 (cIAP1 and cIAP2), encoded by BIRC2 and BIRC3, respectively, are important regulators of cellular survival and apoptosis. These proteins contribute to cancer cell survival by suppressing apoptotic signaling. While individual knockouts of BIRC2 or BIRC3 in cancer cells have been investigated, the consequences of simultaneously targeting both paralogs remain poorly understood. Thus, a single-gRNA CRISPR/eCas9 strategy was developed in which one gRNA targeting a shared sequence in BIRC2 and BIRC3 was used to simultaneously disrupt both genes in human colorectal cancer HCT-116 cells, and the resulting cellular and transcriptomic effects were compared with those of the individual knockouts. Individual and dual-targeting CRISPR/eCas9 constructs were experimentally validated by immunofluorescence analysis, RT-PCR, and RT-qPCR, while fluorescence microscopy and T7EI analysis were used to evaluate single-cell-derived clones. Apoptosis was evaluated using flow cytometry, and RNA sequencing was performed for differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis. The single-gRNA dual-targeting strategy resulted in concurrent loss of cIAP1 and cIAP2 expression and produced a stronger reduction in cell survival and induction of apoptosis than targeting either gene individually. In addition, the expression levels of TNFRSF25, TRAF2, TNFSF15, and MIR663AHG were significantly upregulated following simultaneous BIRC2/BIRC3 targeting. RNA-seq analysis provided detailed insight into the molecular alterations associated with concurrent cIAP1 and cIAP2 depletion. Overall, these findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of targeting two highly homologous genes with a single gRNA and reveal that simultaneous disruption of cIAP1 and cIAP2 produces biological effects that are more pronounced than those observed following individual targeting.

title: De novo MAP2K4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome and impaired JNK signaling in iPSC-derived neurons.
authors: Nomakuchi, Tomoki T; Rippert, Alyssa L; Santos De Leon, Sabrina A; Gonzalez, Elizabeth M; Li, Dong; Angireddy, Rajesh; Finoti, Livia Sertori; Faletra, Flavio; Musante, Luciana; Tuula, Rinne; Amor, David J; von Wintzingerode, Lydia; Jamra, Rami Abou; Stover, Samantha R; Buchan, Jillian G; Hayek, Jennifer; Leon, Eyby; Attie-Bitach, Tania; Rio, Marlene; Baujat, Genevieve; Wallach, Elisabeth; Smail, Amandine; Dias, Kerith-Rae; Pfeifer, Ulrich; Peterson, Amanda; Ahrens-Nicklas, Rebecca C; Bhoj, Elizabeth J K
abstract: MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. These neurons showed reduced JNK pathway activation and impaired maturation in the neurogenin 2 (NGN2) system, characterized by persistence of progenitor-like cells and disrupted neurite morphology. Our findings establish MAP2K4 as a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder-associated gene and identify impaired JNK signaling as the underlying mechanism. More broadly, this work expands the spectrum of JNK pathway disorders and underscores the critical role of JNK signaling in human brain development.

title: A cross-species AAV platform for precise microglial interrogation.
authors: Yu, Fengting; Wang, Ruiyu; Di, Run; Xu, Ke; Gao, Jinquan; Shang, Huiping; Yuan, Zhengwei; Dai, Ruicheng; Wu, Wenting; Weng, Danwei; Gao, Xinwei; Li, Heng; Yu, Tao; Zhang, Yuanqing; Wang, Xiongfei; Luan, Guoming; Zhao, Fei; Luo, Minmin
abstract: Targeting microglia with adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) remains challenging because of inefficient transduction, off-target expression, and inconsistent payload performance. Here, we develop an integrated, Cre-independent AAV platform that combines a compact 446-bp microglia-specific regulatory element (MSRE), a high-yield AAV2/9.m capsid, microRNA-mediated neuronal de-targeting, and a microglia-tailored codon-optimization strategy. Following direct intracranial delivery, the optimized vector achieves robust, long-lasting transgene expression with greater than 90% microglial specificity across multiple mouse brain regions, including in an Alzheimer's disease model. With doxorubicin-assisted delivery, the platform also enables efficient and selective microglial targeting in rats, rhesus macaques, and human ex vivo brain slices. Codon optimization supports the expression of otherwise challenging functional payloads, enabling calcium imaging, chemogenetic manipulation, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. This cross-species toolkit provides a versatile resource for investigating microglial biology and developing microglia-directed therapeutic strategies.

title: Structural basis and rational engineering of a thermophilic Cas13a for robust RNA detection.
authors: Oladeji, Seye J; Gonzalez, Diego H; Deng, Xiangyu; You, Zheng; Zhang, Yuxuan; Golla, Devin A; Smith, Jamie; Zhang, Yi; Gao, Xue; Lillehoj, Peter B; Gao, Yang
abstract: Cas13a enzymes are particularly attractive for nucleic acid detection due to their robust collateral activity. Recently, there has been a surge in the discovery and engineering of thermostable Cas13a proteins for nucleic acid detection. The thermostable Cas13a from Thermoclostridium caenicola (TccCas13a) was identified; however, its native target sensitivity and collateral activity are relatively low and require optimization for molecular diagnostic applications. Here, we report comprehensive biochemical characterization and structure-guided engineering of TccCas13a. Our analyses reveal its intrinsic thermostability, nucleotide substrate preferences, and tolerance to structured target RNA substrates. Rational engineering of the spacer-target RNA binding channel improved target engagement and enabled determination of a 3.13 A cryo-electron microscopy ternary structure. Furthermore, extensive structure-guided engineering of active site-proximal regions yielded a variant with over  approximately 100-fold enhanced target sensitivity and collateral activity across diverse biological matrices. Together, our work provides mechanistic insights and establishes TccCas13a as a platform for next-generation RNA diagnostics.

title: Single-cell CRISPR screen maps epigenetic regulators of lineage specification and malignancies in human HSPCs.
authors: Yuan, Shiru; Yang, Shangda; Huang, Yaojin; Ma, Baowei; Wu, Qian; Zhang, Xinghui; Yin, Tong; Chen, Lianting; Zhang, Baixuan; Sun, Guohuan; He, Yicheng; Duan, Honglin; Hu, Linping; Hao, Sha; Cheng, Hui; Wei, Jun; Cheng, Tao
abstract: Mapping how genetic perturbations influence cell fate is key to understanding human development and disease. Here, we developed a massively parallel single-cell CRISPR (scCRISPR) screening platform in primary human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), profiling 322 regulators across 172,382 single-perturbed cells. The resulting multi-layered regulatory framework captured known associations and enabled functional annotation of regulator-phenotype relationships. Specifically, our atlas revealed that regulators acted within perturbation clusters to govern distinct gene programs that shaped cell fate. As proof of concept, we illustrated several examples. SMYD3 emerged as a negative regulator of long-term regenerative capacity. Analysis of lineage output further identified KMT5B, TRIM24, SETD7, and NSD3 as regulators associated with lineage-biased outputs. Finally, integration with clinical datasets identified PRDM10 as a candidate dependency in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This work establishes a scalable functional genomics platform in a primary human stem cell system.

title: Generation of induced pluripotent stem cell lines TRNDi045-A-40 and TRNDi045-A-41 modeling mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA and type I from parental KOLF2.1J.
authors: Ma, Chris H; Xu, Miao; Lin, Yongshun; Zou, Jizhong; Liu, Chengyu; Lorino, Maryann; Bigger, Brian W; Zheng, Wei; Chen, Catherine Z
abstract: Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS) are lysosomal storage disorders caused by enzyme deficiencies that impair glycosaminoglycan degradation and cause multisystem disease. We generated two human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines from the KOLF2.1J background using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of pathogenic variants: TRNDi045-A-40 carries a homozygous SGSH c.734G > A (p.Arg245His) variant associated with severe Sanfilippo syndrome type A (MPS IIIA), and TRNDi045-A-41 harbors a homozygous IDUA c.1205-1206 GG > AA (p.Trp402Ter) variant causing Hurler syndrome (MPS I). These lines model MPS diseases with different enzyme mutations. The resulting iPSCs are pluripotent, genetically validated, and support studies of disease mechanisms and therapies for MPS IIIA and MPS I.

title: Repurposing Type III CRISPR-Cas as Modular Cellular RNA Biosensors.
authors: Yildiz, Caglar; de Roode, Sarah; Elias, Jinane; Tibbe, Arjan; Staals, Raymond H J
abstract: Over the past decade, CRISPR-Cas based biosensors have emerged as sensitive, specific and programmable platforms for nucleic acid detection, with applications ranging from diagnostic tools, environmental monitoring and various applications in fundamental research. The vast majority of these biosensors are currently limited to in vitro applications, highlighting the need for cellular platforms. Here, we provide a perspective on the potential of type III CRISPR-Cas systems as a platform for real-time RNA biosensing in living cells. We discuss the unique properties that distinguish type III from other CRISPR-Cas types, including their intrinsic cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signal amplification cascade, PAM-free RNA targeting and the extensive biochemical diversity of their downstream CARF and SAVED effector proteins. We outline the fundamental design principles of a genetically encoded type III cellular biosensor, comprising a programmable guide RNA, a multi-subunit sensing complex and a cOA-sensing effector protein capable of generating optical or electrochemical readout signals. A remaining challenge for type III cellular biosensors is the inherent cytotoxicity of canonical cOA-activated effectors. We propose several strategies to re-engineer these outputs towards non-cytotoxic reporter systems. While cellular biosensors present a natural route toward in vivo sensing, they face many challenges beyond the choice of the output signal and hardware strategy. We conclude that type III CRISPR-Cas is a promising platform for programmable real-time RNA sensing in living cells, utilizing its diverse modular effector outputs, representing a significant expansion of the CRISPR biosensor toolkit, while emphasizing appropriate deployment scenarios that enables full potential of these biosensors.

title: Gene Therapy: Routes of Inner Ear Delivery.
authors: Yildiz, Erdem; Arnoldner, Christoph
abstract: Gene delivery and the various routes of administration used to deliver viral vectors constitute a rapidly evolving field, with recent success in restoring hearing in children with OTOF variants in ongoing clinical otoferlin trials. With the rise of gene therapy for major hereditary hearing disorders, both syndromic and nonsyndromic, there has been parallel progress in the development of new delivery methods. Advances in intratympanic injection of antibiotics and corticosteroids, along with nearly half a century of experience in cochlear implantation surgery, have enabled multiple local and systemic approaches to access the inner ear. Recent industry investment in gene therapy and delivery technologies has accelerated scientific progress, underscoring the need for continuous evaluation of the most suitable gene delivery strategies for different causes of hearing loss. Although most gene delivery in animal models has been performed via round window membrane injection, yielding promising results in cochlear hair cell transduction, potential drawbacks remain for clinical translation-particularly limited vector distribution, which may result in a basal-to-apical gradient. Venting procedures such as stapes footplate fenestration or canalostomy have been explored to mitigate these limitations, and recent intrathecal or even in utero injections have been investigated as alternative approaches. Hearing loss can be inherited in multiple ways, and patient treatment with gene delivery, or even the type of gene therapy itself, may vary with the recent success of CRISPR/Cas-based editing tools. Understanding the genetic etiology of inner ear disorders has facilitated the identification of therapeutic targets and innovative delivery approaches. This review summarizes the current understanding of delivery routes for gene therapy, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations as demonstrated in translational and clinical research to date. Furthermore, it examines advances in drug delivery and clinical applications in the context of emerging therapeutics, providing an integrated overview and perspective on the future direction of gene delivery strategies.

title: Quantifying the impact of genetic mutations on enhancer dynamics.
authors: Das, Maitreya; Banerjee, Deepro; Hossain, Ayaan; Jensen, Matthew; Mogre, Saie; Sun, Jiawan; Mao, Joseph; Glick, Adam B; Salis, Howard M; Girirajan, Santhosh
abstract: Transcriptional regulation is mediated by enhancers, yet how genetic perturbations alter enhancer activity and gene expression remains unclear. We develop UDI-UMI-STARR-seq, integrating dual indexes and unique molecular identifiers, and combine it with RNA-seq to profile perturbation-associated changes in enhancer activity and gene expression. We apply this approach to 253,632 fragments representing 46,142 cell type-specific candidate enhancers and assess the impact of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of six transcription factors (ATF2, CTCF, FOXA1, LEF1, TCF7L2, and SCRT1). We identify responsive fragments that are repressed or induced and enriched for p53 family motifs. Enhancer-gene mapping reveals associations between responsive fragments and gene expression changes, including Wnt/p53 targets after ATF2 or LEF1 depletion. A deep learning model recapitulates enhancer grammar, including cooperative motif syntax and flanking sequence context. Applying this framework to 16p12.1 deletion identifies responsive fragments associated with genes involved in neuronal function, providing a scalable readout of enhancer dynamics across genetic perturbations.

title: CRISPR genome editing in food and feed crops: intellectual property challenges, global accessibility, and the Indian perspective.
authors: Mangal, Harshit; Mathur, Shivangi; Chaurasia, Anurag; Sharma, Soumya; Kumar, Sunil; Ranjan, Rajiv
abstract: The ever-increasing global demand for food and feed, coupled with population growth and climate change, necessitates the development of high-yielding and stress-resilient crops. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) technology has emerged as a transformative genome-editing tool due to its efficiency, precision, and ability to generate targeted genetic modifications. This review highlights recent advances in CRISPR genome editing, including base editing, prime editing, and novel Cas variants, together with emerging approaches such as epigenome editing, mitochondrial genome editing, and hypercompact Cas systems, and their applications in improving crop productivity, stress tolerance, and nutritional quality. In food and feed crops, these applications also include crop-specific priorities such as grain and nutritional quality in food crops and digestibility, forage quality, and mineral bioavailability in feed and forage crops. Particular emphasis is placed on the complex intellectual property (IP) landscape surrounding CRISPR technologies, including patents on editing systems, delivery platforms, and proprietary vectors. These intellectual property barriers can restrict research access, technology transfer, and commercialization, particularly in developing countries. The review further discusses patent limitations, licensing frameworks, and strategies to enhance equitable global access through collaborative approaches such as non-exclusive licensing, humanitarian licensing, indigenous technology development, and international partnerships. Overall, the review underscores the need to balance innovation, intellectual property protection, and global accessibility to ensure that CRISPR-based technologies contribute effectively to worldwide food and feed security and sustainable agriculture.

title: Recent progress in microbial succinic acid production: integrating genome engineering and fermentation strategies.
authors: Phosriran, Chutchawan; Jantama, Sirima Suvarnakuta; Cheng, Kuan-Chen; Jantama, Kaemwich
abstract: Succinic acid is a four-carbon dicarboxylic acid and important platform chemical with diverse applications in food and feed, pharmaceutical, textile, and bio-based polymer industries. Growing demand for sustainable and economically viable production routes has stimulated increasing interest in microbial routes for succinic acid biosynthesis as an alternative to conventional petrochemical processes. This mini-review summarizes recent advances in microbial succinic acid production, with particular emphasis on strain development, metabolic engineering, and fermentation-process optimization. Significant progress has been achieved through engineering of both native producers, Actinobacillus succinogenes, Mannheimia succiniciproducens, and Corynebacterium glutamicum and non-native production hosts, such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella oxytoca, and several yeast species, leading to marked improvements in succinate concentration, yield, and productivity. Emerging approaches, including adaptive-laboratory evolution, systems-level omics, and CRISPR-Cas9, have enabled more precise control of carbon flux toward succinic acid biosynthesis while improving cellular tolerance to low pH and elevated succinic acid concentrations. In parallel, advances in fermentation and bioprocess strategies, particularly low-pH fermentation and enhanced CO(2) fixation, together with the valorization of renewable feedstocks such as lignocellulosic hydrolysates, offer promising opportunities to improve process feasibility and sustainability. However, their economic competitiveness remains strongly influenced by feedstock pretreatment, hydrolysis, detoxification, fermentation performance, and downstream processing requirements. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives for industrial-scale succinic acid production are discussed, highlighting the importance of integrating strain engineering with innovative bioprocess design to develop robust, economically competitive, and environmentally sustainable production platforms.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies eIF4G2 as a regulator of CD8+ T cell dysfunction.
authors: Holcomb, Erin A; Jiang, Long; Pearson, Ashley N; James, Jadyn; Tate, Akshay; Wang, Zhuwen; Dasgupta, Anwesha; Clauwaert, Jim; Armas, Nicholas D; Elaimy, Ameer L; Palagama, Dilrukshika S W; Goodwin, Samantha K; Kwiatkowski, Matthew J; Gijon, Miguel; Morgan, Meredith A; Courtney, Adam H; Carty, Shannon A; Huber, Amanda K; Zou, Weiping; Prensner, John R; Green, Michael D
abstract: CD8+ T cells directly target and kill cancer cells and are required for effective antitumor immunity. However, CD8+ T cells may become dysfunctional when exposed to chronic antigen stimulation during cancer. Dysfunction is characterized by reduced proliferation, increased expression of inhibitory receptors, and impaired effector function, yet the genetic mechanisms controlling dysfunction remain poorly understood. Therefore, we developed a murine ex vivo chronic stimulation model that recapitulates features of CD8+ T cell dysfunction observed within the tumor microenvironment. By coupling this system with genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screening, we discovered that the progression of murine CD8+ T cells to a dysfunctional state required eIF4G2, a noncanonical mRNA translation factor. Deletion of eIF4G2 restored CD8+ T cell survival and proliferation during chronic stimulation conditions in vitro. Transcriptomic, proteomic, and flow cytometric analyses revealed that eIF4G2 deletion shifts CD8+ T cell phenotype from a dysfunctional state to a proliferative state. eIF4G2 depletion reduced oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and accumulation of misfolded protein aggresomes during chronic in vitro stimulation. Finally, eIF4G2-depleted cells mediated enhanced tumor control in a murine model of melanoma. These data suggest that targeting eIF4G2 may promote CD8+ T cell resilience and improve therapeutic antitumor immunity.

title: A syngeneic murine glioma model recapitulates key molecular, immunologic, and functional features of human glioblastoma to enable therapeutic development.
authors: Grausam, Katie B; Pioso, Marissa S; Sanchez, Julio C; Li, Marissa; Rincon Fernandez Pacheco, David; Hatanaka, Emily A; Herrera, Gilbert; Lai, Thomas J; Lu, Eddie; Linesch, Paul W; Kobritz, Naomi; Phan, Trinh L; Ashley, Sophie; Andrade, Ariel A; Markus, Lauren; Yao, Jingwen; Fan, Xuemo; Yu, Bohyeon; Diaz, Aaron A; Liau, Linda M; Danielpour, Moise; Nathanson, David A; Prins, Robert M; Breunig, Joshua J; Shiao, Stephen L
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of novel therapies. Here we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-gamma (mIFN-gamma) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

title: Molecular mechanisms and regulatory networks governing Yersinia biofilm formation and host adaptation.
authors: Wu, Haisheng; Wu, Hailian; Peng, Wenxuan; Zhang, Yiquan; Zhang, Qingwen
abstract: The genus Yersinia includes three human pathogens-Y. pestis, Y. pseudotuberculosis, and Y. enterocolitica-where biofilm formation plays distinct roles in transmission and environmental persistence. All three species share the core biofilm machinery-the hmsHFRS operon, encoding enzymes for poly-beta-1,6-N-acetylglucosamine (PNAG) exopolysaccharide production, and the c-di-GMP signaling controlling this production-but their regulatory networks and biofilm outputs differ. Transcriptional control of hms involves an integrated network that includes the Rcs phosphorelay (reshaped by rcsA pseudogenization), PhoP/PhoQ, EnvZ/OmpR, BarA/UvrY, Fur/Zur, CRP-cAMP, RovM/RovA, and multiple sigma factors. Post-transcriptionally, the Hfq-sRNA and CsrA-CsrB/CsrC systems modulate gene expression; the latter is directly validated in Y. pestis and Y. pseudotuberculosis, whereas its role in Y. enterocolitica is inferred from genomic conservation. At the translational and enzymatic levels, polyamines sustain Hms protein production, while redox signals govern the HmsC-HmsD disulfide switch, controlling diguanylate cyclase activity. This multi-layer architecture ensures that biofilm output is tuned to species-specific ecological niches. In host adaptation, Y. pestis transitioned from a foodborne enteric pathogen to a flea-borne lifestyle through key genetic events-acquisition of ymt, pseudogenization of rcsA, inactivation of y2909/y3389, and ureD-which are not shared with Y. pseudotuberculosis or Y. enterocolitica, thereby explaining their different biofilm-dependent transmission strategies. Studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have identified host O-glycosylation modifications as receptors for biofilm attachment. This review summarizes progress on the molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and host-adaptive functions of Yersinia biofilm formation and proposes future research directions to address knowledge gaps. Future priorities include the identification of c-di-GMP effectors, flea-specific signals, 3D biofilm imaging, and CRISPR-based detection.

title: A guide to studying tumour-T-cell interactions using in vitro coculture assays.
authors: Khoshdoozmasouleh, Nooshin; Kearney, Conor J
abstract: T cells are central mediators of antitumour immunity and are the cellular basis of many successful cancer immunotherapies, including immune checkpoint blockade, T-cell receptor (TCR)-engineered therapies and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. However, clinical responses remain variable, and many tumours evade or resist T-cell-mediated control. Understanding how T cells recognise tumour cells, deliver cytotoxic signals, produce inflammatory cytokines and shape tumour cell fate is therefore essential for improving modern immunotherapies. In vitro tumour T-cell coculture systems provide a powerful experimental framework for dissecting these processes under controlled conditions. They allow investigators to manipulate antigen specificity, HLA/MHC restriction, tumour genotype, T-cell activation state, cytokine exposure and drug-mediated perturbation in ways that are difficult to achieve in vivo. However, these systems require careful design, because assay outcomes are strongly influenced by tumour model, antigen expression, effector-to-target ratio, assay duration and readout. This guide provides a practical framework for studying tumour T-cell interactions in vitro, with a focus on CD8+ T-cell-mediated tumour recognition and killing. It discusses commonly used mouse and human antigen-specific models, how antigen expression and presentation can be experimentally controlled, T-cell activation and coculture conditions, cytotoxicity assays, immune synapse imaging, competition assays, cytokine-mediated bystander killing, transcriptional profiling, CRISPR perturbation strategies, therapeutic testing and patient-derived models. The aim is to help researchers choose the most appropriate model, experimental setup and readout for the biological question being asked and to avoid common interpretive pitfalls when studying tumour immune sensitivity, resistance and therapeutic response.

title: A review on recent advances in regenerative medicine for renal diseases: Approaches and challenges.
authors: Roy, Urbi; Pillatt, Ashiq Shibili; Chan, Mike K S; Velure RajaRao, Mohan Rao; Banerjee, Antara; Pathak, Surajit
journal: Developmental dynamics : an official publication of the American Association of Anatomists
abstract: Renal diseases such as acute and chronic kidney disease cause loss of nephrons and kidney function, often leading to renal failure. Current treatments like dialysis and transplantation only manage symptoms and extend survival for a few years. Regenerative medicine offers promising approaches for repairing and regenerating renal tissue by targeting underlying disease mechanisms. For this narrative review, relevant original research articles and review articles were retrieved from online databases such as PubMed, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect by using relevant keywords such as "renal regeneration," "kidney organoids," "stem cell therapy," "gene therapy," "extracellular vesicles," and "tissue engineering." The literature search focused primarily on articles published between 2020 and 2026 to discuss the recent advancements in regenerative approaches for renal disease. Recent advances in regenerative medicine have identified therapies such as stem cells, gene therapy, CRISPR-Cas9, extracellular vesicles, and kidney organoids that promote nephron regeneration, improve vascularization, regulate inflammation, and restore kidney function. This review highlights the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying renal damage, recent advances in regenerative medicine, and the key challenges and future directions for the safe and effective use of regenerative medicine in treating renal diseases.

title: CRISPR-mediated gap-based replacement enables site-specific DNA lesion insertion into long DNA and nucleosomes.
authors: Kim, Youngseo; An, Soyeong; Choi, Jimin; Choi, Moonjung; Lee, Gyeongjin; Takata, Kei-Ichi; Anand, Roopesh; Myung, Kyungjae; Lee, Ja Yil
abstract: Defined DNA lesions are essential substrates for dissecting DNA repair mechanisms, yet existing approaches remain limited in positional flexibility, lesion diversity, efficiency, or compatibility with long and chromatinized DNA. Here, we present CGRID (CRISPR-mediated Gap-based Replacement for Insertion of DNA damage), a programmable strategy for site-specific installation of DNA lesions into long DNA and nucleosomes. CGRID uses paired Cas9 nickases to generate two adjacent nicks, followed by gap formation and replacement with a synthetic lesion-containing oligonucleotide. This design enables easy and efficient insertion of diverse DNA lesions at user-defined positions without pre-engineered nicking sites or substrate redesign. Applied to long lambda-DNA, CGRID supports efficient installation of single lesions and internal double-strand breaks at predefined positions, which are challenging to obtain using existing methods. These molecules enable high-throughput single-molecule analysis of diverse repair pathways including base excision repair (BER), nonhomologous end joining, and microhomology-mediated end joining without hydrodynamic force. CGRID further allows efficient site-specific lesion incorporation into nucleosomal DNA, enabling systematic repositioning of damage within a nucleosome. This shows that nucleosome context and lesion orientation strongly influence APE1 incision efficiency. Together, CGRID establishes a broadly applicable platform for programmable DNA damage engineering, bridging biochemical and single-molecule methodologies, and facilitates mechanistic studies of chromatin-dependent genome maintenance.

title: Hybridization-Mediated Reversible sgRNA Caging Enables Tumor-Selective Gene Editing for Potentiating Antitumor Immunity via cGAS Demethylation.
authors: Zhang, Haoyu; Li, Yajie; Wang, Yehan; Zhao, Ziyin; Yang, He; Hu, Jiawen; Cao, Desheng; Wang, Guanglin; Zhu, Ran; Liu, Xun; Yin, Lichen
abstract: Spatiotemporal precision remains a critical challenge against the gene editing technology used for disease treatment. We herein developed a tumor cell-selective CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system by introducing a complementary single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) containing apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) sites (AP-ssDNA) along the target region of single-guided RNA (sgRNA). The engineered hybrid (AP-ssDNA/sgRNA) could tracelessly release the native sgRNA in tumor cells due to cleavage of AP-ssDNA by the overexpressed apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1), thus enabling tumor-selective gene editing. Subsequently, a biodegradable lipid nanoparticle based on dynamic covalent bonding was developed to codeliver Cas9-encoding mRNA (mCas9) with AP-ssDNA/sgRNA targeting the SUV39H1 gene, which mediated silence of cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) methylation to activate stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and enhanced antitumor immunity. As thus, when coupled with radiotherapy, the gene editing platform provoked robust antitumor efficacy in B16F10 xenograft tumor-bearing mice. This study provides a versatile paradigm for conditionally controlled gene editing and highlights the therapeutic potential of cGAS demethylation in reactivating cGAS-STING pathway for antitumor immunotherapy.

title: Advances in plant metabolic engineering through synthetic biology.
authors: Alsuwat, Hind; Alvarez, Derry; Al-Babili, Salim
abstract: The challenges associated with the escalating global population and climate change in crop production and food security are substantial. This underscores the necessity for improvements in crop nutrition, yield, and resilience to environmental stresses. Plant metabolic pathways directly influence growth, nutrient accumulation, and stress responses, rendering them prime targets for crop enhancement. Advances in plant synthetic biology and gene editing are facilitating more precise modifications of genes, regulatory elements, and metabolic pathways. This review highlights the primary technologies used in plant metabolic engineering and focuses on representative examples of their implementation for crop improvement, including but not limited to CRISPR-Cas systems, multiplex genome editing, knock-in and knock-out strategies, CRISPR-mediated gene regulation (CRISPRi/CRISPRa), base editing, prime editing, RNA targeting technologies, synthetic promoters, and gene stacking strategies. Furthermore, the emerging role of artificial intelligence in the design and optimization of metabolic pathways and genome editing tools will be briefly discussed.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify shared and context-specific regulators of podocyte resistance to oxidative injury.
authors: Zhen, Xuan; Hu, Jiaying; Wang, Xiao; Qing, Jianbo; Wu, Junnan
abstract: Podocyte injury is a convergent driver of glomerular disease progression, yet the genetic determinants that govern podocyte vulnerability to oxidative stress remain incompletely defined. Here, we performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens in differentiated human podocytes exposed to two complementary injury models: Adriamycin (ADR), a clinically relevant inducer of podocyte damage, and hydrogen peroxide (H(2)O(2)), a direct oxidative stress challenge. Human podocytes were transduced with a genome-wide sgRNA library, differentiated under non-permissive conditions and subjected to optimized stress conditions that imposed selective pressure while preserving library complexity. Across five independent replicates per condition, sequencing-based sgRNA profiling demonstrated high reproducibility, balanced library representation and clear treatment-specific selection. The ADR screen identified 819 depleted and 456 enriched genes, whereas the H(2)O(2) screen identified 277 depleted and 215 enriched genes. Integrated analysis revealed both model-specific dependencies and 27 shared depleted genes across the two injury conditions, implicating stress adaptation, chromatin regulation, mitochondrial metabolism, inflammatory signaling and cytoskeletal organization as candidate processes required for podocyte survival. These genome-wide screens provide a functional framework for prioritizing genes that regulate podocyte resilience to oxidative injury and offer a resource for mechanistic studies of glomerular disease.

title: Bioorthogonal Vitamin C Probes Enable Cellular Profiling and Investigation of Lysine Vitcylation.
authors: Wang, Wanting; Ding, Baoli; Yang, Shuqiao; Li, Xuejie; Yang, Jiawei; Zhou, Zhiwan; Xiao, Sidong; He, Xiadi; Zhu, Cheng-Liang; Zhang, Shuai
abstract: Vitamin C is an essential micronutrient, yet its direct chemical engagement with the proteome remains poorly defined. Here, we develop and experimentally benchmark a bioorthogonal probe platform for labeling, profiling, and imaging of lysine vitcylation, a recently identified vitamin C-derived post-translational modification, in living cells. Chemoproteomic analysis and fluorescence imaging reveal a candidate vitcylome enriched in nucleolar proteins associated with ribonucleoprotein biogenesis and RNA processing, and reporter-derived lysine adducts on selected targets were validated by mass spectrometry. Time-resolved analyses demonstrate that intracellular vitcylation undergoes unexpectedly rapid remodeling, indicating active cellular regulation. Furthermore, a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies glutathione S-transferase P1 (GSTP1) as an upstream regulator of global vitamin C-derived protein modification, linking vitcylation remodeling to cellular electrophile handling and redox homeostasis. Collectively, this platform provides a chemical framework for profiling, visualizing, and investigating protein vitcylation in living cells, and reveals vitcylation as a dynamic, spatially organized and regulated metabolic modification.

title: CRISPR integration of an FLT3 CAR into the TRAC locus generates CAR T cells for AML.
authors: Noer, Maya G; Christensen, Kimmie B; Mikkelsen, Nanna S; Skjelbostad, Sigrid Fu; Rothemejer, Frederik H; Wittenborn, Thomas; Famme, Simon; Mikkelsen, Kasper; Barington, Torben; Thomsen, Martin K; Barnkob, Mike B; Moller, Bjarne K; Bak, Rasmus O
abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains a therapeutically challenging hematological malignancy with high relapse rates, especially in patients harboring mutations in the FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) gene. FLT3, a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in hematopoietic cell proliferation and survival, is frequently mutated or overexpressed in AML, contributing to leukemic proliferation and poor prognosis. Although FLT3 inhibitors have demonstrated clinical benefit, resistance often develops, underscoring the need for alternative treatment strategies. METHODS: In this study, we developed and evaluated allogeneic anti-FLT3 CAR T cells engineered by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeted integration into the T cell receptor alpha constant (TRAC) locus (TRAC-CAR T). This approach enables CAR expression under the endogenous TRAC promoter while simultaneously disrupting native TCR expression, thereby allowing the use of allogeneic T cells with reduced risk of graft-versus-host disease. RESULTS: TRAC-CAR T cells demonstrated efficient disruption of TCRalphabeta expression, robust surface CAR expression, and superior integration efficiency compared to safe harbor AAVS1-targeted and lentivirally transduced CAR T cells (LV-CAR T). Functionally, TRAC-CAR T cells exhibited potent and selective cytotoxicity against FLT3-positive AML cell lines in vitro, achieving comparable killing relative to LV-CAR T cells. In a xenograft AML mouse model, TRAC-CAR T cells effectively reduced leukemia burden and prolonged mouse survival, with efficacy matching that of LV-CAR T cells. Notably, TRAC-CAR T cells exhibited reduced exhaustion marker expression. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these results highlight TRAC-integrated anti-FLT3 CAR T cells as a promising off-the-shelf immunotherapy candidate, combining precise gene editing, efficient manufacturing, and potent anti-leukemic activity.

title: Optimized gGBE enables robust G-to-Y conversion in mammalian cells and zebrafish embryos.
authors: Li, Min; Jiao, Yao-Ge; Tao, Rui; Hu, Yun; Fei, Jun-Yi; Wang, Chun-Ting; Yao, Shao-Hua
abstract: Base editing is a powerful and precise genome-editing tool capable of introducing single-base substitutions with high resolution. Depending on the base-modification domains employed, base editors can mediate both transition and transversion base editing in mammalian cells. While deaminase-derived base editors have enabled efficient transition editing in the zebrafish genome, glycosidase-derived transversion editing remains a significant challenge. In this study, guided by structural insights into the Cas9 complex, we engineered a series of glycosidase guanine base editor (gGBE) constructs by inlaying the N-methylpurine DNA glycosylase (MPG) domain into Cas9 protein. Among these variants, we identified a high-performance gGBE in which MPG was inserted between residues G1246 and S1247 of the PI domain in Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9, which we named gGBE-PIGS. This variant improved editing efficiency by up to 3.5-fold in mammalian cells and 13-fold in zebrafish embryos, without compromising editing precision. Furthermore, we developed a gGBE-editing-responsive GFP reporter to monitor editing efficiency and enrich for gGBE-edited cells and embryos. Using a combination of the optimized gGBE-PIGS and the GFP reporter, we successfully generated zebrafish models carrying mutations homologous to human amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated variants. Together, these findings highlight the robustness and versatility of the gGBE platform for precise base editing and underscore its promising potential for in vivo disease modeling and therapeutic genome engineering.
