title: In vivo CRISPR screens identify dual functions of DNMT3A in mediating tumor immune evasion.
authors: Zhao, Jianhong; Deng, Yanrong; Chen, Haonan; Zhou, Xiaojun; Yin, Siyuan; Qian, Qun; Xie, Xiaoyu; Chen, Quanjiao; Zhang, Jinfang; Fan, Lifang; Ren, Xianghai; Chen, Baoxiang; Jiang, Congqing
abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has achieved remarkable clinical efficacy across multiple cancers but remains ineffective for most patients, and the mechanisms underlying resistance remain incompletely understood. Here, we perform in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 screens in female mice and identify DNA methyltransferase 3 A (DNMT3A) as a key driver of tumor immune evasion through both methyltransferase-dependent and -independent mechanisms. DNMT3A represses TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF1B expression, enabling tumor cells to evade TNFalpha-induced killing. Independently of its methyltransferase activity, DNMT3A interacts with NFYA to activate cholesterol biosynthesis, leading to zymosterol accumulation in tumor interstitial fluid. Zymosterol impairs SREBP2 cleavage and promotes HMGCR degradation in CD8(+) T cells, thereby suppressing cholesterol biosynthesis and compromising their antitumor effector functions. Targeting DNMT3A with antisense oligonucleotides overcomes resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, these findings establish DNMT3A as an integrated epigenetic and metabolic checkpoint in tumor immune evasion and a potential target for immunotherapy.

title: Author Correction: UNCOVERseq enables sensitive and controlled gene editing off-target nomination across CRISPR-Cas modalities and systems.
authors: Kinney, Kyle J; Jia, Kun; Zhang, He; Schmaljohn, Ellen; Osborne, Thomas; Thommandru, Bernice; Murugan, Karthik; Sanchez-Pena, Andrea; West, Sean; Chen, Shengyao; Codipilly, Roshani; Sturgeon, Morgan; Turk, Rolf; McNeill, Matthew S; Behlke, Mark; Jacobi, Ashley; Cromer, M Kyle; Rettig, Garrett; Kurgan, Gavin L

title: Examination of the expression of G-protein-coupled receptor (GPR) 37 across whole-body organs using GPR37-deficient mice by Western blotting.
authors: Kitamura, Kai; Nakajima, Ryusuke; Miyawaki, Shingo; Saito, Shouichiro
journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
abstract: G-protein-coupled receptor (GPR) 37 is a G-protein-coupled receptor implicated in diverse physiological and pathological processes, including myelination and Parkinson's disease. Although its expression has been reported in the central nervous system (CNS), testis, and immune cells, the distribution of GPR37 at the protein level in peripheral tissues has remained unclear, partly because it is technically difficult to detect GPR37 specifically, which shares highly similar domains with other G protein-coupled receptors. In this study, to survey the protein expression of GPR37 in the major organs, we generated GPR37‑deficient mice by deleting the exon 1 start‑codon region using CRISPR/Cas9, and the protein expression of GPR37 in the major organs was compared between wild-type and GPR37‑deficient mice by western blotting. We confirmed GPR37 expression in the CNS and testis and newly demonstrated its protein‑level expression in the eye and inner ear, the latter representing a previously unreported organ in mammals. Across tissues, the 40 kDa short form of GPR37 was the predominant variant, whereas the 75 kDa form was restricted to the eye, revealing tissue‑specific differences in molecular forms. These findings provide reliable evidence for the tissue distribution of GPR37 and establish a robust framework for validating GPCR expression in vivo, offering new insights into its potential roles in neural, reproductive, and sensory systems.

title: Development of CRISPR/Cas13-based analytical tools to study RNA-protein interactions.
authors: Yamamoto, Keita; Shikata, Shiori; Hao, Yangying; Tomita, Takuya; Kanai, Rina; Verhoeyen, Els; Saeki, Yasushi; Goyama, Susumu
abstract: RNA-protein interactions (RPIs) are as important as protein-protein interactions (PPIs) for the formation of membraneless organelles (MLOs) and play vital roles in diverse biological processes. Despite remarkable advances in PPI analysis technologies, the development of tools for RPI analysis has lagged behind. To address this challenge, we integrated three established PPI technologies-bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), NanoBiT, and split-TurboID-with RNA-targeting CRISPR/dCas13. We applied these platforms to paraspeckles, a representative MLO formed through interactions between the long non-coding RNA NEAT1 and the RNA-binding protein NONO. BiFC-dCas13 functions as a fluorescence-based recorder that enables quantitative detection of NEAT1-NONO interaction events. NanoBiT-dCas13 precisely monitors dynamic changes in the NEAT1-NONO interaction through a reversible luminescence readout. Split-TurboID-dCas13 induces proximity-dependent biotinylation of proteins surrounding paraspeckles, identifying the N6-methyladenosine reader YTHDC1 as a paraspeckle-associated protein. Furthermore, BiFC-dCas13 was readily reconfigured to detect additional RPI pairs, demonstrating the modularity of the platform. Together, these complementary systems provide versatile approaches for recording, monitoring, and discovering RPI-associated biology and molecular environments.

title: Global Malat1 deletion in two genetic mouse models reveals sex-dependent effects on select ethanol-related behaviors.
authors: Gil, Daniela V; Baratta, Annalisa M; Ferguson, Carolyn; Miskanic, Martha; Iker, Andrew; Homanics, Gregg E; Farris, Sean P
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a widespread psychiatric condition, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its development remain poorly understood. While prior studies have largely focused on protein-coding genes, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) remain underexplored in AUD. Malat1, a highly abundant and evolutionarily conserved lncRNA, is elevated in post-mortem brain tissue of human AUD subjects and rodents chronically exposed to ethanol; however, its causal contribution to AUD-relevant behaviors remains unknown. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we generated two complementary global Malat1 knockout mouse models to assess its role in ethanol intake and related phenotypes. Constitutive knockout selectively attenuated acute functional tolerance rate and every-other-day two-bottle-choice (EOD-2BC) ethanol intake in females. These results were supported by an inducible adult conditional global knockout model, which reduced EOD-2BC ethanol consumption in females without altering taste preference. Together, our findings provide the first causal evidence that Malat1 regulates select ethanol-related behaviors in a sex-specific manner, supporting further investigation into its underlying mechanisms in AUD.

title: A nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat gene OsCNL1 contributes to strain-specific resistance to bacterial blight in rice.
authors: Zhao, Pu; Wang, Dengji; Li, Jianmin; Chen, Tianyi; Lu, Jialing; Zhou, Yongli
abstract: Bacterial blight (BB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), remains a major threat to rice production, and continued discovery and functional validation of resistance genes remain important for durable disease management. Here, we functionally characterized OsCNL1 (LOC_Os11g37759), a rice coiled-coil (CC)-type nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) gene associated with BB resistance in the resistant line B5N494. OsCNL1 encodes a 968-amino-acid CC type NLR protein and showed pathogen-responsive expression after PXO99A inoculation. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of OsCNL1 in B5N494 reduced resistance, whereas introduction of a genomic OsCNL1 fragment into susceptible backgrounds and overexpression of the full-length coding sequence enhanced resistance to PXO99A. These reciprocal loss- and gain-of-function assays indicate that OsCNL1 is a genetic component that positively regulates BB resistance against specific Xoo strains. Resistance-spectrum assays further showed that the effect associated with OsCNL1 is strain specific and strongly influenced by host genetic background. No major agronomic penalty was observed in the transgenic materials when compared to wild type under the field conditions. Furthermore, heterologous and in planta assays pointed to a potential physical association between the CC-containing region of OsCNL1 and the non-transcription activator-like effector (non-TALE) XopAE, providing a preliminary framework for future mechanistic studies. Overall, our results suggest that the functionally validated CNL-type NLR OsCNL1 participates in strain-specific BB resistance and has potential in resistance pyramiding strategies for rice BB management.

title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT.
authors: Rajan, Arvind Arul Nambi; Piacentino, Michael L; Bronner, Marianne E; Hutchins, Erica J
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin, which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3' untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

title: Enhancer Hijacking in Hematological Malignancies.
authors: Mulet-Lazaro, Roger; Delwel, Ruud
abstract: Cell identity is established by tightly regulated transcriptional programs. Disruption of the regulatory mechanisms governing these programs leads to aberrant behavior and, frequently, cancer. Enhancer hijacking, the process whereby a gene comes under the control of an ectopic enhancer, is a major cause of transcriptional dysregulation. Although recognized since the 1980s, its detection has been traditionally hindered by the low resolution of karyotyping and incomplete knowledge of enhancer biology. This has changed with the development of high-throughput sequencing, leading to a surge in newly identified enhancer hijacking events over the past two decades. Furthermore, functional dissection of enhancers using techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9 has shed light on their mechanistic underpinnings, with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) emerging as a paradigm for this phenomenon. In this review, we outline the historical development of enhancer hijacking, highlight representative examples in hematological malignancies, and discuss the insights derived from this research, particularly in AML.

title: The AF-2 domain of estrogen-related receptor interacts with PPRC1 to modulate larval epidermal marking in Bombyx mori.
authors: Wu, Jinxin; Liu, Die; Xu, Haoran; Zeng, Lingqing; Lin, Ping; Zhao, Ping; Shen, Guanwang
abstract: Estrogen-related receptors (ERRs) have no natural ligands, vertebrate ERRs rely on their activation function-2 (AF-2) structural domain to recruit coactivators for transcriptional regulation. While metabolic regulation in insects differs significantly from that in vertebrates, it remains unclear whether the regulatory function of insect ERR requires coactivators. Using silkworms as the research subject, this study aims to analyze the molecular mechanisms of ERR-regulated metabolism in insects and refine the metabolic regulatory network. This study applied CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology to knock out the AF-2 domain of BmERR in the lepidopteran silkworms and examined its effects on functional role, associated interacting factors, and related physiological processes. Disruption of the BmERR AF-2 domain inhibited the expression of melanin metabolism-related genes BmTH, BmDDC, BmAA-NAT, Bmebony, and Bmtan, leading to the accumulation of tyrosine and dopa, thereby causing aberrant melanin metabolism and loss of epidermal markings. By contrast, BmERR overexpression enhanced the pathway, resulting in intensification of epidermal markings. The homologous gene of the ERR coactivator, BmPPRC1, showed highly consistent expression with BmERR in the epidermis. The immunofluorescence signal of BmPPRC1 was localized to the nucleus and highly overlapped with that of BmERR. BmPPRC1 interacts with the AF-2 domain of BmERR, and deletion of this region weakens the regulation of melanin metabolism-related genes in silkworm embryonic cells. The ERR function and mode of action are evolutionarily conserved, and its AF-2 structural domain binds equally well to the coactivator BmPPRC1, providing new perspectives for studying the modulability of insect mottle formation.

title: Aberrant recursive splicing in a human disease locus.
authors: Boone, Philip M; Harripaul, Ricardo; Yadav, Rachita; Grzybowski, Michael; Hanafy, Mahmoud K; Lee, Amanda C; Choi, Esther Y; Collins, Ryan L; Polesskaya, Oksana; Makhortova, Nina; Larson, Matthew O; Kayir, Hakan; Wang, Yizhi; Avila, Rodolfo A; Frie, Jude A; Eed, Amr; Albeely, Abdalla M; Vemuri, Sunitha; Ayoub, Samantha M; Lemanski, John M; Ben-Isvy, Daniel; Zhao, Xuefang; Sanchis-Juan, Alba; Handley, Maris; Erdin, Serkan; de Esch, Celine; Mohajeri, Kiana; Chen, Clementine; Tovar, Paulina Gonzalez; Salani, Monica; Moyses-Oliveira, Mariana; Tai, Derek J C; Currall, Benjamin; McGraw, Christopher; Slaugenhaupt, Susan; Doan, Ryan; Gao, Dadi; Gusella, James F; Sanchez-Roige, Sandra; Young, Jared W; Khokhar, Jibran Y; Geurts, Aron M; Palmer, Abraham A; Talkowski, Michael E
abstract: Recursive splice sites are rare motifs postulated to facilitate splicing across massive introns and shape isoform diversity. The necessity of recursive splicing (RS) and its role in human disease are unsubstantiated. Here, we use CRISPR to model intronic deletions eliminating an RS site (RS1) in CADM2 and conferring risk for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and other neurobehavioral traits. Ablating RS1 in human induced neurons alters the gradient of RNA abundance across CADM2's first intron, decreases CADM2 expression, and impacts transcript usage. Decreased CADM2 expression is reflected in reduced exon usage downstream of RS1 and global alteration to genes involved in neuronal processes. In vivo rodent models harboring Cadm2 RS1 deletions exhibit an attenuated effect on Cadm2 expression and modest changes in behavior and functional brain connectivity. This study demonstrates RS as a noncoding regulatory mechanism in a gene associated with a spectrum of neuropsychiatric and behavioral traits.

title: mTREX2 co-expression promotes large deletions in CRISPR/Cas12a editing of the highly polyploid sugarcane genome.
authors: Ali, Qasim; Trujillo, Carolina; Altpeter, Fredy
abstract: The LbCas12a(i)-mTREX2 system enhances large deletions, and the LbCas12a(i)-RRV enables efficient editing of lw1 in sugarcane. Sugarcane (Saccharum spp. hybrids) is a major feedstock for biofuel production and the primary source of global table sugar; however, its highly polyploid and complex genome constrains the effective deployment of functional genomics and precision breeding strategies. While CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing has been reported in sugarcane, Cas12a-based editing remains unexplored despite its advantages in targeting AT-rich genomic regions. In this study, we report efficient CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated targeted mutagenesis of the lw1 gene in sugarcane. The lemon white1 (lw1) is a key regulator of chlorophyll and carotenoid biosynthesis, and targeted lw1 mutagenesis results in a visible phenotype. We compared the editing performance of intron-containing LbCas12a-R (LbCas12a(i)-R) and LbCas12a-RRV (LbCas12a(i)-RRV) variants and assessed the impact of Mus musculus Three prime repair exonuclease 2 (mTREX2) co-expression on editing efficiency and deletion profiles. Editing efficiencies ranged from 31 to 85%, where LbCas12a(i)-RRV consistently outperformed LbCas12a(i)-R in both overall editing efficiency and allelic editing efficiency. Co-expression of the mTREX2 shifted the mutation spectrum toward larger deletions, increasing the frequency of moderate-to-large deletions. The >/= 51 bp deletion class increased ~7-fold in both variants. Capillary electrophoresis-based genotyping provided a cost-effective, high-throughput alternative to next-generation sequencing (NGS) and accurately predicted allelic editing efficiency and indel size. This first report of CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated genome editing in sugarcane provides a framework for future engineering of AT-rich cis-regulatory elements in the polyploid sugarcane genome.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-based nanodelivery systems for precision gene editing in neuroinflammation.
authors: Sahu, Sanjana; Jain, Parag; Dharme, Karan Kumar; Yadav, Krishna
journal: Inflammation research : official journal of the European Histamine Research Society ... [et al.]
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neuroinflammation is a characteristic feature of many neurological diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Uncontrolled activation of microglia and astrocytes results in the production of proinflammatory mediators that contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. PURPOSE: CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technology provides highly precise targeting of genes involved in these pathways, enabling the deletion, correction, or modulation of disease-associated genetic alterations. Nonetheless, effective delivery of CRISPR components to the central nervous system (CNS) remains a major challenge because of protective barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), as well as concerns regarding genomic instability and immunogenicity. METHODS: Nanotechnology-guided delivery platforms, such as lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, dendrimers and polymeric carriers, have been developed as promising strategies to address these challenges. These nanosystems can improve biodistribution, pharmacokinetic behavior, and cellular uptake, while potentially reducing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. RESULTS: The preclinical studies demonstrate successful modulation of key neuroinflammatory targets, including the NLRP3 inflammasome, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, and the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, with potential therapeutic relevance to neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, novel techniques, such as mitochondrial base editing, prime editing, and epigenetic modulation, expand the scope of CRISPR-mediated therapeutic strategies. Although outcomes from animal models are promising, translation to the clinical setting requires careful consideration of safety, ethical concerns, and long-term efficacy. CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights the potential of integrating CRISPR/Cas9 with nanodelivery systems to advance precision medicine for neuroinflammatory disorders, while emphasizing their potential for therapeutic applications in complex CNS conditions. Ongoing studies aimed at optimizing delivery and reducing off-target effects will be essential for advancing these approaches toward clinical practice.

title: High-efficiency secretion expression of FAD-dependent glucose dehydrogenase in Pichia pastoris via signal peptide optimization and redox cofactor enhancement.
authors: Wei, Chun; Zhang, Zhenao; Xu, Jiahao; Zheng, Jianyong; He, Tianhao; Wang, Yuqi; Liu, Dongchen; Chen, Xueting
abstract: FAD-dependent glucose dehydrogenase (FAD-GDH) is a promising glucose sensing enzymes owing to its excellent thermostability and substrate specificity. To produce recombinant FAD-GDH with higher enzymatic activity by Pichia pastoris to meet commercial demands, three complementary strategies were proposed. First, the OST signal peptide, which outperformed ADV and MSB, replaced alpha-MF to yield much more efficient secretion, enhancing enzyme activity and protein yield up to 201.4% and 214.0% compared to the levels obtained with the original secretion signal, respectively, in shake-flask cultures. Second, to address the low specific activity of FAD-GDH, mixed feeding with riboflavin, adenosine, and yeast extract during induction period of fermentation had improved enzyme activity and specific activity to196.6% and 161.4%, respectively, while maintaining cell viability, compared with the control without additional feeding. Third, to further enhance specific activity of FAD-GDH, endogenous FAD synthase was ectopically overexpressed under the control of either the GAP or AOX1 promoter via CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genomic integration. The strain with AOX1-drivenFAD synthase (WCG-AOX1-FAD1) exhibited the most significant improvements, with enzyme activity of 1023.46 +/- 95.85 U/mL (239.4% of WCG-OST) and specific activity of 886.31 +/- 25.42 U/mg (233.4% of WCG-OST), both representing relatively high levels among similar studies. The synergistic application of these three strategies provides a reference for the industrial production of various cofactor-dependent enzymes.

title: Experimental Methods for CRISPR Enzyme Assays with Fluorescence Readout.
authors: Jiang, Qi; Avaro, Alexandre S; Bae, Hyunjun; Sorensen, Angelina; Santiago, Juan G
abstract: Fluorescence-based CRISPR diagnostic assays have become a popular platform for nucleic acid detection due to their programmability, configurability, specificity, and compatibility with standard laboratory equipment. However, reported enzymatic kinetic rates and limits of detection for CRISPR trans-cleavage assays vary by several orders of magnitude across the literature. This variation in performance parameters is coupled with, and exacerbated by, inconsistent calibration, incomplete correction of measurement biases, and nonstandardized or incomplete data analysis procedures. We present an experimental protocol and quantitative analysis framework for fluorescence-based enzyme assays using routine laboratory instrumentation, including thermocyclers and fluorescence microplate readers. Building on previous studies of CRISPR enzyme kinetics and fluorescence calibration, we describe procedures for flat-field and background correction; comprehensive fluorescence calibration, including correction for the inner filter effect; quantification and implications of reporter degradation; extraction of Michaelis-Menten kinetic parameters; and determination of assay's limits of detection. We provide step-by-step experimental guidelines and open-source Python implementations for each stage of the workflow. Using representative Cas12 trans-cleavage datasets, we demonstrate that explicit fluorescence calibration and correction procedures substantially reduce systematic bias in measured kinetic rates and improve consistency between experiments. Our framework aims to establish standardized practices for quantitative fluorescence-based CRISPR assays and provides researchers with practical tools for reproducible kinetic characterization and rational assay design.

title: Synergistic Integration of Recombinase Polymerase Amplification and CRISPR-Cas12a Enables High-Sensitivity Detection of Mycoplasma bovis.
authors: Yaghoubi, Diba; V Pillai, Viju
abstract: Mycoplasma bovis is a major pathogen of cattle, causing substantial economic losses in the global cattle industry and emerging as a serious threat to North American bison (Bison bison). Effective outbreak management is hindered by the lack of rapid diagnostic methodologies deployable in field settings. Current testing approaches are limited by slow turnaround times for microbial culture and the dependence of qPCR on centralized laboratory infrastructure, both of which are poorly suited for field settings. To address this gap, we developed a highly sensitive, isothermal diagnostic platform coupling Recombinase Polymerase Amplification with CRISPR-Cas12a detection targeting the conserved uvrC gene. The optimized assay requires less than 1 h at 37 degrees -39 degrees C and achieves an analytical limit of detection of approximately 8 copies, comparable to that of the gold-standard quantitative PCR. Clinical validation using 110 samples from bison and cattle demonstrated 100% concordance with PCR and complete differentiation from closely related species, including Mycoplasma canis and Mycoplasma felis. Overall, these data establish the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay as a sensitive and specific isothermal approach for detecting M. bovis in clinical specimens, providing a field-adaptable framework for future instrument-free surveillance in resource-limited agricultural settings and supporting improved herd health management in both commercial cattle and bison conservation operations.

title: Structural basis for ITP-selective hydrolysis by a CRISPR-associated Nudix hydrolase.
authors: Wu, Wanqian; Xia, Shenglan; Li, Duo; Lin, Junchao; Cao, Chen; Kong, Jianping; Lu, Meiling; Xiao, Yibei; Li, Zhaoxing
abstract: The nucleoside diphosphates linked to moiety-X (Nudix) hydrolases are a superfamily of proteins defined by the characteristic Nudix box sequence, most of which are involved in clearing the cell of potentially deleterious metabolites and in preventing the accumulation of metabolic intermediates. The Nudix hydrolase associated with CRISPR-Cas-associated adenosine deaminases (CAAD) from Limisphaera ngatamarikiensis (LngNH) mitigates CAAD-induced toxicity by hydrolyzing ITP to IMP and pyrophosphate. Here, we determined crystal structures of LngNH in the apo form and in complex with ITP using catalytic mutants and validated key interactions by site-directed mutagenesis. The hypoxanthine of ITP is deeply buried in a hydrophobic pocket and engages a distinct hydrogen-bond network, whereas the triphosphate tail is coordinated by conserved residues and divalent metal ions. Together, these findings provide a structural framework for CAAD-linked nucleotide sanitization and suggest that CRISPR-associated Nudix hydrolases function as local self-protection modules that limit toxicity from noncanonical inosine nucleotides.IMPORTANCENucleotide quality-control enzymes protect cells from harmful metabolic by-products. Here, we characterize a CRISPR-associated nucleoside diphosphates linked to moiety-X (Nudix) hydrolase that removes ITP, a toxic noncanonical nucleotide generated during antiviral defense. Biochemical and structural analyses show how this enzyme specifically recognizes and hydrolyzes ITP while avoiding related cellular nucleotides. Our findings suggest that CRISPR-associated nucleotide deaminase systems require "self-protection" mechanisms to prevent damage from their own antiviral activities. These results expand our understanding of how bacteria maintain nucleotide homeostasis during immune responses and reveal an additional regulatory layer within CRISPR-associated defense systems. The structural framework reported here also provides a foundation for future studies of nucleotide sanitization enzymes in microbial physiology and antiviral immunity.

title: BdPiwi is essential for gametogenesis and post-embryonic development in the oriental fruit fly, Bactrocera dorsalis.
authors: Fu, Junhong; Wang, Jinsheng; Ling, Shishi; Pan, Yile; Jia, Lanqi; Sheng, Yehui; Andongma, Awawing A; Zhan, Shuai; Xu, Li; Wang, Yaohui
abstract: BACKGROUND: The PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathway is a conserved transposon silencing mechanism essential for genomic integrity and gametogenesis. While Piwi proteins are known to play essential roles in insect germline development, their functional characteristics remain largely unexplored in agricultural pests. Here, we investigated BdPiwi in Bactrocera dorsalis, a highly invasive pest whose exceptional reproductive capacity underpins its global pest status. RESULTS: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that BdPiwi is evolutionarily conserved among insects and contains the canonical PAZ and PIWI domains. Spatiotemporal profiling showed ubiquitous expression across developmental stages, with predominant enrichment in adult ovaries. Based on CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis, we found that BdPiwi loss caused severe gonadal arrest and complete sterility in both sexes-females lacked detectable oocytes and males produced no mature sperm. Transcriptomic analysis uncovered widespread transcriptional upregulation, extensive transposon derepression, and dysregulated immunometabolic genes likely contributing to oogenic failure. Additionally, mutants exhibited prolonged larval duration and abnormal eclosion. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that BdPiwi is a pleiotropic regulator governing gonadogenesis, fertility, and metamorphic transition in B. dorsalis. This study expands the functional repertoire of Piwi genes in insect pests and provides a promising molecular target for genetic-based management of this devastating invasive species. title: Targeting CLK1 by CRISPR tools and pharmacological inhibition modulates the innate immune response and dengue virus replication.
authors: Pozzi, Berta; Lucero, Agustina Magali; Buggiano, Valeria; Pelaez, Miguel Angel; Garcia, Cybele; Srebrow, Anabella
abstract: Alternative splicing is a key regulatory mechanism known to be altered upon viral infection. These alterations can arise both from direct viral interference with the splicing machinery and from cellular responses such as activation of innate immunity. Here, we investigated splicing changes shared between dengue virus (DENV) infection and interferon (IFN) treatment in cultured cells, the latter serving as a model for virus-independent innate immune activation. Among the common events, we identified an increased production of non-coding mRNA isoforms from the CLK1 gene, which gives rise to a kinase that phosphorylates splicing factors including SR proteins and spliceosomal components. Consistent with this finding, IFN treatment led to a reduction in CLK1 protein levels. Using stable cell lines with CRISPR/dCas9-mediated modulation of CLK1 expression, we found that silencing CLK1 enhanced the induction of immune response genes, while its over-expression attenuated it. Inhibition of CLK1 kinase activity with the pharmacological inhibitor TG003 further potentiated IFN-induced gene expression and reduced DENV replication. Altogether, these results identify CLK1 as a proviral negative regulator of IFN-stimulated gene expression and suggest that its inhibition could enhance antiviral defenses and become a target for therapeutic strategies.

title: Keap1 Deficiency Promotes Macrophage M2 Polarization and Protects beta Cells.
authors: Huang, Baoliang; Mou, Lunpan; Huang, Xiaoyan; Su, Siyu; Hong, Zhenzhen; Zhang, Yi
abstract: BACKGROUND: Progressive pancreatic beta-cell injury is a core feature of Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Imbalance between macrophage M1 and M2 polarization, driven by chronic inflammation, is a key contributor to this injury. The Keap1-Nrf2-ARE pathway regulates macrophage polarization and inflammatory responses, but whether it affects pancreatic beta-cell survival through macrophages is unknown. METHODS: We generated a Keap1-knockout THP-1 line using CRISPR-Cas9, differentiated the cells into M0 macrophages with PMA, polarized them toward M2 with IL-4/IL-13, and cocultured them with MIN6 cells injured by LPS. RESULTS: Keap1 knockout increased M2 polarization efficiency and reduced the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio of NF-kappaB p65, with lower IL-1beta and TNF-alpha mRNA expression. After coculture with LPS-injured MIN6 cells, the Keap1-KO-M2 group showed higher MIN6 viability and less apoptosis. The antiapoptotic protein Bcl-2 rose, whereas the proapoptotic factors Bax and cleaved-caspase3 declined; MDA content fell, whereas HO-1 and SOD levels climbed. CONCLUSION: These findings indicate that Keap1 deficiency attenuates LPS-induced pancreatic beta-cell injury by increasing macrophage M2 polarization efficiency and expanding the M2 population.

title: Genome-wide mapping of Cas9-induced sister chromatid exchange across single and over 200 genomic sites in human cells.
authors: Chovanec, Peter; He, Shiyang; Yin, Yi
abstract: CRISPR/Cas9-induced DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are widely used for genome engineering, yet their capacity to provoke sister chromatid exchange (SCE) remains incompletely understood because exchanges between identical sisters leave no sequence change and are invisible to conventional sequencing. Using sci-L3-Strand-seq, a scalable single-cell template-strand sequencing platform, we mapped SCE following targeted Cas9 cleavage. Cas9 targeting of a unique genomic locus strongly enriched SCE at the break site, reaching 41% in the same cell cycle and 17% in the subsequent division, indicating frequent non-local inter-sister repair. Targeting 237 repetitive Alu sites produced mild enrichment of on-target SCE, whereas cells with elevated SCE burden showed significant enrichment at programmed cut sites, suggesting context-dependent recombination at repetitive loci. Reciprocal daughter-cell pair analysis revealed large-scale structural alterations on chromosomes with induced SCEs and at SCE junctions, indicating that Cas9-induced SCE does not universally reflect error-free homologous recombination. Disruption of LIG3, LIG4, XRCC1, and XRCC4 at Cas9 cut sites did not measurably alter SCE frequency, consistent with delayed functional loss following editing. Together, these findings identify Cas9-induced DSBs as potent local triggers of SCE and reveal structural outcomes invisible to conventional sequencing.

title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design.
authors: Ustuner, Enes; Oz, Mustafa
abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

title: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-Based Genome Editing in Inherited Cardiovascular Diseases: Therapeutic Advances, Emerging Editing Platforms, and Translational Challenges.
authors: Fakiyesi, Tosin; Ozioko, Mmaduabuchi; Ogunseye, Oluwapelumi D; Adeyemi, Olaoluwa; Adedoyin, Ibukunoluwa; Badejo, Adeolu A; Anifalaje, Olorungbami; Adegbesan, Abiodun; Olalude, Oluwakemi; Tiamiyu, Rachael; Hassan, Almustapha
abstract: Inherited cardiovascular diseases (ICVDs) are a broad category of hereditary disorders resulting from pathogenic mutations that alter cardiac anatomy, electrical conduction, and metabolic pathways. The main types include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), cardiac channelopathies, and familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) and are associated with heart failure, malignant arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death, particularly in young people. Current treatments, such as pharmacological therapies, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, and heart transplantation, have significantly improved outcomes; however, these treatments are mainly targeted toward symptom control and the prevention of complications without correcting the underlying genetic defects. Recent advancements in genome editing have transformed precision cardiovascular care, with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based technologies emerging as potential methods for targeting and modifying disease-causing variants. Emerging platforms, such as base editing, prime editing, and epigenome editing, have widened the therapeutic potential of genome engineering by enhancing editing precision and reducing some of the constraints of the traditional CRISPR-Cas9 strategy. In the setting of inherited cardiovascular disorders, promising early results have been obtained in preclinical studies using human induced pluripotent stem cell and animal models, including correction of MYBPC3 and MYH7 mutations in HCM; targeting of TTN-, RBM20-, and LMNA-associated mechanisms in DCM; restoration of ion channel function in inherited arrhythmia syndromes; and modulation of lipid-related genes such as PCSK9, LDLR, and ANGPTL3 in FH. However, major challenges remain, including off-target effects, effective delivery to cardiac tissues, immunological responses, interpretation of genetic variants, and ethical concerns. This review provides a translational, integrated view of the evolution of CRISPR-based genome editing technologies, their application to ICVDs, current preclinical and clinical advances, and the challenges that need to be addressed to achieve safe and effective translation into cardiovascular therapeutics.

title: Comparative Evaluation and Optimization of a CRISPR/Cas-Based Assay for Rapid Detection of Tilapinevirus tilapiae (TiLV) in Indian Isolates, Validated Against Conventional Nucleic acid Detection Methods.
authors: Thangadurai, Kaliyamoorthy; Bedekar, Megha Kadam; Manojkumar, Chandraprakasham; Namdeo, Meshram Supradhnya; Limbola, Maharshi; Jeena, Kezhedath; Rasal, Kiran Dashrath; Rajendran, Kooloth Valappil; Kumar, Kundan
abstract: Tilapia lake virus (Tilapinevirus tilapiae; TiLV) remains a significant threat to global tilapia aquaculture, underscoring the urgent need for rapid, sensitive, and field-ready diagnostic approaches. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-Cas12a assisted reverse transcriptase-recombinase polymerase amplification assay (Cr-TiLV) targeting a conserved region of segment 6 of the TiLV genome. The integration of RT-RPA with Cas12a significantly enhanced analytical sensitivity, enabling the detection of viral RNA at levels as low as 10 copies. Diagnostic assessment using 40 clinical samples demonstrated that the Cr-TiLV assay achieved sensitivities of 86.67% and 82.29%, and accuracies of 90% and 85%, respectively, relative to semi-nested PCR and RT-qPCR, with specificity approaching 99.9% for both benchmark methods. Although less sensitive than RT-qPCR for samples with low viral loads, the assay consistently detected low to moderate viral concentrations and showed substantial concordance with semi-nested PCR. Operating isothermally at 39  degrees C and requiring minimal laboratory resources, the Cr-TiLV assay offers a rapid and field-deployable diagnostic solution with strong potential for routine TiLV surveillance in resource-limited aquaculture settings. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12088-026-01550-y.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic Analysis Identifies ENO3 as a Candidate Lactate Metabolism-Associated Biomarker in Colorectal Cancer Metastasis.
authors: Qian, Jiahao; Wang, Miaomiao; Liu, Jiaqi; Gao, Meiling
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Metastasis is the primary cause of mortality in colorectal cancer (CRC), a leading global malignancy. Although metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, the stage-associated transcriptional features of metabolic pathways during CRC progression remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize transcriptionally inferred metabolic heterogeneity during CRC progression and identify candidate molecular factors associated with metastasis. METHODS: We performed an integrated transcriptomic analysis using TCGA and GEO datasets and compared metabolic pathway signatures across normal tissues, primary tumors, and metastatic lesions. An exploratory tumor lactate metabolism score (TLMS) was developed using Cox regression and LASSO analysis. Consensus clustering identified metabolic subtypes, and their associations with computationally estimated immune-cell signatures were assessed. The functional consequences of ENO3 loss were preliminarily evaluated using CRISPR/Cas9 knockout, cell proliferation assays, and an NSG tail-vein experimental lung colonization model. RESULTS: We observed a stage-associated reversal-like transcriptional pattern: primary tumors showed broad suppression of metabolic pathway signatures relative to normal tissues, whereas metastatic lesions showed reactivation of several signatures, including the pentose phosphate pathway. A six-gene lactate metabolism-related signature stratified patients into prognostic groups within the TCGA cohort. The high-risk group showed higher ssGSEA-inferred neutrophil abundance and enrichment of a neutrophil extracellular trap (NET)-associated transcriptional signature. ENO3 expression was associated with poor outcome, while ENO3 knockout reduced MC38 cell proliferation and experimental lung colonization in NSG mice. CONCLUSIONS: CRC progression is accompanied by stage-associated changes in transcriptomically inferred metabolic programs. TLMS and ENO3 represent exploratory candidate biomarkers that require independent clinical validation and further mechanistic investigation, particularly with respect to lactate metabolism and the tumor immune microenvironment.

title: Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy Aptasensors for Nucleic-Acid Detection: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
authors: Alam, Md Saiful; Hassan, Kazi Mohammed Mehedi; Tarafdar, Monika; Hossain, Mohammad Imran; Parvez, Mohammad Anwar; Rahaman, Mostafizur; Hasnat, Mohammad A
abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.

title: Placental TRPV2 supports trophoblast function and normal fetal development.
authors: De Clercq, Katrien; Perez-Garcia, Vicente; Panda, Amitesh; Gevaert, Seppe; Witvrouwen, Jill; Van Mechelen, Pilar; Lopez-Tello, Jorge; Maksym, Katarzyna; David, Anna L; Van Den Broeck, Evy; Luyten, Katrien; Segal, Andrei; Poovathingal, Suresh; Wojno, Marta; Katanosaka, Yuki; Vennekens, Rudi; Pasque, Vincent; Sferruzzi-Perri, Amanda N; Voets, Thomas; Vriens, Joris
abstract: While placental functioning arbitrates fetal outcome, the molecular players that underpin normal placental development remain poorly understood. Here, we provide evidence that the Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 2 (TRPV2) channel plays an important role in normal placental development, determining fetal size and survival. Its absence severely affects placental morphology, causing fetal growth restriction and embryonic lethality, which was found to be allocated to a non-redundant role in the trophoblast, but not in the embryo. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Trpv2 deletion in mouse trophoblast stem cells demonstrated that Trpv2 contributes to the differentiation towards Syncytiotrophoblast layer II (SynTII) cells, which was confirmed by the growth restriction phenotype in SynTII-specific Trpv2 knockout animals. Finally, TRPV2 was functionally expressed in human trophoblast cells and enriched in trophoblast populations undergoing syncytial differentiation. Together, our findings identify an important role for TRPV2 during placental development and consequently fetal outcomes.
